My daughter’s in Newcastle, and I’ve been thinking about moving there. But the timing just hasn't worked out. That’s understandable. I wonder how it will affect people like us, working in education and the public sector. Exactly. I’ve been having discussions with my colleagues at the school. Some of them are worried about funding and how the changes will impact our jobs. It’s all very uncertain. I can only imagine. I think we just have to keep going and make the best of what we have. I’m going to talk to my daughter about moving up there soon. Maybe it's time for a change.

So, I've got this idea for a mousetrap game we could make. It's not like the classic one with the stick and the cheese, more of a board game where you navigate through different challenges to catch the mouse. What do you think?      That sounds interesting. I mean, I've never been into board games, but I do like the idea of something creative. Though I'm not sure about the mechanics. How do you plan to structure it?      Honestly, I think it's a cool idea. Maybe you could use tokens or something. You know, like moving around a board with different spaces—like traps, shortcuts, and maybe even some surprises. It could be like a mix of strategy and luck.      Yeah, I’m in. You know, I once made a mousetrap out of a cardboard box and some string. It worked for a week—until the cat knocked it over. Maybe for the game, we could make it look like a real trap to add some fun.      Sounds like a great plan. I’ve always loved the idea of combining creativity with a bit of mischief. But let's not forget the story behind the mousetrap. You know, my grandfather used to tell me about how he used to build these elaborate ones in the 1950s. He claimed he once caught a mouse in a trap that took three days to set up.      Oh, I love that. My uncle used to tell stories like that too. He said once he made a mousetrap that had a little flag that went up when the mouse got caught. The neighbors thought he was crazy, but he was proud of his work. I think you could do something like that with the game.      You know, I’ve been thinking about working abroad. My sister mentioned that the UK isn’t the only place with opportunities. Maybe I should consider a job in America? I mean, it's a chance to see the country, and meet people from different backgrounds.      That’s a bold move. I mean, I've always wanted to go to the US. I took an exchange program there for a semester, and it was incredible. The culture is so different. But I also heard about the cost of living and the language barrier. Is it really worth it?      It’s definitely worth it if you're into the culture.

You’ve really outdone yourself this time. It was all for you. I thought it was time we did something a little different, just us.

So, what do you think of that rugby match last night, Oisin? I swear, the way they handled the ball was like a bunch of footballers on a playground.      Yeah, it was a bit of a mess, honestly. I mean, I love rugby, but that game was like watching a traffic jam with no one in charge. I didn’t even know who was playing for which team half the time.      You’d be surprised. I didn’t either when I was in school. My brother used to talk about it for hours. He said it was the most exciting thing in the world.      That’s the thing. It’s like a mix of football and wrestling, but with more rules. If you don’t know the rules, it’s harder to follow.      I remember when I was teaching, we had a few boys who were obsessed with rugby. One of them once tried to run with the ball through the hallway, and I nearly had a heart attack.      Sounds like my cousin. He was on a school team, and he thought he was the next Tony Blair. He ran with the ball like it was a bat.      That’s the thing about kids. If they love something, they’ll do anything for it. Like, someone once told me they’d rather get a black eye than miss a game.      That’s the spirit. Anyway, speaking of games, your birthday is coming up, right?      Yeah, it’s in two weeks. I was thinking maybe we could do something special.      That’d be nice. Maybe we could do something outdoors? I’ve been wanting to take the kids stargazing again. It’s been a while since we all got together.      I’d like that. The night sky here in Ballincollig is incredible. I remember when I was teaching, I used to take the kids out and talk about the constellations. It was a real bonding moment.      That’s a great idea. We could even make it a family thing. Maybe we can bring out the old cards and sign them for Oisin. He’s been wanting to have a birthday card collection for years.      Yeah! I have a few signed ones from my old team. I could bring them over.      Perfect. It’ll be a nice way to remember the day. And, Oisin, you’re going to bed early, right? The night sky is going to be worth it.

So, do you know what’s going to happen with the baby? I mean, it’s been a while since we last talked about it, and I’ve been so busy with work lately. Yeah, I know. I’ve been meaning to ask you—do you think we should start baby-proofing the new flat yet? I mean, we’re moving in a few weeks, so maybe we should get a head start. Definitely. It’s so much, you know? I can imagine. But at the same time, it’s amazing how much you learn when you have a baby. I mean, I’ve been learning Spanish for my job, and it’s not even close to the kind of learning you do with a baby. It’s like, you just absorb everything—it’s so natural. That’s true. I’ve been thinking about taking a language course too, but I’m not sure if I’m ready. It’s one thing to study languages for work, and another to actually use them in a real conversation. You know? I get that. I used to struggle with that too. But once you start speaking, it just comes naturally. It’s like, you don’t even think about it anymore. I mean, I’ve been working with different dialects from all over the UK, and it’s fascinating how different they sound. That must be amazing. I mean, I’ve heard how different accents can be, but I’ve never really thought about it in that way. I guess it’s part of the job, right? Absolutely. And it’s also part of my life as someone who grew up in Aylesbury. I’ve always been interested in how language shapes identity, and how it changes depending on where you come from. Yeah, I can see how that would be interesting. I grew up in Lincoln, so I’ve always felt that connection to the East Midlands, even though I’ve been living in Cambridge for years.

So, I've been thinking about dialects and accents lately. I was just in Chester and heard this really strong North West accent, and it was like,  wow , I could barely understand a word. It made me realize how much of a difference regional dialects can make.      Yeah, I totally get that. I teach English as a foreign language, so I’ve had to study a lot of different accents. But I still get confused sometimes. Like, I can tell the difference between a Londoner and a Bristolian, but the East Midlands? It’s like a whole new language.      Man, I’ve got a bit of a weird mix myself. My mum’s from Bedford and my dad’s from Cyprus, so I’ve got that English-Cypriot twang. Sometimes people just don’t get it. If I say “Beds” for “beds,” they think I’m British, but if I say “betta” for “better,” they think I’m from somewhere else.      That’s wild. I mean, I grew up in Bedfordshire, so I’d say I’ve got that sort of South-Eastern English accent. But I tend to drop the “r” at the end of words. Like, “car” becomes “cah.” Mate, I’ve been told I sound like a character from  Downton Abbey .      Or  Fawlty Towers ! I’ve been called that too. But honestly, I think it’s more about how you pronounce certain words. Like, I always say “ bath ” with a hard “th” sound. That’s not  actually  a thing, but people get confused. I think it’s just a language thing.      Yeah, and I’ve got this thing where I drop the “g” sound in some words. Like, “butter” becomes “butter.” It’s weird, but I think it’s just the way I was brought up. I mean, I’ve got a cousin who’s a teacher and he’s got a  proper  accent. It’s like trying to catch a cricket ball in the dark.      You know, I’ve been thinking about accents and how they can go hand in hand with your job. I’m an artworker, so I work in a creative field. But I’ve noticed that people sometimes assume I’m from a certain place just based on how I speak. Like, if I say “chips” instead of “crisps,” they think I’m from the North.      Oh, that’s so true. I’ve done that too.

I’ve even started meal prepping on Sundays. That’s a smart move. I should try that. It’s not just about saving money – it’s about making better choices in general.

So, I was just telling my granddaughter about the time her gran tried to fix the plumbing in the kitchen. She thought it was just a simple job, like putting together a toy!      I remember that! You were wearing your apron and everything, Gran. You spilled the water on the floor and then tried to mop it up with the same cloth. It looked like a river in the kitchen!      Oh, it was a disaster! I thought I was being helpful, but really, I just made things worse. I still remember the sound of the water dripping like a leaky tap, and then my husband came in and said, “That’s not a leak—you’ve got a flood in the kitchen!”      Yeah, and he had to call the plumber. I still don’t know how we managed to survive that day. But I suppose it taught me a lesson—some things are better left to professionals.      It did teach us all a lesson. We learned that if you want to fix something, you should ask the right person. And that, my dear, is why I’ve always been so careful with my GCSE Maths exams. I know my stuff!      Yeah, but you still got confused between the clock and the phone, didn’t you?      Oh, come on, that was a different time! I had to run up to the school to check the time, and when I came back, it was 10 minutes later. I thought the phone had gone out.      That’s not a phone, that’s a kettle! You know that, Gran.      Yeah, and the kettle didn’t even boil. It just bubbled for hours.      Oh, I tried to fix it. I thought it was just a faulty switch. I even put it on the stove!      And it exploded!      Yeah, go on, tell us how you got the fire brigade involved.      I did! I called them, and they came and took it away. I didn’t even know it was dangerous.      I think you still have a scar from that.      Oh, I’ve seen it. It’s right above your eyebrow.      Oh, I’ll have you know that was an accident, not a scar! I can’t believe we’re still talking about that old sailing story. I still get flashbacks every time I see a boat on the river. Oh come on, it was an unforgettable experience! I can't believe it's already April. You know, I was just thinking about how quickly time flies. We had such a lovely winter, didn't we? Oh, it was a bit of a rollercoaster, to be honest. I can't believe we've been on the road for six hours already. I’m starting to think we should’ve taken the train instead of driving all the way here. Oh, I just got an email from the university about the new language project. It’s going to be a big one, they want to expand their research on regional dialects in the UK. Yeah, and it’s not just about the words, it’s about the tone, the slang, and the rhythm.

I just checked the map again, and we’re only about a 40-minute drive from Tarnow. Should be easy enough, but I’m still a bit nervous about the roads. I’ve never been this far east in Poland. I just can’t believe how much money is being thrown at football clubs these days. You know, with all the sponsorship deals and the fancy kit designs. I just got a message from my cousin, and she’s mad at me because I didn’t answer her texts. I got so caught up in my own problems today, I completely forgot to respond. You know what’s worse? I just made a really lovely coffee, and I think it’s going to be the best cup of coffee we’ve had in ages. I’ve been experimenting with some new beans I got from that specialty shop in Lincoln. So, I think we need to make a decision on where to place the new hospice. I know we’ve got a few options, but I’d like to hear your thoughts. Oh, look at this! I still can’t believe it’s been ten years since we went to the Royal Ascot together. I just watched this new horror movie last night, and it gave me nightmares for days. You would not believe the twist at the end—like, totally unexpected. Oh no, you’re not going to tell me what it was, are you? I’ve got a feeling I already know what you’re talking about. You wouldn’t, would you? I thought I was being clever with the title. I can’t believe it’s already 10 o’clock. I’ve been trying to wind down, but my head’s still buzzing from the day. Did you ever get that email from the school about the new iPad for the classroom? So, I've been meaning to ask you — have you read that new book by that Scottish author, James Macdonald? The one about the Highlands and the old wars? I mean, we grew up here, and we’ve been friends since university—so it’s time we actually do something proper together.      Aye, that’s the thing. We’ve got this shared love of books and travel, and we’ve never really taken it beyond the café or the weekend trip. It’s time we made something real. Maybe we can even bring a few friends along.

Okay, I've just finished applying for that job in Manchester. I thought it would be a good move, you know, to get out of London and maybe find something more stable. I've been thinking a lot lately about how times have changed, haven't they? When I was younger, things were much simpler. But I suppose we’re not the only ones. Everyone’s got their own story. I just wish there was more support for people like us. It’s not fair, is it? Not at all. I think the government should do more. They talk about helping people, but they don’t really act on it. They just keep talking about it, and nothing changes. I agree. I’ve been trying to get some help from the local council, but it’s been a struggle.

So, I've been thinking about the new space we're converting in the East Wing. I know it's got to be flexible enough for different tenants, but I’m not sure how we’ll handle the storage issue. So, I've been thinking about the meal we're going to have tonight. I was going to make that stir-fry with the chicken and veggies I bought earlier, but I wonder if we’d all like that. I just got a new phone, so I'm sorting out my contacts. I was thinking, do you know if you got the new one yet? Or are you still using that old one from university? I just got a call from the hospital. My dad’s having another scan. It’s been a real rollercoaster, hasn’t it? I’m trying not to get too worked up, but it’s hard when you’re used to being the one who’s always in control. I’m so sorry to hear that. I can only imagine how tough it must be. My mum had a similar experience with her cancer. It was really hard on the whole family. I remember feeling so helpless, just wanting to do something to make it better. Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s like he’s still around, but in a way that’s sad and comforting at the same time. That’s a beautiful thought. My dad always said he wanted to be buried in the garden, but I never got around to talking about it. I feel guilty about that. I can understand that. I’ve been thinking about my own family too. My sister mentioned that she’s been trying to lose weight, but it’s hard when you’re dealing with all this. I’ve been helping her with some healthy meals, but I’m not sure if it’s working.

So, I've been thinking about our trip to the Alps next month. I’ve been doing some research on the best places to ski and where to find decent wine to pair with the meals. It’s a bit of a challenge, honestly. I mean, you don’t want to end up with cheap plonk when you're out of the country.      Well, I’d say a bit of plonk is fine, as long as it’s not too bad. I remember when I was in the Pyrenees, I got this cheap red that was, let’s say, not the best. It was like drinking paint.      Wow, that sounds terrible. I’ve never even tried wine before. I mean, I know it’s supposed to be good with food, but I don’t know how to pick it.      Me neither. I guess I just stick to beer. It’s easier, and I don’t have to worry about the taste.      You could try something like a Chardonnay or a Pinot Noir for the lighter stuff. And I’ve been looking into a few local vineyards near the slopes. They have some decent labels that are not too expensive.      That’s a good point. I actually got some local wine from Belgium once—it was amazing. I think it’s the terroir that makes the difference.      Terroir? What’s that?      It’s like the environment where the grapes are grown. The soil, the climate, the altitude… it all affects the flavor. I’ve been reading a lot about it, actually. It’s pretty fascinating.      So, like, if you grow grapes in the Alps, you get a different wine than if you do in the Mediterranean?      Exactly. And that’s why some places are better for certain types of wine. But I think it’s also about personal taste. I personally prefer something full-bodied.      I agree. I like a good Malbec or a Cabernet Sauvignon when I want something bold. But I’ve been trying to branch out a bit more.      That’s cool. I think I’ll just stick to beer, but maybe I’ll try a glass of wine at your place next time.      Yeah, I’m up for that. I mean, if it’s not too bad.      You’ll be fine. I’ll even bring my own bottle to make sure it’s good.      Great. I can’t wait to taste it.

I just found this old photo of us in Japan last summer. Do you remember that trip? It’s so hard to believe it’s been over a year already. Oh, I remember! That was such a wild adventure. So, I was just telling my mates about that time I tried to skinny dip in the River Lagan in Belfast. I thought it’d be cool, like some kind of rebellious thing. Exactly. I’ve also heard about some places that have even stricter rules. I read somewhere that some theme parks won’t let you bring any food at all, even if you’re just eating your own. It’s like they want you to buy everything from them. That’s crazy. I mean, I get that they want to control the revenue, but it’s just so unnecessary. I think it’d be better if they just had clear signage and allowed people to bring their own snacks as long as they’re not open containers. I agree. But then again, I’m a PhD student, and I know how complicated these policies can get. Some of the border security stuff I’ve read about is way more strict. I mean, they can’t even let people bring certain gadgets into the country without going through a full inspection. I know, right? It’s like security is everywhere these days. Even in a pub, you’d think we’d be safe from anything. But I guess with all the travel and tech these days, it’s just the way it is. Yeah, and I guess it’s better to be safe than sorry, even if it’s a bit frustrating.

I can't believe we've been meeting up here so often. It’s always nice to catch up, but I feel like I've missed out on so much recent news. I’ve been meaning to ask you about your family—how are things with your brother? I heard he’s been unwell again. Oh dear, I’m sorry to hear that. He’s been in and out of the hospital with a chest infection. It’s been really tough on the whole family, especially with the funeral of his father still fresh in everyone’s mind. You know, it's hard to process all of it at once. I can only imagine. I’m so sorry for your loss. I still can't quite believe my uncle passed away last year. It felt like everything was happening too fast. I was so caught up in my own life, and I think I turned my back on the family for a while. I know exactly what you mean. It's a strange thing, isn’t it? One day you're there, and the next, the whole dynamic changes. I still have so many memories of my father—especially the way he used to take us kayaking on the river. He had this old wooden canoe that he’d fix up every summer. That sounds like such a special thing. My father used to take me rowing on the river near our home in Dorchester. I remember the way the water felt beneath the oars, the silence of the morning, the sense of freedom. I've been thinking about taking up rowing again lately—maybe it's time I got back into it. That's a great idea. I recently started taking kayaking lessons in the evenings, and I have to say, it's been a real confidence booster. It's not just the physical aspect—it's the mental clarity it brings. I barely noticed the rain yesterday when I was out on the water. That’s fantastic. I’ve been trying to get myself into better shape, and maybe rowing could be the ticket. I’ve been looking for the right sort of clothing too—something that keeps you dry in wet weather. Have you found any good gear? I’ve bought a few things online, but I’m still not entirely happy with the waterproofs. I think I might need to try some more practical clothing.

Dad, I just got a text from my friend saying her results came through. She’s got an A in all her subjects, and she’s applying for uni in September. I’m so proud of her. That’s brilliant! You know, when I was your age, I didn’t even know what uni meant. I just wanted to get out of Bolton and find a job. But I guess it’s better to have options. Yeah, I know. But it’s so stressful. I’ve got my results day tomorrow, and I’m worried about how I’ll cope. I mean, I’m still trying to figure out whether to study English or business. You’ll figure it out, love. When I was your age, I used to send text messages all the time and I couldn’t even spell properly. But now, I’ve got to admit, I still can’t spell “emoticon” right. Yeah, I saw that on my phone the other day. It’s so weird—emoji’s have taken over all our conversations. I mean, I can’t even read a text without seeing a smiley face. It’s not just texts. I saw a Vodafone ad the other day – it had a whole bunch of emojis and none of the words. It was like a language of its own. I know! And I’ve heard that people are even using Morse code on WhatsApp now. It’s so complicated. I just use the dictionary app when I can’t find the right word. Hey, you know what I missed out on? Buying second-hand stuff on eBay. I used to buy all my clothes from there when I was your age. It saved me money and got me some decent stuff. I’ve got my eye on some new shoes on Amazon. I’ve got student finance, so it’s not too bad. But the delivery is going to take forever. I’ve already got a glass water bottle on the way. Oh, I’ve got one of those too. I keep it in the fridge. It’s the best thing since sliced bread. You know, it’s funny how things change. I remember when I used to buy my food at the market. Now I just order it online. That’s true. I’ve been to the university campus this week, and it’s so big.

Yo, man, it's been ages! You've been in Japan for ages, right? How's that going? Yeah, man, it's been like six months. I've been studying Japanese in Tokyo. It's intense, but I love it. That’s awesome. I heard Tokyo is crazy busy. Do you get used to the crowds? Oh, yeah, I’m starting to. It's like a different kind of chaos. You know, there's always something going on. Didn’t you say you wanted to go to university? Why did you go to Japan instead? I did, but I got a scholarship to study Japanese. It's a bit of a dream come true. Plus, I wanted to experience the culture first-hand. That’s cool. But I’m about to start my master’s. I’ve been stressing about exams and all that. I know the feeling. I used to stress about exams back in uni. But now, I just try to stay focused. Yeah, I guess I need to find a way to stay calm. It’s like everything is on my shoulders. You’re not alone. I had to deal with that too. But I found that hanging out with friends helps a lot. True, but I’ve been trying to catch up with people. I’ve been to a few restaurants lately. Oh, you’re into food? I love trying new places. Have you had any good eats in London? Yeah, actually, I went to this little Thai place on Brick Lane. The pad thai was out of this world. Nice. Maybe I should check it out. Speaking of food, have you thought about where you’re going after uni? I’m thinking about staying in London. I have some friends here and I like the vibe. That’s cool. I’m not sure yet. Maybe I’ll stay in Tokyo or go back to Jamaica. Either way, I guess the future is uncertain. Yeah, but the point is to go with the flow. And if you ever need help with anything, just let me know. Thanks, man. You’ve always been there for me. Anytime. We’re in this together. Yeah, man. Let’s catch up more often. I miss our old hangouts. Definitely. I’ve missed those too. Let’s plan something soon. For sure. Maybe a trip to some new restaurants? Sounds like a plan.

So, I just got a photo from Facebook of that trip we took to Buckfast Abbey last year. It’s the one with the giant white cross and the waterfall. I can’t believe we managed to get there on time. Remember how we had to take the bus from Exeter because the car was in the shop?      Oh, yes! I still laugh about that. You know I said we’d leave at 7 a.m., and we didn’t even make it out of the house until 8:30. I think the cat was more eager to get there than us.      You mean the cat that used to sleep on your head? That was a real contender for the title of “most stubborn creature on Earth.” I still remember when you tried to take him to the Abbey, and he just sat there staring at the mossy stones for half an hour.      That’s the one! I think he was judging the place. Anyway, we should plan another trip soon. Have you thought about where we might go next? I was thinking maybe the Lake District or somewhere in Cornwall.      I was just saying the other day that I’d love to go on a cruise. We’ve been talking about it for ages. It’s not like we’re old enough to be retired, right?      Speaking of old, I still have a few pounds saved up from when I was working, and I’ve been thinking about booking one of those retirement cruises. I heard they’ve got good food and plenty of opportunities to chat with other people. You know, like real conversation, not just staring at a phone.      That sounds nice. But I’m still not sure about sea travel. I’ve always found the idea of being on a boat a bit scary. I mean, what if the weather turns bad?      Well, we could always start small. Maybe a day trip on a lake or something. Or maybe even a road trip. I saw a post about visiting the Torquay Heritage Museum. It’s not far from here, and the tickets are cheap.      Torquay? That’s where I started my career as an accountant. I remember walking those coastal paths every morning. It was cold, but the views were worth it.      I’d love to go back there. I’ve been meaning to visit the old school I used to teach at.

So, how was Belgium? I’ve been dying to hear all about it! You two got to see all those pretty cities and stuff, right?      It was absolutely amazing, luv. We stayed in Bruges for a few days, and it’s like stepping back in time. The cobbled streets, the canals... it was like a fairytale.      And the food was  to die for . We had this incredible steak in a little family-run restaurant. It was so good, I almost choked on my wine.      I bet you did. I’ve heard that the Belgian waffles are legendary too. Did you try those?      Oh, we did. And I’ll be honest, I expected them to be sweet, but they’re actually breakfast food—like a real proper fry-up. Haha!      Yeah, I had to explain that to my mum when she saw me eating one for dinner. She said it was “unhealthy,” but I told her it was  authentic .      I can see that. Speaking of authentic, how did you manage with the Sat Nav? I’ve heard stories about people getting lost in Belgium.      Oh, it was a nightmare. We had to rely on Google Maps and the locals. One time, we drove past a market and thought we’d missed the turn, but it turned out to be the  best  market in the whole town!      And the cycling was incredible. We hired bikes and did this route from Bruges to Kortrijk. The countryside was just stunning.      That sounds amazing! I’ve always wanted to do that. Do you think I could join you next year?      Absolutely, luv. You’d be perfect for that. Just remember to take a phone with you.      And a good map. I still can’t believe how hard it was to find my way around with my phone. I ended up calling a friend just to ask for directions.      I’ve had some issues with my new phone too. It’s been dropping signal everywhere. I’m thinking of getting a better one.      You should. Or just learn to drive. You know, like I did. Always better to have a backup plan.      Oh, I’d rather not. I’ve had enough of driving abroad. Maybe we can plan a cycling trip next year.      Yes, that sounds like a plan! I can’t wait to hear more stories from you both.      You’ll get your stories, luv. And maybe a few more maps.

I just finished chopping the onions, and I think I’ve made a mess of the kitchen. I can’t believe I got the knife stuck in the board again. You know, I remember when we first moved in, you were so careful with the kitchen tools. Maybe you’re just getting a bit more adventurous in your cooking these days? Oh, I’m not sure if it’s adventure or just a lack of focus. I was just trying to make a proper sauce for the lasagna, and now I’ve got to clean up this disaster. Do you want to help? Only if you promise not to let the knife go rogue again. I’ve had enough of that. Speaking of which, did you get that new perfume I mentioned? It’s supposed to be the one with the vanilla and amber notes. Yes, I did. It’s lovely, actually. I wore it tonight when I came home. I think it smells like a warm hug. Do you like it? I do. It actually reminds me of the time we went to that little boutique in York. You remember, the one with the mismatched décor and the owner who thought she was a mixologist. Oh, I remember. She said she was ‘a blend of aroma and alcohol,’ and I believed her for a moment. Anyway, I think the perfume is perfect for the evening. Should I put some candles on the table too? Yes, but not too many. I don’t want the room to feel like a spa. Just a few to set the mood. Oh, and I saw some beautiful white lilies at the market earlier. Would you like me to bring them over? That would be lovely. I’ve been wanting to add some flowers to the room. I think it’ll make the space feel cozier. Perfect. And while I’m at the shop, I’ll pick up a few more things for the meal. I’ve been thinking about how we haven’t had a proper gathering in a while. That’s true. It’s been a long time since we had friends over. I think it’s time we bring some of the old Facebook friends over for dinner. They’ve been messaging me a lot lately. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. Maybe we can invite a few of them. It’s been nice to catch up, even if it’s just online.

I've been meaning to ask, have you ever been to Australia? I've heard so much about it from my nephew, who worked there for a few years. Oh, I've been there a couple of times. Not for work, but I always wanted to see the Outback. My wife and I went to Queensland a few years back. It was incredible—so different from the UK. You don’t get that kind of wide open space here in England. Oh, I’ve been there too! My sister-in-law works in Sydney and sent me a photo of the Sydney Harbour Bridge. It’s like something out of a postcard. I always thought Australia was the land of kangaroos and beaches, but the cities are pretty modern too. That’s true. I had a friend who moved there and started a business in Melbourne. He told me about how the dress code is very strict for business men—formal suits, ties, everything. I couldn’t believe it. You don’t see that kind of formality in England anymore. Yeah, I remember reading about that. I think it’s because of the influx of international business. You can’t go wrong with a suit and tie, especially in the cities. But I suppose it’s a little too much for some people. True. I actually had a student from Australia once who was studying English here. He said that in his hometown, people dress quite differently. You don’t see the same kind of business suits. It’s more casual, even in business settings. I can imagine. I’ve heard the Yorkshire dialect is quite different from the South. I’ve been to Bristol a few times, and the people there are very friendly. I think they’re the most polite Southerners I’ve ever met. Oh, I know! I grew up in Manchester, so I’ve heard the northern dialect for years. It’s quite distinct from the way people speak in London or Bristol. You can tell where someone’s from just by how they speak. I agree. I’ve had a few students over the years whose accents were so strong that I sometimes thought they were from the North. It’s fascinating how much dialect can tell you about someone’s background. It really does. I had a colleague once who was from Sheffield, and he used to say that the Sheffield dialect is one of the hardest to understand.

I just checked my Instagram again, and I'm so tired of seeing the same people posting about their ‘glamping’ trips and vegan smoothies. It’s like everyone’s trying to be something they’re not. I know, right? I follow a few bloggers who post about eco-friendly living, but honestly, I can't tell if they’re genuine or just trying to sell something. It’s like the whole social media scene is just a performance. Exactly. And don’t even get me started on the influencers. You know, the ones who post flawless photos of themselves doing yoga in the middle of nowhere, but then you see their captions saying they're dealing with anxiety and depression. It's so contradictory. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. I think it’s more about the image they’re trying to project than the real person. Sometimes I wonder if they even watch the shows they’re promoting. I mean, I’ve seen some of them talking about TV shows they don’t even know the plot of. I’ve been thinking about starting a podcast lately. I mean, not like the big ones, just something casual where I can talk about books or travel. But I’m scared of being too niche. What if no one listens? That’s understandable. I started one a few months ago, just about language and culture. It’s been okay. I’m not getting a huge audience, but it’s been a good way to connect with people who are into the same things. You don’t need to be huge to have an impact. That’s true. I guess the key is just to be real and not try too hard. I’ve been listening to a few podcasts lately about mindfulness and personal development. They’re not the most exciting, but they’re really thought-provoking. I like that. I’ve been doing a bit of that myself. It’s amazing how much you can learn from just sitting and listening. I think I’ll start a podcast soon too. Maybe something about teaching English and working in Poland. That sounds interesting. I’d love to hear more about that. Maybe we can even collaborate on something one day. It’s funny, isn’t it? We’re both teaching English, but in completely different ways. Yeah, it’s kind of ironic.

Okay, so I just got a message from Pippy. She wants to know if we can get a photograph for her Blue Peter badge. She’s really excited about it, and I think she’s going to see ANON’s Travelling Circus this weekend.      Wait, isn’t ANON the babysitter? I thought she was going to be here this afternoon. Is she not coming?      Yeah, she said she had to go to a meeting with her dad. But she mentioned she’s got the circus tickets. Didn’t she say she was getting a photo too?      Yes, she did. She said it’s for her Blue Peter badge. But the thing is, I need to get a passport photo for her. I was just wondering if you two would like to come with me to the post office. It’s near the park, and it’s a nice walk.      That sounds fun. I’d love to go. But, uh, do I have to wear anything special?      No, I think it’s just a regular photo. But maybe we should dress nicely? Like, not in pajamas.      Exactly. I thought about that. So we’ll need to bring something to wear. I was thinking maybe we could go after lunch. Would that work for you?      Sure! I can ask my mum if she’s free. Wait, isn’t it supposed to be sunny today? Should we bring an umbrella just in case?      It might be. But I think it’s going to be alright. Although, I have to say, I’m a bit nervous about the passport photo. I’ve never done one before.      You don’t have to do it alone. I can help you. I’ve seen the machine before. It’s like a robot with a camera.      That’s what I thought. But I’m worried I’ll mess it up.      Don’t worry, Mum. I’ll keep you company. And if you do mess it up, we can just do it again.      Yeah, I’ll help you too. And maybe we can get some snacks from the café next door.      That sounds perfect. Alright, I’ll let you know when we’re heading out. Oh, and while we’re at the post office, we might need to get a few stamps for the circus tickets.      Wait, isn’t that the one where the ringmaster has a hat with a unicorn on it?

I just had this weird conversation with my mate about ED, you know, erectile dysfunction. It’s like, why is it such a taboo topic? I mean, we’re all students, we’re all in our late teens, we’re supposed to be into this stuff, right? Yeah, I know. I mean, I’ve been thinking about it too. I had this chat with my cousin last week. She’s like, “Oh, you’re too young to worry about that.” But she’s in a relationship, and she’s been struggling with it for months. It’s not even about age, is it? No, it’s not. I think it’s just that people don’t want to talk about it. Like, if you’re a guy and you can’t get hard, you’re like, “Oh, I’m just not into it,” or “I’m too stressed.” But it’s not always that simple. I mean, I’ve read a bit online, and it’s like, there are so many causes—stress, anxiety, even diet. It’s not just about being lazy or not caring. Exactly. I mean, we’re not even in the same place when it comes to that. Some of us are sexually active, some aren’t, and some are just figuring it out. I think it’s important to be open about it, you know? If you’re struggling, you shouldn’t feel embarrassed to talk to someone. Like, maybe a doctor or a therapist. Oh, totally. But I think the real issue is that people don’t want to open up about it. Especially with friends. Like, if you’re a guy and you say, “I’m having trouble with this,” people might think you’re being dramatic or just not man enough. It’s a bit of a double standard, isn’t it? Absolutely. I mean, I’ve seen so many guys just hiding it, not even talking to their partners. And it can be so much worse for the person on the receiving end. They might feel like they’re doing something wrong or that they’re not attractive. It’s a real mess. Yeah, and I think it’s starting to change, you know? More people are talking about mental health, about anxiety, about stress. But ED is still this weird thing that people don’t want to mention. It’s like we’re still stuck in the past.

So, I just got the veg box delivered today, and I was so excited. But honestly, it felt like a lot of stuff I don’t even like. I mean, who even eats raw kale? I mean, it’s not like I’m the biggest fan of leafy greens.      Yeah, I know, I felt the same. But I think it’s worth it in the long run. I mean, if you’re trying to save money, it’s easier to cook from scratch, and you can’t beat fresh veggies.      I get that, but I’m not sure I’m ready to switch completely. I’ve been trying to stick to the Slimming World plan, and honestly, the ‘extra’ options are so expensive. Like, the 0 calorie syrup? I feel like I’m paying for a bubble bath.      Oh, I know, it’s a bit of a scam, isn’t it? I tried the free food and ‘syns’ thing, and it was honestly kind of a waste. I mean, I thought I was saving money, but I ended up buying way more things I didn’t need.      And then there’s the scales. I mean, I’ve tried everything, and they just don’t seem to match up. Sometimes I feel like I’m losing weight, and other times, I feel like I’m gaining. It’s like the scales are playing tricks on me.      Honestly, I think it’s just the fluctuation. Like, your body is always changing, so the scales aren’t the best indicator. But hey, I still try to be mindful. I’ve been cooking a lot of cauliflower cheese, and I’m even eating the roast with the double peas from the freezer. It’s not terrible.      Speaking of which, have you thought about the ‘treat day’ this Saturday? I was thinking maybe we can go to that new café in Notting Hill. I saw a review online, and it said they have some really good vegan cakes.      Oh, I’d love that! But we have to plan ahead. I tried to use Siri to schedule it, but it kept asking me for my birthday. I think it was confused.      Haha, seriously though, I made a list of things we need to buy. The Quorn range is getting cheaper these days, and I think it’s a good way to save money while still eating healthy.

I've been thinking a lot about our holiday plans. I really want to go somewhere with good food and a bit of culture, maybe somewhere in Europe. I’m feeling like I need a break from the usual tourist traps. I hear you, but I’ve been thinking about something different. What if we take a road trip? I’ve always wanted to see more of the countryside. Maybe drive up to the Lake District? A lot of people say it’s peaceful and beautiful. That sounds lovely, but it’s not exactly the kind of place I’m looking for. I’d rather be somewhere with more... activity. Maybe a city with a good literary scene? I’ve been meaning to read more, and I like the idea of being around books and writers. I get that, but I’m also thinking about the domestic sphere. If we go to a city, I’d need to bring the kids along. I’d rather not have to worry about childcare all the time. Maybe a place where we can both relax without the kids? That’s true, but I don’t want to leave the kids behind either. Maybe we can find a short break somewhere near. I was thinking of the South Coast—like Brighton or Bournemouth. There’s a lot to do, and the weather is usually good. I’m not sure. I’ve always been interested in the idea of getting a tattoo. It’s something I’ve been putting off for a long time. What do you think about the idea of getting one? A tattoo? That’s a big decision. I’m not sure I’d ever get one, but I can see the appeal. It’s personal, right? You can have something that means something to you. What would you get? I was thinking of something symbolic. Maybe something that represents my journey or my family. I’ve been thinking about the idea of ‘home’—I’ve moved around so much. That could be a beautiful tattoo. But I think it’s important to think about how long you’ll want it to stay. Politics is another thing I’ve been thinking about. With the elections coming up, it feels like the world is shifting. I’m not sure where I stand. Yeah, it’s frustrating. I think it’s important to be informed, but it’s also hard not to feel overwhelmed by all the noise.

I just got a postcard from the Scottish Highlands last week. It’s a bit of a blur, but it showed those beautiful mountains and some traditional tartan. I thought I’d show it to you, just to see what you think. That sounds lovely! I remember you talking about a trip there during your break. Did you manage to visit the Isle of Skye? Yes, I did. A real treat. The landscapes were absolutely stunning. But I can’t help but think about the future of Scotland. You know, the independence movement. It’s a bit of a hot topic these days, isn’t it? Definitely. I’ve been keeping up with the news. It’s a bit of a divisive issue, but I think it’s important for people to have a say. I mean, if they want to be independent, who are we to stop them? I suppose that’s the argument. But I worry about the economic implications. Scotland’s economy is pretty strong, but it’s intertwined with the rest of the UK. I’m not sure how it would hold up on its own. Yeah, I hear you. But as long as the people of Scotland have the right to decide, I think it’s a democratic process. Anyway, let’s not get too political. We’re here to enjoy the night, aren’t we? True. It’s been a long week at the college, and I’m looking forward to the weekend. I was just wondering—do you think we should plan a small gathering? It would be nice to have some friends over for dinner. That sounds like a great idea. I’ve been meaning to do something like that. I was thinking of a weekend trip to the countryside, maybe a picnic. Do you think you could help with that? I’d be happy to. Maybe we could do something like that for the upcoming weekend. I’ll check the weather forecast and let you know. Also, I was going to ask—what about our friend Margaret? I think she’d enjoy a picnic too. Absolutely. She’s mentioned wanting to get out of the city for a while. I’ll send her an invite. Speaking of invitations, have you thought about the birthday arrangements for the next few weeks? I’ve been putting it off, to be honest. I was planning to go to a restaurant, but I’m not sure if that’s the right time.

I just saw a news story about the Syrian refugees coming into the UK. I was thinking, maybe we could do something to help. You know, like drawing a chair for them? A chair? Like, a real chair? No, not a real chair. It’s a symbolic thing. You know, the idea of giving someone a seat, a place to sit, to feel welcomed. A simple act of kindness. I don’t get it. Why a chair? Well, imagine you’re a refugee. You’ve left everything behind, you’re tired, you’re scared. And then you walk into a new place, and the first thing you see is a chair. It might be the first time you feel safe to sit down, to rest. It’s a small gesture, but it can mean a lot. But how do we do that? Do we draw it? Exactly. We can draw a chair and put it in the school art display. They have a project called "Draw a Chair for Refugees," and it’s spreading across the country. It’s a way for kids to show empathy and understanding. I can draw a chair. I draw dinosaurs all the time. That’s great! And maybe we can add a message. Something like, “This chair is for you. You’re welcome here.” It’s not just a drawing—it’s a message of hope. Can I write something too? Like, “Welcome to our school”? Of course. That’s wonderful. It’s about showing compassion and making them feel part of our community. What if they don’t like it? That’s the beauty of it. It’s not about what they like—it’s about what we can do to help. And it’s not just about the drawing. It’s about the conversation, the awareness. I think I want to draw a blue chair. Because blue is calm. Perfect. And maybe we can make a banner with all the chairs. Then we can present it at the school fair. Can I bring my dinosaur drawing too? Of course! Maybe we can make a whole room of chairs—drawn chairs, real chairs, and even posters. It’s going to be a beautiful display. I can ask my teacher if we can do it in art class. That’s a great idea. Let’s talk to her next week. And maybe we can even include a note from the class saying how much we care.

I just got a message from Lucy. She’s so excited about her new baby, and she’s already talking about baby names and everything. I can’t believe she’s actually doing it—she was so against having kids just a year ago. I know, it’s wild. But I guess she’s just grown up. I mean, we both went through that phase of being like, “Wait, is this what we really want?” but now she’s all in. She even started a baby shower group with a few of our mutual friends. Yeah, and it’s so fun to see how they’re all changing. It’s like watching these little mini versions of themselves pop up, only cuter and more chaotic. My sister had a baby last year, and it’s like the whole family’s gone through this transformation. I know, it’s incredible. But I was thinking the other day—how do we even keep up? I mean, we’re both lecturers, so we’re busy as hell, and now we’re also trying to support these friends through all this. I feel like we’re missing out on some of the more… I don’t know, glamorous parts of parenthood. I know what you mean. But I think we’re in a good place. I can't believe we've been stuck in this traffic for over an hour. It's like the whole road is a parking lot. I’m starting to think we should have left earlier. I know, I know. I told you we should have left at 7 instead of 8. But it’s not like we could do anything about it. Besides, I reckon this is the only time of year when the roads are actually busy. Not that I mind, but it’s just frustrating. Honestly, I can't even remember the last time I saw such a traffic jam. I think it’s because of all the people trying to get to the fair. And don’t even get me started on the parking situation. My uncle lives in a flat with no outside space. He tried to get a disabled parking permit once, but they said he couldn’t because the car wasn’t registered in his name. Yeah, I remember when I was in London, there was a big issue with disabled parking permits and people just faking them. I think the council was cracking down, but it’s still a mess. I’ve had enough of it. My cousin lives in a care home and they’re always having problems with the council housing. They’ve been waiting for a new property for over two years now. They’re not even sure if they’ll get one. It’s ridiculous. You’d think with the way things are going, the government would prioritize elderly and disabled people. I agree. I work with a lot of people who need support, and it’s heartbreaking to see how little they’re getting. I mean, the council houses are still an option, but they’re so scarce. And when they do get one, there’s a waiting list that can take years. It’s not just about housing, it’s about accessibility too. I remember when I was in my finals, I had to use a disabled parking space at the university. I had to prove I was disabled, and it took weeks. I think it’s a bit of a bureaucratic nightmare. Exactly. And if you’re over 60 and you’re not working, you’re not even considered for anything. It’s like the government doesn’t even care. That’s not true. They do care, but they don’t have the resources.

I've been thinking a lot about the allotment we were talking about last week. I think it's time we actually got started. I've been doing some research online and I found a few plots that are available in the local area. Do you remember where the community garden is? Oh yes, I remember! It’s just down by the old railway track. I think it's called the Greenfield Community Plot. I've heard a few people talk about it. I’ve even seen a few of them working there. It’s a nice spot, quite secluded and not too crowded. That sounds perfect. I was thinking of getting a plot for us. I've got the idea of planting some herbs and vegetables like tomatoes and courgettes. I love cooking and I think having fresh produce would be a real treat. That’s a great idea! I was thinking of starting with some fruit trees. Maybe a couple of apple trees and some raspberry bushes. I’ve always wanted to grow my own fruit. Plus, they look lovely in the garden and make great additions to the scenery. Yeah, I think we can combine both ideas. I could take care of the vegetables and you could focus on the fruit. I’m pretty sure there are some local gardening groups that can offer tips too. That sounds like a plan. I think we can start by visiting the community garden next weekend. I can go with you and we can check out the available plots.

Right, so I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to plan that secret weekend trip to York? I remember you kept checking your phone like it was a surveillance camera. But I swear, if we’d actually gone, that would’ve been the best thing ever. Oh, I was just being responsible. I mean, we’re students, not criminals. But seriously, I feel like we’ve been planning so many things and never actually doing them. It’s like we’re always talking about the next big adventure, but we never take the leap. Yeah, I know what you mean. Like, we’ve got this whole "somedays" thing going on. "Some day we’ll go to the seaside," "Some day we’ll go hiking in the Lake District," "Some day we’ll even try that new coffee place in Sheffield." You did try that coffee place last week, remember? You were so into it, you even ordered a flat white. I was like, “What even is a flat white?” and you were like, “It’s like the holy grail of coffee.” And you liked it, didn’t you? But if we do this, we’re doing it properly. I’m not going to be the one who forgets again. Deal. So, what’s the plan? Do we grab a takeaway and watch a movie, or are we actually going out? Well, we made a plan, didn’t we? So, let’s make it count. I’ll text the others. Let’s see if they want to join.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to play  Call of Duty  together last week? I swear, I was just trying to aim properly, and then suddenly I was hit by a rocket launcher from behind. It was like  Mission Impossible !      Oh, you were just bad at it. I mean, you were a bit nervous, right? I remember you kept saying “I’m not a bad gamer, I just got distracted by the pizza delivery!”      Yeah, I remember that. You were literally juggling a pizza box and a controller at the same time. But hey, at least you got the pizza delivered on time. I still don’t know how you managed that.      That’s the story of my life, honestly. I try to focus on gaming, and then something random happens—like my phone rings, or my cat jumps on the keyboard. I swear, the cat’s got a grudge against me.      Yeah, I think she takes it out on you because you’re always playing games and not paying attention to her. She’s like, “Hey, I’m here, you know!”      She’s got a point. She’s the one who walks into the room every time you’re trying to win a match and starts barking. It’s like she’s trying to help.      I remember when we first moved in together. You tried to teach me how to play  Valorant , and she ended up in the middle of the screen, trying to bark at the enemies. It was such a weird moment.      Yeah, that was one of the weirdest things I’ve ever seen. My cat’s got better reflexes than I do in some games.      You know, I think we should start a gaming group. Like, just us. We could call it “The Casual Gaming Collective.” No pressure, just playing for fun.      That sounds cool. I mean, we could play on weekends, or whenever we feel like it. Maybe even start a tournament or something.      Yeah, but we need to make sure we all agree on the games. I mean, I’m not into  Call of Duty  so much, but I do like  Overwatch  or  Fortnite .      I can be flexible. I like most things, as long as there’s some action. Maybe we could mix it up a bit—some co-op, some competitive, some just chill.      I like that idea.

I just watched that new film about the 1960s. It was  so  convincing, don’t you think? I mean, the costumes, the music—it all felt real. Yeah, I remember seeing it at the cinema. It was a bit slow in the middle, but the ending really got me. I felt like I was right there in the protest marches. Oh, I’d have loved to have been there. You know, I used to go to the cinema every week when I was younger. Back in the days when the pictures were still showing films like  Lawrence of Arabia  and  Doctor Zhivago . That sounds like a real treat. My lectures are all about production schedules and budgeting. It’s not like I get to see films like that anymore. Oh, I know what you mean. But you’re lucky, you’ve got a good job and all. You know, I used to work in the service sector, minding shops and things. Not that I’m complaining, mind you—just reminiscing. Thanks, I guess. It’s not the easiest job, but it pays the bills and gives me time to watch films. I mean, it’s not like I have a lot of time for hobbies. I know the feeling. But you’ve got to make time for yourself, love. You can’t just live for work. I used to say that to my daughter all the time. She’s got a job now, though, and she’s doing well. That’s good to hear. I’m jealous, honestly. I’ve been thinking about going back to school for a bit. I’ve got a postgrad in media studies, but I’ve been too busy. That’s a great idea. You should do it. It’s never too late to learn something new. I started learning to cook when I was in my early sixties—well, I think I did. I tried to make a soufflé once and it collapsed. Oh no! Did you take a photo? No, but I did take a video. You should have seen it! The mess was  everywhere . I think it was more of a casualty than a success. I’d love to see it. Maybe we can watch one of those old films together sometime. I’ve got a few classics I’ve been meaning to catch up on. Sounds like a plan. Let’s make a list and see what we can watch.

So, I just got back from this weekend trip to the spa. I know it's not exactly the first thing you'd think of when you're hanging out with friends, but it was actually pretty chill.      Oh, a spa? You mean that place with the hot tubs and the massage? I thought you were going to take me to that one in Basingstoke.      No, no, no! That’s the one I wanted to go to. But my mum said she wasn’t going to pay for me to go to a spa again after the last time I came back with a sunburn and a headache. So I went solo to this one near Stratford. It’s got a nice little pool and some yoga classes.      That sounds nice. You know, I’ve been thinking about getting a spa treatment for my back. I’ve been working too much lately, and I’m starting to feel it.      Oh, you should! I mean, if you have the time and the money. I told my sister I was going to the spa, and she said, “You don’t even have a back!” But she’s only joking, of course.      You know, I was just thinking about that. My partner works in a really busy office, and he barely has time to take a bath. He’s always talking about how he wants to go on a weekend getaway, but every time we try to plan something, someone has to work.      That’s so frustrating. I mean, what’s the point of a relationship if you can’t even plan a weekend together? I guess it’s all about communication, though.      I agree. Communication is key. I mean, I’ve been trying to get my boyfriend to talk about his week more. He’s so quiet sometimes, and I don’t know what’s going on in his head.      That’s true. I think sometimes people just don’t know how to express themselves. I remember when I was in an interview once, and I was so nervous, I just kept saying yes to everything. I didn’t even know what the questions were asking.      Oh, I’ve been in interviews too. My job as a Language Research Coordinator requires a lot of interviews. It’s funny how people can act so differently in front of a camera or a microphone.      That must be interesting.

I just had to load the washing machine again. That thing’s been acting up all week. I think it’s got a blockage somewhere. I’ve tried everything—checking the filters, even taking the back panel off. But it keeps throwing up water when it’s supposed to spin. You’re not the only one. My washing machine’s been giving me the same problems. I’m actually thinking of getting a new one. It’s been costing me more in repairs than it’s worth. I’ve had it for like five years now. Five years? That’s ancient! I’ve only had mine for two, but it’s already giving me trouble. I swear, the only reason I haven’t thrown it out is because I still have a few pairs of clothes left that are waiting to be washed. I feel you. I think I’m going to go with a front loader this time. The ones I’ve seen in the shops are really quiet and efficient. I’ve heard they’re more modern and less prone to breaking down. Although, I’m still not sure if I can afford it. Yeah, I can see the appeal. I’ve been meaning to do the same. But then again, I’m not in a rush. My parents have one and it’s been working fine. I guess it’s just a matter of time before mine bites the dust. Speaking of family, did you hear about my cousin’s wedding? It was last weekend. She got married in the countryside. The whole family turned up. I had to wear a suit, which I haven’t done in years. It was a bit of a struggle getting back into the groove. Oh, that sounds like fun. I’m sorry I couldn’t make it. I was stuck with work. But I did get a call from my mum telling me all about the food. She said the catering was amazing. She even tried the dessert and said it was like something out of a film. Yeah, she mentioned that too. I’ve been telling her I should start a catering business. She said, “If that’s what you want to do, then do it.” I think she’s trying to encourage me. I’ve been thinking about it a lot lately. That’s sweet of her. My mum’s always been supportive, even if she doesn’t understand my work.

I just got a call from the estate agent. They said there’s a small cottage in Hunsonby that’s available, and the price is lower than I expected. Maybe I should take a look? That sounds promising. I heard the housing market in Cumbria has been more stable than in the south, especially since the VW scandal. It’s like people are avoiding the bigger cities now. Yeah, I heard about that too. It’s a shame, really. The scandal had a big impact on the economy, and it hit the northern regions particularly hard. I remember reading that some car parts factories had to close, and that led to a lot of job losses. Exactly. It’s funny how things like that can change everything. I left the teaching job last year, and I’ve been thinking about moving somewhere quieter. The noise and stress of city life just wore me down. I can understand that. I work from home a lot now, and being in the north is actually quite nice. The cost of living is lower, and the community feels more like a real place. Plus, being closer to the countryside gives you that peace and quiet. I agree. But I still feel like I’m watching the world move on without me. I got laid off from the oil industry a few years back, and I’ve never really found another job. It’s hard to stay motivated when you feel like you’re stuck. I know what you mean. I was someone who always worked, and retirement has been a bit of a shock. I had to adjust to not having a routine. But now I’m looking at this cottage, and it might be exactly what I need. That’s a great mindset. Sometimes, the hardest part is just taking the first step. If you’re considering it, you should take a look. I’d be happy to come with you and help you look around. I’d like that. I could use a change of scenery too. Maybe it’s time I stopped waiting for the world to change and started changing it myself. That’s the spirit! I’ll call the estate agent and arrange a viewing. It’s about time I started living the life I’ve always wanted, instead of just surviving. I’ll help you get settled. Let’s make this a new beginning, together.

I just don’t know how we’re going to manage without a pension. I mean, it’s not like we can keep living off the same savings forever, is it? I know, mate. It’s like the government’s set us up to be reliant on the state. But with the way things are, even if we do get the full pension, it’s not going to be enough. You know how much inflation has been doing lately? I’ve heard about that. It’s all so confusing. I just don’t understand how people manage when they’re retired. I mean, I used to earn a decent wage, but now I’m just sitting here, watching the news and feeling like we’re being pushed aside. It’s not just the pension, though. I’ve been thinking about the housing developments they’re pushing through in the area. I don’t like the idea of all these new flats taking over the old town. It’s changing the whole vibe of the place. I remember when we used to walk to the shops and have a cup of tea at the corner café. Yeah, I remember that too. It’s sad to see all that gone. But what can we do? The council says they need to build more housing because of the demographics. I just hope it doesn’t turn into one of those places where nobody knows their neighbour. I’m worried about that too. We’ve all been trying to stay in bed and breakfasts to keep the cost down, but it’s getting harder. I mean, not everyone can afford to stay in a B&B every night, especially with the prices these days. I know, but I think we’ve got to try and make the best of it. I’ve been looking into the different areas where we might be able to move. Maybe something in the countryside? I’ve heard it’s cheaper up there. Yeah, I’ve thought about that. Though I don’t know if I’d want to move. It’s not like I’m ready to pack up and leave everything behind. I just miss the old days, you know? I get that. I keep thinking about the family too. I miss seeing the kids and grandkids. I’ve been trying to stay in touch through the phone, but sometimes it just feels like there’s so much distance.

So, I just saw this video online about evolution and human biology. It was super interesting, but also kind of weird. Like, they showed how our bodies have changed over time, but it felt like they were making it sound like we’re just some kind of animal—sort of like we’re not even humans anymore?      Yeah, I saw that too. It was basically saying that we evolved from apes. I mean, I know that’s true, but it’s weird how people get upset about it. Like, why does it matter if we came from monkeys? It’s just science, right?      Honestly, I think some people take it too seriously. Like, they’re like, “Oh, evolution is a lie!” or something. But it’s not like we’re saying we’re not human—we’re still human. I mean, the video didn’t say anything about us not being special or anything. It just explained how we got here.      That’s the thing, though. Some people use evolution to justify racism or sexism. Like, they say, “Well, we’re just animals, so it’s okay if some people are better than others.” But that’s not even real science. Evolution is just about survival—it doesn’t say anything about superiority or hierarchy.      Exactly. I mean, I’ve heard some people say that if we evolved from apes, then we’re not that different from them. But then again, we’re not the same. We have this thing called culture, and language, and everything. That’s what makes us unique.      Also, some people get really worked up about religion and evolution. Like, they say it’s a conflict between science and faith. But I don’t think it has to be. You can believe in a higher power and also accept that life evolved. It doesn’t have to be either/or.      Yeah, I think some people are just scared of what evolution means. They don’t like the idea that we’re all connected and that we’re not perfect. Like, we’re all just trying our best to survive and make the best of what we have.      And then there’s the whole internet thing. Like, these videos go viral, and people get so caught up in arguing about them. I mean, I get it—it’s catchy, and it’s interesting, but it’s not like we can just ignore what we’ve learned about science.

I just had a really weird experience at the hospital last week. I was there for a check-up, and they said I might need some tablets for my blood pressure. But I’ve been feeling fine, you know? Oh no, are you okay? I heard the waiting times are terrible there. But I’m glad you’re not too unwell. I’ve been meaning to ask you—have you heard about that new acupuncture place in town? I read somewhere it helps with stress and fatigue. Honestly, I haven’t. But I’ve been meaning to try it, especially with all the stress from work. It’s been a hectic few months. I’ve been thinking about switching to a different job, but I’m not sure if I’m ready for that. You know, I had acupuncture once when I was in my early sixties. It felt strange at first, but after a few sessions, I noticed a real difference. I used to have a lot of back pain, and it helped so much. You should give it a go. Yeah, I had that too. My wife used to get regular treatments, and I swear it did wonders for her. But she’s not around anymore. I miss her. Speaking of which, have any of you heard from our cousin who lives in the Highlands? I haven’t seen her in ages. No, I haven’t. I did try to message her a few weeks ago, but she didn’t respond. I wonder if she’s been in an accident or something. That would explain why she hasn’t been around. You know how she is, always adventure-seeking. I know, she’s always been a bit of a risk-taker. I remember she tried skiing when she was 60, and she ended up in the hospital with a broken leg. She barely even got up from the snow. It was quite the story. Oh, I remember that! She was so embarrassed. She said she was just trying to ‘get back in shape’ after all those years waiting on the sidelines. But really, she was just being reckless. I still worry about her sometimes. Well, I suppose we should all be careful. I’ve been trying to get my MOT done early because I know how bad the roads are getting. And I’ve got new tyres ready to go in.

You know, the people who lived in the Americas a long time ago didn't always have the same rights as everyone else. Some people were treated very badly because of the color of their skin.      What do you mean, Mum? Why were they treated badly?      Well, it was a long time ago, in a place called the United States. There was a system called slavery where people were forced to work for others without being paid. It was wrong, and it lasted for a very long time.      Was it because they were Black?      Yes, in many cases, it was. People of African descent were taken from their homes and forced to work on plantations. They were treated like animals and had no freedom. It’s a dark part of history, but it’s important to understand so we don’t repeat it.      But why would people do that? I mean, it’s not fair to treat someone like that.      It was a combination of greed and ignorance. Some people believed that people with darker skin were less human, so they thought it was okay to treat them badly. But that belief was wrong, and we now know that everyone deserves to be treated with respect.      So why didn’t they just stop it?      That’s a good question. It took a long time for people to realize how wrong it was. People started to fight for freedom and equality, and that led to the Civil Rights Movement. It was a long struggle, but eventually, the system was abolished.      Do you think people still treat others badly today?      Sometimes, yes. There are still people who discriminate based on race, gender, or other differences. But we’re learning, and we’re trying to do better. That’s why it’s so important to talk about these things and teach our children the right values.      So we should fight for fairness?      Exactly. And that’s why we’re all here, talking about it. The past helps us understand the present, and it gives us the strength to make the future better for everyone.      I like that. So we can be kind to everyone, no matter who they are?      That’s the best part of all. Kindness and fairness make the world a better place. And that’s what we should always remember.      We will. I promise.      Good. Let’s keep learning and growing together.

I just watched this new show on BBC iPlayer last night, and I have to say, it’s absolutely brilliant. It’s about a group of friends who start a podcast about their lives, but it turns out there's some dark secrets hiding beneath the surface. Oh, really? I’ve been meaning to check that out. I’ve heard a lot about it on social media. I think it's called  The Quiet Life ? Something like that. No, no, it's  The Second Season . I’ve been telling everyone about it. It’s so gripping, and the dialogue is just... perfect. It feels so real. I can’t get enough of it. That sounds like the type of show I’d enjoy. I’ve got a bit of a soft spot for drama, especially if it’s heartfelt and emotionally driven. I’m always looking for something that makes me feel something. I tend to watch more comedies these days. Life’s been a bit heavy lately. But I do enjoy a good plot twist now and then. I watched that  Ted Bundy  series the other day, and it was really intense. Ted Bundy? That’s a real eye-opener. I read a book about him a while back, and it got me thinking about how some people can be so charming on the surface, but really have a dark side. It’s kind of horrifying. That’s what I love about true crime shows — they make you question what someone might be hiding. Although, I have to say, I’ve started to avoid a lot of it recently. It’s just too much for my peace of mind. I can understand that. I do enjoy the suspense though. It’s like the show we were talking about earlier — it keeps you guessing and makes you care about the characters. I think it’s a reminder that we’re all just people with complicated lives. Exactly. I think that’s what makes them so compelling. It’s not just about the crime or the secrets — it’s about the people behind it. It makes you reflect on your own life, doesn’t it? It does, in a way. I mean, you think about the people you know, and the ones you’ve never met. You never know what someone’s going through. That’s the beauty of it. And it’s all the more reason to stay curious and keep an open mind about people.

So, I was just telling the kids about George Stephenson—the man who built the first real steam engine. You know, the one that actually moved trains? I think it was called the “Rocket” or something like that.      Is that the one that ran the Liverpool and Manchester Railway?      Exactly! That's the one. It was a big deal in the 1830s. The whole idea of having steam-powered trains pulling carriages—it was revolutionary. I mean, imagine going from one city to another in a few hours instead of days. It changed everything.      Yeah, I’ve heard about that. My dad used to talk about how his grandparents used to take the train to work. It was the main way people traveled then.      That's right, and Stephenson was the engineer behind it all. He was from a humble background, I believe. A blacksmith, maybe?      Wasn’t he? I think he started off as a coal miner or something, then got into engineering. It's pretty impressive that he became such an important figure.      Oh, absolutely. He was kind of a workhorse. He didn’t just build the locomotive—he designed tracks, stations, even the way the trains were powered. It was a lot of work for one man.      Wait, so what’s the deal with Harry Potter? I remember you talking about it last week. Is it like a real thing or just a story?      It’s a story, but it’s so popular, people make it sound like it's real. I mean, it's just books and movies, but it’s a big part of pop culture now. I think it started in the 90s, right?      Yeah, and it’s been around for a while. I have a friend who acts like he's a wizard. He used to say he could do spells. I told him, “You’re not even a real wizard, you’re just a kid who loves magic.”      That’s the kind of thing. Kids love the idea of being wizards or having magical powers. It's a great escape from reality.      I like it. I think I want to be a wizard when I grow up. Maybe I can ride a broomstick and do spells.      Well, if you do, make sure you wear a cloak and a hat. That’s how they all do it. And don’t forget about the wand.

Alright, I’m just finishing up the beans. I think we’re ready to eat. Should we start with the chips or the salad? I think the salad first. But I’ve had some work problems lately. I’m in the middle of a project, and it’s been so stressful.

I just had the most amazing lunch today. The new café in the village has this really good fish and chips. I got the traditional with mushy peas and a bit of tartar sauce. So, I've been thinking—do you ever notice how people's accents can tell you so much about where they're from? My teacher said it was all about perseverance.      And my friend Lily, she’s been really good at succeeding. She got her Bronze in swimming, even though she’s scared of the deep end.
