So, I was just telling my cousin about the gym again—the one in Doncaster. It’s been ages since I went, but I swear I still remember that guy who kept trying to sell me protein powder. He looked like he’d been through a war.      Protein powder? You mean the guy who tried to convince you that all your gym sessions were a waste unless you were drinking that neon-red stuff?      Exactly! I mean, I'm not saying it's not good for you, but the way he talked about it like it was a miracle pill… I almost bought it, just to see what would happen.      You’d have been the first person in the world to go to the gym and then end up in the hospital from a protein overdose. I remember when I started going to the gym in Lewisham—my first session, I was so nervous I almost passed out from the weights.      You’re not the only one. I think I still have the wheezing from that first time I tried the treadmill. What did you do, run for ten minutes and then hide in the changing room for an hour?      Oh, I did worse. I actually tried to do a pull-up and ended up on the floor. I still have the bruise on my wrist from that.      Well, I guess we’re both not exactly gym experts. But I have to say, I think I’d rather be working out than dealing with my ex. That’s actually what I was thinking earlier—maybe I should get back into it.      Why? What happened with your ex?      It wasn’t that bad. We just… grew apart. I mean, we were together for three years, and at the end, it felt like we were just going through the motions. I think I need to focus on myself more, you know? Like, being active, getting out more.      That makes sense. You should try joining a group class or something. I met my partner in a yoga class. It was weird at first, but now it’s one of the best things that ever happened.      Maybe you could come with me? I’ve been looking for someone to do a spin class with. Just to stop me from falling asleep on the bike.      Deal. But I’m warning you—don’t expect me to keep up with you.

So, what do you think of that pizza we had after the Domino Drive? It was proper good, wasn’t it?      Yeah, it was alright, I guess. I mean, the pizza was okay, but I’d rather have gone for a bite at the chip shop. Still, it was nice to get out and about.      Ah, you’re too picky, lad. You know what I say—pizza is pizza. And besides, the Domino Drive doesn’t come around every week, so we should make the most of it. Still, I’ll be honest, I’m not sure I’d go for a second slice. My tummy’s not what it used to be.      You’re telling me. I’ve been trying to lose a few pounds myself, but the Pizza Hut just keeps luring me in. I swear, it’s a bit like that old log that keeps sliding out of the fireplace—no matter how many times you try to put it back, it’s just gonna slide out again.      That’s one way to put it. I’ve seen that log go on and on for weeks. But I reckon it’s got more to do with the way it’s placed. I mean, if it’s not sitting right, it’s bound to come out.      You’re not wrong. I remember the time I tried to put one back and it went flying straight into the fire. That was a proper mess—looked like a firework went off in the living room.      I’d say that’s the highlight of the week. Anyway, speaking of fire, I’ve been meaning to ask you—you know that new hair cut you got? You look a bit different.      Yeah, I know. It was supposed to be a bit of a style, but the barber thought he was doing a ‘youthful’ look. I think he confused me with a bloke out of a music video.      Aye, that’s the trouble with these modern barbers. Used to be, you went in, you said, “I want a trim,” and that was it. Now they’re trying to give you a full face lift.      I suppose they’re trying to keep up with the times. But I’ll say this—no matter how much you change your hair, you’ll always be my nephew. And that’s something I’ll never forget.      Thanks, Auntie.

I just can’t get over how much I miss the pubs in Sunderland. They had this one place called The Grapes, and it was always packed with people from all walks of life. You’d hear everything from local football debates to full-on political arguments. It felt like a real community. Yeah, I remember that place, but I think it was more like a pub in Birmingham where I grew up. We had places like The King’s Head, which was always buzzing, especially on a Saturday night. But I think it’s a bit different now, don’t you? Places are more about the ambiance than the vibe. I guess that’s true. I mean, the pubs in Cambridge are lovely, but they feel more like a tourist spot than a local hangout. It’s not the same as sitting at the bar with the regulars, swapping stories over a pint. It feels too clean, almost too proper. You’re right about that. I think in places like Sunderland, you had that sense of being part of something bigger. Also, the food was always better. I mean, do you remember those Sunday roasts? They would serve everything—roast beef, Yorkshire pudding, and even a few veggie sides if you wanted to be fancy. Oh yes! And the veg – I swear, they knew how to cook greens. I don’t know why the supermarkets have such bad produce these days. I mean, I’ve been trying to grow my own veg, but it’s just not the same. I remember once I tried to cook a vegetable curry, and it turned out so bad, my nan laughed at me and said, “Back in the day, we used to throw the greens out if we didn’t like them.” That sounds like something she’d say. I’ve been trying to cook more vegetarian meals recently. I mean, it’s not like I’m a vegan, but I do enjoy the variety. I think the key is to use the right spices and not be afraid of experimenting. Do you think there’s a way to bring that Northern flair into modern cooking? Absolutely. I think it’s all about using the right ingredients and knowing how to handle them. And maybe even a bit of a dash of British stubbornness. That’s what makes the food so unique. I mean, I still can’t believe how much I miss the local celebrities too.

So, I've got a word game trick up my sleeve. If you think of a word that has three syllables and ends with 'tion', I'll tell you a joke about it. Ready?      I’m ready! What’s the word?       Education.  Alright, here’s the joke: Why did the teacher get kicked out of the classroom? Because she kept  educating  the students  education !      That was a  education  in puns! Wait, did you just say 'education' or 'education'? You’re mixing up the syllables!      I think the real issue here is that you’re playing  Articulate  with your own language! Let’s stick to the rules, shall we? You have to say the word correctly in three syllables. Or are you just trying to confuse us?      You know, I used to play this game at the charity events I used to run in Singapore. It’s a great way to get people laughing and thinking—especially when the rules are a bit fuzzy. But I still think it’s better than the one where you have to say a word with only one vowel. That was  painful .      Oh, I know that one! I’ve done that with my support group. It’s the  pain  in the neck, but it’s also a  pain  in the brain. And let’s be honest, someone always ends up saying ‘pay-nee’ instead of ‘pain’—and then the whole table bursts out laughing.      So, is the point of this game to make us all sound like we’re from the 1950s or just to keep us from talking about what we really want to talk about?      Well, it’s not just about making us sound like we’re from the 1950s. It’s about keeping the brain sharp and the laughs coming. Plus, it’s a way to remember the rules of the game, even if we end up breaking them.      That’s what I love about it—there are no real rules, just a whole bunch of rules that you can choose to go against. I think that’s why it’s so addictive. You’re always on the edge of breaking the game and making it your own.      Exactly! That’s the beauty of it. You can turn it into a game of wit and strategy, or just a game of chaos and laughter. Either way, it brings us together.      So, are we going to play another round or are we just going to keep talking about how fun this game is?

So, I think I just won! I had the king of hearts and the queen of spades. You can't beat that, can you?      Well, I don’t know about that. You might have the cards, but I’ve got the luck. I swear, I’ve seen the cards move on their own.      Please, you’re just too proud to admit you lost. I watched you shuffle like you were trying to steal the deck.      You’re all just too competitive. I’m just here to enjoy the game and the company, not to win. Though I do have a secret weapon.      Oh? What’s that?      My ability to remember every card that’s been played. I’ve been playing since I was a kid in Cardiff, you know. My mum used to play with me every weekend.      That’s impressive. I used to play with my dad, but he always cheated. I never could quite figure out how.      You didn’t, did you? He was a teacher too, right? So he must’ve had a way of hiding the cards in his pocket.      Yes, I’m sure he had a card hidden in his pocket. And I’m not sure he ever gave it back.      Okay, enough of the stories. Let’s get back to the game. I think I’ve got a good hand. I’ve been waiting for this moment all week.      Alright, let’s see. I’m going to deal this out properly this time. No more shenanigans.      And here I thought the only rule was no cheating.      No, the real rule is no talking during the game. Unless you’re trying to figure out the next move.      Then I guess I’m just here to figure out the best move. And if that means cheating, so be it.      Alright, let’s get serious. I’m going to go with the two of clubs. Anyone want to follow?      I’ll take that. But if I win, you’re all buying dinner.      Deal. But only if you actually win.      You want to bet on that? I think I just saw a king in the trash pile.      You’re all mad. But I’ll admit, it’s fun.      Yeah, it’s the chaos that makes it worth it. And besides, we’re not all here for the cards. We’re here for the memories.      That’s true. Even if we’re all trying to win, we’re all here for the same reason.

Hey, did you see the latest episode of  Stranger Things ? It was so intense! I couldn’t stop watching it all night.      Oh, I saw it! It was wild. I mean, they finally revealed the truth about the Upside Down, and it’s messing with the timeline. I don’t even know what’s going on anymore.      I haven’t watched it yet, but from what I’ve heard, it’s like a mix of horror and sci-fi. I was supposed to start an apprenticeship in accounting next month, but I’ve been too busy studying for my A Levels.      You’re going to be an accountant? My cousin works in finance, and she said it’s a stable job. I’m actually still working on my degree in engineering, but I’ve been thinking about switching to something more practical.      Wait, you’re still in university? I thought you were done last year. You didn’t say anything about it.      I did, but it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I’m doing a dual degree in engineering and computer science, and it’s been a lot. I’m also helping out at my uncle’s company, which is why I’m still in school.      That’s amazing. I’ve been working part-time as a care support worker since I was 16. It’s not the easiest job, but I love helping people. I’ve been thinking about going to university for social work, but I’m not sure if I can afford it.      I know, it’s so expensive. I’m actually applying to a few universities next year. I’m pretty sure I’m going to study architecture. My sister is an architect, and she’s been helping me with the applications.      I’m applying for an apprenticeship in accounting. I’m not sure if it’s the best choice, but it’s a good way to earn money while learning. I’ve already got an offer from a local firm.      That sounds better than waiting for university. I’m thinking of doing a retail apprenticeship too. I’ve been working at the local store on weekends, and it’s not bad. I just don’t know if I’m ready to commit.      You know what’s funny? I’ve been telling people I’m going to be an engineer, but honestly, I’m considering switching to something more creative.

So, I was walking down the High Street the other day, and I saw this group of cyclists zooming by like they were in a race. I thought, “Oh, what a bunch of madmen!”      I can imagine. I tried cycling to work once, but it felt like I was being chased by a bus. I ended up walking most of the way because I was too scared of getting hit.      Yeah, I’ve had the same experience. I tried to cycle to the shops last week, and a car almost sideswiped me. I’ve been stuck with the idea that driving is safer ever since.      I know what you mean. I used to drive everywhere, but these days, I just walk. It’s not that I’m old, it’s just that I don’t want to risk getting into an accident.      You’re not that old, though. I mean, you’re still in your sixties—personally, I’d be happy to be cycling around by then.      Oh, I know, but I’m not the adventurous type. I remember when I was younger, I used to drive everywhere, and I thought I was the best driver in the world. Now I just stick to the pavement.      You know, I used to drive when I was younger too. It was my job, actually. I was a delivery driver for a while, and I used to enjoy it. But after a few close calls, I just stopped.      That’s scary. I’ve always been pretty good at driving, but I’m not sure I’d want to be in that position.      I know what you mean. I remember when I was younger, I was always rushing to get somewhere, and I never thought about the dangers. But now, I just take my time. It’s not about being late—it’s about being safe.      I guess that’s the thing, isn’t it? We all have to find our own way of getting around. Some people love driving, others prefer cycling, and then there are those of us who just walk.      Yeah, and it’s amazing how different people approach things. It’s just a matter of what works for you.      To walking safely, cycling wisely, and driving carefully.      And to never giving up on the things we love, even if they’re a little risky.      And to surviving all of it.      That’s the spirit.

So, I heard you’re from Lincoln? That’s in the East Midlands, right? I’m from Aylesbury, so I’m pretty familiar with the region. I’ve actually been to Lincoln a few times for work—mostly for conferences and meetings.      Oh, really? I’ve never been to Lincoln, but I’ve heard it’s got a lot of history. I’m actually from Lincoln too—though I grew up in the suburbs. My parents moved there when I was a kid. It’s a small place, but it’s got a nice vibe.      Interesting. I’ve never been to Lincoln, but I’ve spent a lot of time in the Midlands, mostly around Shropshire where I was born. I did my PhD in linguistics, and I’ve always been fascinated by dialects. It’s amazing how regional accents can vary so much within the same country.      Yeah, I agree. I’ve noticed that even within England, there’s a huge variation in dialects. I’m from the South-East, so I speak pretty standard English, but I’ve been to the North and noticed such a difference in pronunciation and vocabulary. It’s like a different language in some ways!      I’ve always found that fascinating too. I think it’s part of what makes England such a rich place culturally. I actually worked on a project a while back that looked at regional variations in speech. It was really eye-opening. There’s a lot of overlap, but also distinct differences.      Yes, and it’s not just about accents. There are differences in vocabulary and even grammar. For example, in the West Country, people tend to use different terms for things compared to people in London. I’ve always thought that studying language variation can tell us a lot about the history and social dynamics of a region.      That’s a great point. I do a lot of language research as part of my job, and I’ve seen how dialects can be a marker of identity. I think it’s something that people often underestimate. You can tell a lot about someone’s background just from the way they speak.      I think that’s true. I’ve lived in London for most of my life, so I’ve picked up a lot of the city’s slang and speech patterns. It’s definitely different from the way I spoke in Lincoln.

I can't believe it's been two years since we last saw each other. It feels like it's been forever. How's everyone doing? It's been way too long, honestly. I miss everyone, especially the kids. I can't believe we've got to this point. I mean, we've had this coffee machine for years, and now it's finally giving up the ghost. Yeah, and now with the removal costs for the old one and the new one, it’s like we're paying for two machines. I don't even know if we should get another one at all. I was thinking maybe we could store the old one and just get a smaller, cheaper model. But I’m not sure if the kids would even want it now. They’re always rushing out the door. That’s true. You know, I used to think we were in a better place. I mean, we've got the right to demand better, but I feel like we're stuck in this cycle where no one really listens. I know. It’d be nice to see some more life in there. That sounds like a good idea. I can help you paint one up if you want. I've got some leftover paint from the house. Oh, and I made a fruitcake with some dried fruit and nuts. It's quite different from the usual ones. I used some dried cherries instead of currants. That sounds interesting. But it's not like we're old enough to be worrying about that, are we?

So, I've been meaning to ask you, how do you say "one, two, three" in Turkish? I've been trying to learn a bit of the language for the summer, just in case I need to order something or ask for directions.      Oh, that’s a good idea. I’ve been practicing with my granddaughter. She’s been fascinated by the language. Let me think... One is "bir," two is "iki," and three is "üç." But I think it’s "üç" with a soft "ü" sound, like the "u" in "cup."      Thanks, that’s helpful. I’d hate to make a mistake and confuse the waiter. You know, I remember when I first came to Cyprus, I ordered "salam" and thought it was a type of cheese. Turns out it’s just a greeting.      Oh, I remember that story! You were at the restaurant in Limassol, weren’t you? I told the waiter, “Please, give me a salad,” and he said, “Salam, baba,” and I thought he was rude. But then I realized it was just a greeting.      Yes, that was the one. I was so embarrassed. But at least I got a good laugh out of it. Speaking of which, did you hear about Mrs. Thompson at the café down the road? She’s been acting strangely lately.      No, I haven’t. What’s going on?      Well, she’s been talking about being able to see spirits. I don’t know if it’s a fluke or if she’s finally gone mad. She said she’s been practicing dowsing and believes she can see her late husband.      That’s interesting. My sister-in-law used to believe in shamanism. She said she could talk to the spirits of her ancestors. But I think it was just a way to cope with the loss of her father.      I suppose it’s all about how you interpret things. But I do wonder if the recent deaths in our circle have made people more interested in spirituality.      Maybe. I’ve been thinking about how fate works lately. You know, I’ve had this feeling that everything happens for a reason. But then again, I’ve been wearing my hearing aids more and more, and I’m not sure if it’s the aids or just the way I see the world now.      Hearing aids can change everything. I’ve found they help a lot, especially in noisy places like restaurants.

So, I've been thinking about the house a lot lately. I know it's not the most modern, but I feel like we could do a few things to make it feel more like  our  place. Maybe we could redo the kitchen? I’ll help you with the candles. I’ve got some materials at home. I could even make some bookmarks as well. You know, they always appreciated thoughtful gifts.      That’s the spirit. I think we should also try to plan a family gathering this Christmas. It's been a while since we've all been together properly. I’d love to have the whole family over for a roast dinner and some games.

Alright, so I just saw this article about catfish and Jeremy Kyle. I was like, "What? That’s got to be some kind of mix-up!" Yeah, I saw that too. I was wondering if it was a real thing or just some prank. I mean, Jeremy Kyle is a TV show, right? Oh yeah, he’s that daytime chat show with all the drama. But I think “catfish” is a term from online stuff, like when people pretend to be someone else on social media. Exactly! So the article was saying that some people were using catfishing tactics on Jeremy Kyle’s show. That’s wild. I mean, how do you even do that? You can’t really fake being someone else on TV! It’s got to be a mix-up. I mean, Jeremy Kyle is known for drama, but catfish is more like an online thing. Still, it’s funny how people can conflate the two. I wonder if the article was trying to say something deeper. Like, maybe people are using catfishing tactics in real life, not just online? That’d be concerning. Yeah, there’s a lot about people being fake these days. I mean, it’s everywhere. You can’t trust anyone anymore, can you? I know, it’s kind of scary. But I think it’s more about people being too insecure or desperate to be someone else. It’s like a modern version of identity crisis. Maybe. But I still think the article was just a bit of a joke. Although, if it’s a real thing, that’s a whole different story. Let’s hope it’s just a mix-up. I’d go mad if I had to deal with catfish on a TV show. I mean, what do they even do? I don’t know, but I’d have to watch it to find out. Maybe it’s a new show, or maybe they’re just making it up for clicks.

So, I was thinking, do you remember when we first came to London? It was like, what, five years ago? I remember you getting lost on the Tube, and then we ended up in a little café in Southwark. You said you wanted to make a life here, and now look at us—living in the same flat, cooking lunch every day like it’s a ritual. Oh, I remember that very well. I was so nervous, wasn’t I? I thought I’d never survive in this city. But then I met you, and somehow, it all worked out. You know, I still think about Vienna sometimes. That’s where I grew up, you know. I used to dream about Paris, just like I do now. You ever think about going back? Honestly? I have. I mean, I love London, but sometimes I feel like I’ve lost a bit of the language. You know, the way I used to speak German, or even Italian, like I was still living in those places. I’ve been thinking about going to Italy again. Maybe to Venice. I’ve got a friend who’s a classics scholar—she’s got a little villa there. That sounds lovely. I’ve always thought Venice is magical. Though I’m not sure I’d ever go back to Austria. I mean, I left for good, and I never looked back. But I still remember the way the language felt—like it was part of the air. You know, I used to speak three languages growing up: German, Italian, and English. That’s amazing. I’m only just starting to understand a little German. My sister is studying it at university. She says it’s harder than French because of the grammar. But I keep trying. I even started using a language app. It’s kind of funny. Language apps? I remember when I was a student, we had to learn Latin. That was real learning. Do you ever miss that kind of challenge? I guess. Sometimes I wonder what I’d go back to university for if I didn’t have to work. But I think I’d go back just to be around the kind of people who make you think. You know, like you. I mean, you’re like a walking library. Well, I was a Classics student once. And I still think about ancient Rome and the way the world used to work.

I can't believe we've got another 40 minutes of this. I was just trying to take a nap, and now I'm stuck in traffic again because someone decided to reverse into the car in front of us. I don’t know how people even do that without being frightened half to death. I saw that! That was absolutely reckless. I've had enough of people driving like they're on a dare. I remember when I was younger, I used to drive like that too. Now, I just want to get to my destination safely, even if it takes me longer. You know what’s even worse? When you're stuck in a car with people who are talking about dangerous driving. It's like everyone's a critic, but no one's actually got the skills to back it up. Oh, come on, you know the rules. Everyone knows you shouldn’t do that. It’s dangerous, and it’s just so disrespectful. I can't believe there aren’t more consequences for this kind of behavior. I think the problem is that people don’t learn from the past. I had a friend who used to do that, and he got into a serious accident. It took him months to recover, and he’s still not back to full health. That’s why I’m so careful now. I still think it's important to take your time and not rush. I mean, if you're trying to get somewhere, you don’t have to do it in a dangerous way. There are always other ways to get there. I agree. I think the biggest issue is that people don’t respect the road. I mean, I had to get an MOT last week, and I was told there were a few things wrong with the car. I had to pay a solicitor to make sure it wasn’t my fault. It was a huge hassle. That sounds complicated. I’ve always been lucky with my car, but I know it can be a pain if you don’t take it seriously. I tried using a Sat Nav once, but it sent me into a bad town. I’ve never been back. I’ve heard of that. Some towns are just terrible for people who don’t know the way around. I remember once I had to get to a relative’s house, and I got lost for hours.

I've been thinking a lot lately, you know. I've had a few days to myself, and it's just got me feeling a bit nostalgic. Remember when we used to walk down by the old mill in Costessey? Now, I don’t know what I’m going to do with all this free time. I suppose I could try gardening more, but I haven’t got the energy for it. You know, I was thinking the same thing. Maybe we could start a little garden together? I still have some seeds from last year, and I’ve been meaning to plant some tomatoes. It’s a shame we haven’t done it yet. That sounds like a plan. Oh, you did a great job, you know. I remember when you used to tell us those stories in the classroom. They always made the kids laugh. You had a real gift for storytelling. Yeah, I used to enjoy that. It’s strange how something like that can be forgotten so quickly. I suppose I just need to find a new way to use my time. Maybe I can help out with the local community garden or something like that. That’s a good idea. I know there’s a group that’s been trying to get more volunteers. They’ve been working on a community initiative to help the elderly. I think it could be a good way to stay active and meet people. I like the sound of that. I’ve been feeling a bit isolated lately. It’s hard when you don’t have a routine. I suppose I could start going to some of the local meetings. Maybe I’ll even meet some new people.

I just got a new record from a local indie label. It’s got this really raw, gritty sound that reminds me of the old days when music was all about feeling and passion, not just polished production. I think it’s a real gem. That sounds interesting. I’ve been meaning to check out more local artists. I’ve been so wrapped up in my PhD work that I haven’t had much time to listen to new music. But I do miss the days when I used to go to gigs every weekend. You should come to the next one I’m going to. It’s at the old warehouse on the edge of town. The vibe is always great, and the people are really into it. You’ll probably meet some interesting folks. Yeah, I’d love that. I’ve been feeling a bit disconnected from the music scene lately. It’s strange how being in a PhD program can make you lose touch with the everyday things you used to enjoy. I get that. It’s like, you’re so focused on your work that you forget to take a step back and enjoy the little things. Speaking of which, have you been keeping up with your friends from university? Honestly, not as much as I’d like. Life has been pretty chaotic lately. But I did see Jen last weekend at the market. She’s been gardening a lot, and she’s actually got quite the green thumb now. That’s great! I’ve been meaning to start my own little garden in the back yard. I’ve read a few books on it, but I’m still figuring out the best way to get started. It’s one of those things I’ve always wanted to do but never had the time. You should do it. It’s a great way to unwind and connect with nature. I’ve been trying to grow some herbs, and it’s been a real joy. Plus, the fresh herbs make such a difference in cooking. Definitely. I’ve been thinking about how the weather has been lately. It’s been so unpredictable, isn’t it? One day it’s sunny and warm, and the next it’s raining all day. Yeah, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I think the climate is changing more than we ever imagined.

I just got a message from my colleague, and it’s about that job they had to cut because of the funding crisis. You know, they had to let go of three people, including someone who was really good at their job. No way, that’s rough. I can’t believe it. I mean, I know the university’s been struggling, but that’s still people’s livelihoods on the line. I’ve been thinking about this a lot since I started my PhD. You know, the fees, the pressure to get a job, the stress of not knowing if you’ll even be able to afford your living costs after you finish. Yeah, I get that. I’ve been thinking about it too. It’s not just about the money, though—it’s the uncertainty. I mean, I was lucky enough to get into a good research manager role straight after my postgrad, but not everyone is as fortunate. I still remember when I was in uni, worrying about whether I’d even be able to afford to live in Sunderland, let alone go to university in the first place. I know, and I think that’s why I’ve been thinking about doing a part-time job while I’m studying. It’s not ideal, but at least it gives me a little bit of financial security. Plus, I’ve been thinking of doing some freelance work in my field, just to keep my skills sharp and see if there are any opportunities out there. That’s smart. I’d say the same thing. I mean, I also did some freelance stuff after uni, just to keep my foot in the door. It’s not glamorous, but it helped me get my first job. I guess it’s all about trying to balance things out. Exactly. And I’m not saying it’s easy, but you have to keep your options open. Speaking of which, have you seen the new West End musical coming up? I was talking to my sister about it last week. She’s been trying to get tickets for months. It’s about the lives of people working in the arts, sort of like the real-life struggles we’re all going through. Oh, I heard about that! I’m not sure if I can afford it, but I’d love to go. It’s funny, isn’t it?

Hey, do you think this book would be good for the kids? I mean, it’s about family trees and stories, right? Yeah, it’s pretty cute. I think it could be a great way to start talking about our family history with the kids. It’s got those little pictures, which are always a hit with them. I like that. I was thinking, maybe we could add some of our own family photos too. You know, like the ones from when we were kids. It might make the book feel more personal. That’s a good idea. I’m not sure about that. I think my son might get confused. But I can help. I know that my ex-husband and I had a pretty complicated relationship, so maybe we can talk about that too. Yes, it’s important to be honest. I think it’s better to tell the kids the truth, even if it’s hard. They’ll understand eventually. Also, we can talk about how different people have different family styles. Some have two parents, some have step-parents, some are single parents. Yeah, I guess that’s part of what makes our family so different. I mean, we all have our own stories, and it’s nice to share them. It might help the kids see that families can be different, and that’s okay. I agree. I think the book can be a starting point, but our stories are just as important. We can always add more as the kids get older.

Right, I can't believe I forgot to shave this morning. I was running late and just grabbed the razor, thinking I'd be fine. But I ended up looking like a Victorian gentleman with a beard. I even bought a new razor — the one with the really sharp blades. I’m sure it’s a  very  sharp razor. But I still can’t get over the fact that I’m doing this to myself.

So, do you remember when we were kids and we used to play that alphabet game where you had to say a word starting with each letter? It was so much fun. How’s your research going? It’s going well, honestly. I’ve been working with a team on a project about human behavior in social contexts. It’s pretty complex, but I love it. And you know, talking about that, I’ve been thinking a lot about the issues in football. I mean, the racism and the violence. It’s a real problem, isn’t it? It is. I’ve been following some of the discussions about it. It’s sad to see that even in 2025, people still face racism just because of the color of their skin or where they’re from.

I've been thinking a lot about the old mill in Wotton. I need to get some solid advice before I even start the proposal. I know you've worked on a few similar projects, so I’d really value your input. Oh, I'd be happy to help. We've had some interesting challenges with the medieval cottages in the village. But first, what exactly are you planning to do with the mill? A full restoration or just a partial renovation? It's a bit of both. The structure is sound, but the internal systems are in dire need of updating. I was thinking of converting the upper floors into luxury apartments and keeping the lower floor as a community space. But I'm not sure about the best approach for funding. That’s a clever blend of preservation and modern use. I’d recommend looking into the Heritage Lottery Fund. They’re always looking for projects that blend historical significance with community benefit. Have you considered applying for a grant? Not yet, but I’ve heard mixed things about the application process. I’m worried about the competition and the need for a detailed business plan. Do you have any tips on how to make the proposal stand out? Definitely. Start by clearly outlining the historical value of the site and its potential impact on the local area. You should also include a detailed timeline, cost breakdown, and a long-term maintenance plan. Oh, and don’t forget to highlight the community involvement aspect—people love that. That makes sense. I also need to think about the bidding process. Are there any particular pitfalls to avoid when working with local authorities? Be prepared for their scrutiny. They’ll want to see that you’re not just about profit but about responsible stewardship of the heritage. Also, make sure your plans align with local conservation guidelines. I know it can be tricky, but it’s worth the effort. I appreciate the advice. I was also thinking about using some traditional materials. Do you think that would be a good idea, or would it be better to go for modern ones that are more sustainable? That’s a good question. Traditional materials can add a lot of authenticity, but they also come with higher costs and maintenance. You might want to strike a balance—use traditional finishes where possible, but opt for more modern, durable materials in areas that require frequent upkeep, like the roof or plumbing.

I just poured the water into the kettle. You want a cup of tea? Yes, please. I’m feeling a bit sluggish after that long meeting with my supervisor. You’re not the only one. I’ve been up since six, trying to get some research done before the team meeting. You’re doing the heavy lifting again, aren’t you? I’ve been stuck in the library for the past three days, trying to source some data for my thesis. It’s the price of being a research manager, I suppose. You know, I often think about how much I’ve changed since I was a PhD student. Yeah, I remember you being pretty obsessed with linguistic patterns back then. You used to talk about dialects like they were your favorite pastime. I still do, but now I’m looking at it from a more practical angle. Like, how do these dialects affect communication in different contexts? That’s interesting. I’ve been reading about sociolinguistic variation and how people use language to mark identity. It’s fascinating how something as simple as a word choice can tell you so much. Exactly! I remember when I was doing my postgrad work, I studied the differences in speech patterns between people from the North East and the Midlands. It was such a contrast. I think that’s why I’m drawn to dialects. They’re like little cultural fingerprints. You can tell a lot about a person just by the way they speak. It’s amazing how much being from a certain place shapes the way you communicate. I still have a slight Northern accent, even though I’ve been living in Cambridge for years. I can hear it. You still use a lot of “’ere” and “’ow’s” instead of the standard “here” and “how’s.” It’s endearing, really. I know, I tried to change it when I started working in the city, but it just came back. It’s like trying to unlearn a habit. It’s not a bad habit, though. It adds character. I think I’ve been trying to get rid of my Birmingham accent, but it’s stuck too. You know, I’ve been thinking about taking a break from work and going on a holiday. Maybe to the Scottish Highlands? I’d love to hear how people speak there. That sounds perfect. I’ve been meaning to go somewhere like that.

I just got a call from the school about the tennis tournament. They mentioned they need parents to help with the catering for the event. I’m not sure how much that’ll cost, though. I just can’t get over that film we saw last night. It was so intense, wasn’t it? That scene where the protagonist confronted the antagonist—unreal, but I couldn’t look away. I know, it really got under my skin. But you know, I think it was also a bit of a commentary on how we teach history. I was sitting there thinking about that debate in Cambridge the other week. They were arguing whether history should be more about narrative or facts. Oh, that debate. I remember hearing about it. It's fascinating, isn't it? I think the key is balance. You can't just teach dates and events; you need to tell a story that people can relate to. My son, he's in education, and he’s always saying that the national curriculum is too rigid. I agree. I remember when I was in school, we had this teacher who made history come alive. He’d bring in maps, videos, even invite local historians. It was inspiring. But now, with the national curriculum, it feels like everything is so prescriptive. Yeah, I think that's part of the problem. Especially with the push for early education. My wife, she’s in teaching, and she's always talking about how students struggle with critical thinking. It's like they’re just memorizing facts, not really understanding the context. It's not just about the curriculum, though. I think the universities are part of the issue too. They've become so focused on grades and assessments that students aren’t given the chance to explore their interests. I had a degree in marketing, and I didn’t even know what I wanted to do when I started. But I did some internships while I was studying, and that really helped me figure it out. That’s true. I think combining academic learning with real-world experience is key. I’ve been teaching for years, and I always encourage my students to think about how what they’re learning applies outside the classroom. It makes it more relevant. You know, I was thinking about that as I was watching the film. The protagonist had this entire back story that was told through flashbacks, and it really made you think about how history is told. Well, I've been thinking about the war again, you know. It's strange how time slips away, isn't it? I remember when I was a lad, serving in the war, just a boy really, thrown into it all. No one ever told us what to expect.      Oh, I remember hearing about that from my father. He was in the army too, though he didn’t talk much about it. I always felt like he had a lot to say, but he kept it buried. You know how men are.      It's amazing how different our experiences were. My father was a businessman, so he never had to fight, but he had to make tough decisions. I still remember the war being a big deal in the news back then, but I never felt the same way about it as you did, John.      Not the same, no. I was at the front, saw things that no one should see. And the way people talk now, it’s like they don’t even remember. They talk about it like it’s just some distant story, not a real part of our lives.      I think it’s more about how we live now. We have so many distractions, so much to do. Back then, it was all about survival, and now it's about making the best of what we have. But I do agree, the war was a big part of our generation.      It was. And also, the way people lived before. I remember when we were kids, our parents used to talk about the old days. They'd say things like, “Back in my day, we had to work harder,” or “We had less, but we were happier.” It’s funny how that idea still lingers.      It does, doesn’t it? My mum always said we had to be grateful for what we had, even if it wasn’t much. I used to think she was just trying to make us feel better, but now I see what she meant.      And speaking of the old days, I was just looking at the furniture in the living room. It’s all so much older than I expected. I can almost imagine my grandfather sitting there, telling stories about his youth.      That’s a beautiful thought. I can almost picture it. It’s like the furniture holds memories, doesn’t it?      Yes, and the weather’s been so kind lately.

I can't believe it's the last time we're driving from Mum’s to Dad’s. It feels like just yesterday we were kids, running around the garden like mad things. Yeah, remember when we used to argue over who got to sit in the front seat? You always wanted to be in the front, and I’d try to convince you it was safer in the back. Oh, you were such a drama queen back then. I still remember that time you got stuck in the back because you were too busy trying to teach me how to drive. You even told me I was being reckless. That was  not  me. I was just trying to look out for you. You were still a kid, and I didn’t want to see you get hurt. Besides, I was the one who ended up getting stuck in the back when you tried to take the wheel. Ha! You were practically glued to the seat. I swear, if you hadn’t stopped the car, we might have ended up in a ditch somewhere. Let’s not talk about that. We’ve got more important things to discuss. I need to talk about the mortgage. Did you get the final deal with the bank? Yeah, it’s all set. I had to sign a bunch of forms, but it’s all good. I even got a better rate than I expected. We’re going to be okay, I think. That’s great to hear. I just hope the house doesn’t fall apart on us. I had a bad dream last night about the roof caving in. Hey, you’re still living in the same house as me, right? I mean, unless you want to move in with me, we could sort something out. No, no, I like my own space. But I do miss the old days. Remember when we used to cook for the whole family? I used to make this amazing lasagna that would last for days. You always made it too much. I still remember the time we had to throw out half of it because it was just too heavy. It was one of the worst meals ever, but it was  your  lasagna. Yeah, go on. You’re still bitter about that. I’m just saying, it was  your  lasagna, not mine. Fine. I’ll take that as a compliment.

I just got the list of guests for the birthday meal, and I think we need to adjust the table plan. There are more people coming than we expected, so maybe we should split into two tables instead of one long one. Yeah, that makes sense. We can't have everyone squeezed around one table. Do you have a rough idea of how many people that would be? Let me check. There's my sister, her partner, their two kids, my brother, his wife, and their two teenagers. Then there's the aunt, uncle, cousin, and the neighbor who's been helping out with the house. That’s like 12 people. We’re definitely going to need two tables. Okay, so I’ll make a new plan. I’ll start by splitting the guests between the two tables, making sure the older folks are seated together and the kids are at a table with some snacks. What do you think about the menu choices so far? I’ve been thinking about the Great British Bake Off for the dessert. Maybe we could have a themed menu with one of the shows’ signature dishes. Like, maybe I can make a Victoria sponge as it’s a classic. For the main course, I was thinking of fish and chips. We can buy fresh fish from the local market – do you have any ideas on where? There’s a fishmonger on the High Street that’s been recommended by a few people. I can check that out. Also, I was wondering about the candles for the birthday cake. Should we use traditional ones or maybe some LED ones so it’s easier to see in the dark? LED ones would be better, especially since we’re rearranging the cupboard space. I’ve been trying to clear out some old items to make room for new ones. Maybe I can use the extra space for the candles and the cake stand. That sounds like a good plan. And while we’re talking about rearranging, do you think it’s a good idea to move the photographs to another shelf? I’ve been feeling a bit overwhelmed with the dementia diagnosis, and being surrounded by old memories is a bit heavy sometimes. I completely understand. I think it’s a good idea to make the space feel fresh and welcoming. We can keep some of the photos in a box or on a separate table just in case.

I swear, I’m going to go through a mental breakdown before I get my wisdom teeth out. I’ve been reading up on it, and it’s like they’re telling me I’ll be in pain for weeks and that it’s gonna be a nightmare. What’s your take on it, L? I know, I know, I’ve been there. But honestly, it’s not as bad as it sounds. I had mine done last year, and it was a bit of a mess, but I survived. You just have to make sure you’re at the right clinic and that the dentist is experienced. You don’t want to end up with some weird hole in your mouth, like the one I had that kept getting infected. Oh no, you had a hole? That’s not good. I was just thinking about my parents, and I was like, “I can’t believe I’m going through this. Why do I have to go through this?” I mean, I’m not even sure if I ever needed them in the first place. I’ve never even thought about them, and now I’m stuck with this plan. I get it. You’re not the only one. I remember when I was going back to uni last year—it was the same. I was like, “I can’t believe I’m back here, I’m not even sure why I came.” But then the moment I saw my old room, everything clicked. You know what I mean? Yeah, exactly. I just don’t know if I’m ready. I was thinking about moving house too. I’m so tired of the flat I’m in now. It’s got holes in the walls, and the balcony’s falling apart. I mean, I’m not even sure if the landlords are even watching this place. Oh, you are not alone. I’ve been thinking about moving too. I just don’t know where to start. I mean, I’m supposed to be going back to uni, but the whole moving process is giving me a headache. I tried to find a place online, but all the ones that look decent are overpriced or in the middle of nowhere. I know, it’s so frustrating. I’m just hoping that once I get my wisdom teeth out, I’ll feel like I can finally focus on moving and getting my life back on track.

Okay, so I was thinking about the Chinese New Year. I’ve been meaning to do something special for the kids, you know, like a little celebration at home. Maybe a few crafts or something we can all do together. What do you think?      That sounds fun! I love Chinese New Year. I remember last year we made little red envelope cards and gave them to the neighbors. It felt really good to do something kind. What kind of activities do you have in mind?      I like that idea! I think making the red envelopes was cool. But I also heard that some people give out little gifts or do random acts of kindness. What’s a good way to do that without spending too much?      Well, one thing I thought of was using the old chess and draughts pieces we have. They’re all in a box, and I was thinking we could sell them online or at a local market. You know, repurpose them as little tokens or even as decorative items. It’s a bit of a creative way to make money, and it’s also a way to give something back to the community.      That’s a great idea! I like that it’s not just about spending money but actually creating something from what we already have. Maybe we could make little kits with the pieces and some cards explaining their history. People might like that.      Yeah, and then we could donate the money we make to a local food bank or something. That would be a real act of kindness. I think we should do that.      Exactly. I think it’s a way to combine education with kindness. Plus, it gives the kids a sense of purpose. I was also talking to my sister about making lactose-free cakes and cookies. I know that not everyone can have dairy, so maybe we can make some special treats for people with dietary restrictions. It would be a nice way to spread some joy.      That sounds amazing! I’ve always loved baking, and I think I could help out with that. What about using some of the leftover ingredients from the lunches we have? That way, we’re not wasting anything.      I love that! Maybe we can even go to the local market and help set up a little stall. I bet the kids would love that.

I just got a new phone, and I'm so excited! I was looking online for a new case, and I found this one with a giant cartoon rabbit on it. I thought it was so cute, but then I realized it was from  Alice in Wonderland . I mean, I love that book, but I guess I'm kind of over the whole story now. Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve read  Alice in Wonderland  so many times, it’s almost like a second language to me. I remember when I was your age, I used to chase the white rabbit around the house every day. I even wore a tiny dress and a little hat, like Alice. You were only six then, and you were obsessed with the idea of falling down a rabbit hole. I still think about that! I used to imagine I was in the story all the time. I’d lie on the floor and pretend I was falling through the ceiling. Mom, did you ever read it to me? Every night! You’d fall asleep in the middle of the story, and I’d have to read it again the next night. I still have that old copy of the book with your name in it, by the way. It’s on the shelf in the living room, right next to the photo of us at the theatre last year. Yeah, I remember that trip! We saw  Alice in Wonderland  on stage. I loved the costumes—especially the Cheshire Cat. I even got a seagull costume for Christmas that year. I tried to mimic the way it moved, but I just ended up tripping over my own feet. That’s your story, sweetie. I still remember the time you tried to chase a real seagull with your toy. You ran all the way to the beach and got covered in sand. Your face looked like a raccoon. I still have that scar on my knee from that day. Mom, do you remember? You said it was a badge of honor. Of course I remember. You had a  huge  scar, and you wore it with pride. I think it’s one of the few things you’ve ever been proud of. Well, it’s still there. I even got a matching scar on my arm from that time I fell off the bike. I was trying to go faster than the other kids, and I didn’t see the pothole.

Well, I've been thinking about the protest group in our area again. They’re fighting against the wind turbine plans, and it's all getting pretty heated. I remember last night when I gave advice to a similar group in another village. They were up against solar panels, and it was a tough battle.      Yeah, I was part of that too. It's all about making sure the local community is heard, but the council seems too biased towards big energy companies. The planning appeal process is like a maze. You have to present evidence, but the timeline is so short. It's hard to get everything together in time.      Exactly. I’ve been reading up on the funding issues. It seems like the government gives a lot of money for subsidies to energy companies, but not nearly enough for research into alternatives. If we’re going to make a real change, we need better storage solutions. Without that, wind and solar just can’t be reliable enough.      That's a good point. I was talking to a few friends last week about how technical innovation is the key. If we can figure out a way to store energy efficiently, then maybe we don’t need as many turbines or panels in the first place. But the problem is, the government isn’t investing enough in that kind of research.      It’s also the politics of it all. The local planners are under pressure from the energy companies, and the council isn't exactly impartial. They want to keep things running as they are. The protest groups have to be strategic. It’s not just about shouting at the council; you need data, you need community support, and you need a plan.      And the Scottish referendum is coming up in two weeks. I wonder if that will influence the local campaign. There's a lot of talk about energy independence, and if the Scottish vote goes one way, it might put pressure on the UK government to rethink its approach.      I can see how it could. The people in Scotland are pushing for more renewable energy and less reliance on foreign oil. If they succeed, it might inspire more local groups to take a stand. But it's not just about the referendum—it's about the long-term vision for energy in this country.      And that's the challenge.

I've been thinking, love, about when you're going to get your licence. You've been asking about it for ages now. I reckon it's about time you started learning. Yeah, Dad, I know. I've had my eyes on a car for a while now. Just haven't had the time to sort out the insurance and all that. But I reckon I'm ready. You should be, dear. I remember when I first got my licence. It was a bit scary, but once you get the hang of it, it's not so bad. I still remember the first time I drove to Woburn. It was a bit of a journey, but I made it. My, yes. You had to take the long way round back then. I used to drive you to school, and I remember every single turn. But I suppose times have changed. Now you can do all that with a sat nav. I suppose so. But I'm not too keen on relying on them too much. I like the old-fashioned way of knowing where I'm going. That's good. I think it's better to know where you're going. It gives you more confidence. But I must say, I'd love to see you behind the wheel. You're such a responsible person. I know, and that’s why I think you're ready. Just make sure you take the time to practice. And don't forget, you'll need car insurance. We can get that sorted when you decide. I was thinking about that. I’d like to go for a comprehensive policy. But I’m not sure if that’s the best option. I’ve heard about third-party only being cheaper. Oh, I’d advise you to go for comprehensive. You never know what might happen. I had a flat tyre once, and it cost me a fortune to get it fixed. You might as well be safe and have the extra cover. Exactly. And once you have your licence, you can start planning your holidays. I know you've been talking about a trip to Cornwall with your friends. That would be perfect with your own car. That’s right. We’ve been saving up for it. It’s going to be a great way to relax and get some sun. I’d love to see the coast again.

So, Dad, I’ve been trying to get my phone to stop buzzing so much with those Facebook notifications. I can’t even read a book without it going off like a party horn!      You think that’s bad? I used to get phone calls all the time from people who thought they were calling me on the landline. You know, before mobiles were everywhere. I still remember the day I got my first one—it was like having a tiny radio in my pocket!      It’s wild how things have changed. I mean, even my brother’s got a smartwatch now. It tells him when to feed the cat and when to take a shower. It’s like it’s watching over him more than I do!      You’re not the only one who’s got to keep up. I’ve been trying to use the app for ordering groceries online, but it’s like speaking to a robot. You have to say the same thing three times, and it still doesn’t get it right.      Speaking of groceries, I’ve been thinking about moving to Brighton again. It’s so much fresher than Gillingham. Plus, the food scene there is amazing. I could actually cook something decent without the kids trying to steal the pasta!      Brighton? You know, I used to live in the old days. Back in the 50s, everyone just cooked from scratch. You had to buy fresh produce and make your own meals. Now, people buy ready meals and expect them to be perfect.      I guess that’s the difference between then and now. I mean, you could even cook without an oven then! I remember my mum making meat pies in a cast iron pan. It was hard work, but it tasted like real food.      Oh, I remember those days. We used to have tea and biscuits every afternoon, and it was a time of togetherness. Now people are too busy with work and screens to even sit down and have a proper meal.      Yeah, I know. It’s sad, but at least I’m not relying on food banks like some people. I mean, I’ve got a part-time job and I’m planning to go to college soon.      It’s not easy, love. But you’ve got the right attitude. I remember when I was your age, I was working at the factory, and I thought I’d never make it.

So, do you remember that time we tried to act out a Shakespeare play in front of our mates? I think it was  Romeo and Juliet , but we completely butchered it. Oh, I remember! You said “To be or not to be” like you were trying to solve a murder, and I was pretending to stab you with a pencil. It was  so  dramatic. Yeah, I think I got more attention for my dramatics than the actual play. But honestly, it was one of those moments where you’re just trying to be funny and end up being  really  awkward. And don’t even get me started on the sarcasm. You said something like, “Juliet, I’m too young to die,” and then immediately followed it up with, “But I’m not dead yet, so I’m not wrong.” It was  so  meta. I know, I know. I was trying to be clever. But you know what really sticks with me? When I tried to teach you how to play golf. I was like, “It’s all about skill, not luck,” and then I immediately hit the ball into a tree. You were like, “Yeah, skill  and  luck.” That was the most cringey moment of my life. I still remember you bragging about how you were going to “win the tournament” and then realize you couldn’t even hit the ball straight. Oh, that was  so  me. I still tell people I have a “winning attitude.” Even though I’d rather just play video games. You know what’s funny is, we both have the same surname—Smith. But you’re always trying to come up with nicknames for yourself. Like “The Great” or “The Master of Everything.” Yeah, I guess I like to think I’m someone who’s always learning. Although, honestly, I’m still trying to figure out where I got my surname from. I mean, I know it’s English, but I’m pretty sure it wasn’t chosen by me. That’s the thing with surnames, man. You don’t get to pick them. But hey, at least we can go out and get some coffee, like our  real  skill. Right, and I’ll be the one who can actually order the coffee properly. You still mess up the order every time. Well, you’re the one who said, “I’ll have a black coffee with a twist of lemon and a side of sarcasm,” the first time we came here.

So, what’s the deal with you lot? You’re always out having fun while I’m stuck in meetings all day. I’m so tired I could sleep for a week.      Look, you’ve got a job that’s  supposed  to be fun. You’re a conference co-ordinator. That’s like organizing parties for people who don’t even like parties. I’m just a labourer, but at least I get to go home and watch Strictly.      Yeah, but you’re not even getting paid to do that. I mean, I’m a production controller at a factory, which sounds fancy but honestly, it’s just a bit of a nightmare. I’m always late for shifts, and the boss is always on my case. I think he thinks I’m a student who’s just there for the weekend.      I don’t know what’s worse—being a co-ordinator or being a production controller. I once had to book a venue for a tech conference, and the place was so far out I had to drive three hours just to get there and back. And then the Wi-Fi was down.      I can’t even imagine. I got stuck in a construction site last week during a huge storm. The boss said we had to keep working, and I was soaked to the bone. I didn’t even have a dry shirt.      That sounds like a real story. I’m still waiting for someone to tell me a real story about work. I mean, I’ve got a postgrad in engineering, but I still get stuck doing admin.      Maybe you should start your own business. I mean, if you want to be your own boss, you could start a transport company. Or maybe you could just rent out your house? I mean, it’s a bit of a fixer-upper, but it’s in a decent area.      I’d probably just end up stuck in a flat with someone who’s got a parrot that screams at 3am.      Or maybe you could just move back in with your parents. I mean, they’re not even that bad. I’m sure they’d rather have you home than someone else.      To the people who actually have lives outside of work.      And to the ones who manage to survive it all.      To the weekend.      And to finally having a weekend that’s not filled with meetings.

Well, I've just been on a call with my niece. She was talking about the eclipse. She said it was absolutely incredible—like the sky turned black and the stars came out like crazy. I told her I wish I could have seen it, but I’ve been stuck indoors with the weather being so awful.      Aye, I know what you mean. I tried to get out with the binoculars but it was so cloudy. I’ve been watching the Cosmos series again, which is quite a good show. It's got some pretty fascinating stuff about black holes and how the universe began.      Oh, I love Cosmos too. I’ve been thinking about the beginning of space—how everything started from that tiny point and expanded. It’s just so mind-blowing. I can’t help but wonder what’s out there beyond the stars.      I suppose it's all very much on everyone's minds these days, especially with the planting programme going on. I’ve been looking after the garden a bit. I’ve planted some new herbs and even a few flowers. I think it's helping me feel a bit more connected to the world.      Yeah, I’ve been doing that too. I put up an owl box in the corner of the garden, thinking it might attract some wildlife. I’ve also been trying to keep the fence with the neighbors in check. It was quite a bit of work, but the view is worth it.      That sounds like a great idea. I’ve had a bamboo plant in the corner for a while now, and it’s grown quite a bit. I’ve been feeding it a bit of compost and watering it regularly. I think it's going to be a real feature in the garden.      You know, I've been thinking about the TV licence. My sister mentioned that she's not paying it anymore because she doesn't watch much. I told her it's a bit of a shame because it's not just about watching TV anymore. It's about being politically correct and supporting the service.      I agree. I think it's important to be aware of things like that, even if you're not watching the TV. It's part of the social contract, you know.      It’s all a bit complicated. I’ve been trying to eat well lately, though.

I just got a text from my cousin. She's coming to town next week and wants to know if there's a good restaurant near the cathedral. You know, somewhere with a view of the skyline? Yeah, I remember she mentioned that before. Why don’t we take her to that little place near the river? The one with the big menu board and the live band on weekends? It’s not too fancy, but it’s got a nice vibe. Sounds good. I’ve had some good meals there. But you know, I keep thinking about that new place that opened up a few months back. The one near the bus stop. They’ve got a really unique menu—like, they do some kind of modern British fusion? Oh, you mean the one with the chef who used to work in London? I heard the reviews are mixed. Some people love it, others say it’s too gimmicky. Maybe we should check it out. It’s not too far from the cathedral, and it’s got a great view of the city from the terrace. I could go for that. But I need to make sure the bus route still runs there. I’ve heard the bus schedule has changed since the council reorganized everything. You know how they always do that without consulting anyone. Yeah, I know. She just moved into a new house out in the countryside and needs a ride. I could help. I’ve been meaning to take her to visit her old place. It’s still standing, though the garden’s a bit overgrown. I’ve been too busy trying to get my head around this new software system at work. It’s supposed to help manage the corpus, but it’s like learning a new language every day.

I’ve been up since dawn, couldn’t sleep a wink. That bloody alarm clock—what’s the matter with it? It’s like it’s trying to murder me. You’re not the only one. I swear, my alarm clock sounds like it’s been dragged through a hedge. I’ve started talking to it. “Please, just let me sleep a little longer,” I say. It doesn’t listen, of course. I tried that once. Ended up with a sore throat. You know, I’ve been thinking about the birds outside. I heard something this morning—sounds like a blackbird, but not quite. Any chance you’ve heard that sound before? Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve been listening to the birds all week, actually. I think it’s a chaffinch. They’re a bit of a character, aren’t they? I’ve been feeding them in the garden, and they come every morning like clockwork. That’s a great idea. I’ve been meaning to start feeding birds, but I’m not sure what to give them. I read somewhere that sunflower seeds are good, but I’m worried they might get too fat. Oh, they’re fine. Just make sure they have fresh water too, and don’t overdo it. I’ve had some fun with the birds—like the one who used to sit on my shoulder every morning. It was a bit of a scare when it flew off during my lecture. I thought I’d lost my mind. That’s adorable. I wonder if the dentist will be okay with all the birdseed dust in my hair. I’ve had a nosebleed twice this week. Not sure if it’s from the dust or the coffee. Nosebleeds? That’s not good. You should see a doctor. I had one last year, and it turned out to be related to throat cancer. Horrible business. But I’m fine now, thanks to early detection. That’s really worrying. I’ll make an appointment. I always thought the elderly women in the neighborhood were just the same, but now I see how different it can be. They are. I’ve been on the lookout for mutual friends, just to make sure everyone’s well. It’s a bit of a habit, I suppose. You know, after all these years, you start to care about everyone. I can’t argue with that.

I can’t believe it’s been five years since we last saw each other! It feels like it’s been decades. How have you been? Oh, I’ve been good, thank you! I’ve actually been through a lot lately. I tried IVF again last year, and it was really tough. I mean, I had to take time off work, and it was just so emotionally draining. I’m so sorry to hear that. I know how much it can take out of you. I’ve been thinking about writing a book about my own experiences with single parenthood. It’s been such a journey, but it’s also been incredibly rewarding. That sounds amazing. You know, I’ve been thinking about doing something similar too. I left my job as a social worker to focus on my family, and I’ve been trying to figure out what I want to do next. It’s hard to change careers at this stage, but I feel like I need to find something more fulfilling. I can relate. I had to make a similar decision when I moved from teaching to writing. It wasn’t easy, but I’ve always had a passion for storytelling. Did you ever think about how social media has changed the way we connect with people? Absolutely. I mean, it’s such a double-edged sword. On one hand, it helps us stay in touch with people we might not have otherwise connected with. But on the other, it can be really overwhelming. I’ve started practicing yoga to help me manage the stress. It’s been a game-changer. That’s great! I’ve been into yoga too. It’s amazing how it can help with both mental and physical health. I try to do it every morning, even if it’s just for ten minutes. I should really start doing that more. I know I’ve been neglecting my own well-being lately. Maybe we can do a class together sometime? That would be perfect! Let’s plan something soon. I’d love to catch up more and maybe even collaborate on something. I’ve got a few ideas for a book, and I think you could help me with the psychological aspects. I’d love that. It’s refreshing to talk to someone who really gets what I’m going through. I think we’ve both had some major life changes, and it’s comforting to share them with someone who understands.

I just came over for a cup of tea, and I must say, the view from your garden is absolutely stunning. It's a real treat to see such a neat and well-kept space in this part of town. Thank you, it's been a long time since I've had the chance to tend to it properly. I used to have more time when I was teaching, but now that I'm retired, I find myself with more free time than I know what to do with. That's the same for me. You remember that time they tried to run the London marathon? It was a disaster, but they were so proud of themselves.      Yeah, I remember. They were like two little soldiers, determined to finish. I just made a really lovely stew. I think it’s going to be the best thing I’ve cooked in ages. What do you think? It smells amazing! I haven’t had a proper meal like this in weeks. Well, I suppose it's about time we had a bit of a chat. The weather’s been so dull lately, I’ve been feeling more down than usual. I've been thinking about the old days, you know. So, how’s the new job going, Lila? I heard you got promoted last month. Oh, it’s going great, thanks! I’m still teaching, but now I have a bit more responsibility. I just finished transcribing those logs from the weekend. I couldn’t believe how much detail they had on the typewriter era. It’s fascinating how much history you can find in old paperwork. Speaking of which, have you tried that new restaurant down the road? It’s supposed to be excellent. I haven’t yet, but I’ve heard great things about their mashed potato. I've been thinking a lot about buying a house these days. It’s a bit of a nightmare, isn’t it? You've got all these taxes and fees, and I can't even remember the last time I saw a proper estate agent who wasn’t trying to scam me. Oh, don’t get me started. I remember when we used to walk into a shop and just say, "What’s a house like around here?" Now they ask you for a deposit before you've even seen the place. It's like they’re trying to scare you off before you even start. I know, I know. I tried looking at properties last year. But by the time I’d spoken to three agents, I’d spent more on fees than the house itself was worth. Yeah, and then there’s this new fangled thing with the pensions. People are being taxed on their pensions now, even if they’re not working. I mean, what’s the point of getting a pension if you can’t even keep it? It’s all about the government trying to balance the books, I suppose. But it’s not fair on people like us who’ve never worked and are just trying to get by. I still remember when the state used to support people properly. Now it’s all about making sure you pay your taxes before you can even get your benefits. I think the problem is also the politics. Everyone’s so divided these days. You can’t even agree on the weather, let alone the way the country is run. I mean, when I was a childminder, I used to hear all the arguments, but now it’s like we’re all just shouting at each other. Speaking of which, have you heard about the new recycling laws? I think people just expect perfection these days. I know, I’ve been thinking about starting a café in Margate. It’s got that vibe, plus it’s not too busy. But I’m worried about the reviews. It’s not even true, but people take it seriously. I remember seeing your café on Instagram. It looks really cool. You have that modern design vibe going on. I was thinking of doing something similar, but I’m not sure how to start. It’s not that hard if you know what you’re doing. I worked with a designer for a while, and he helped me figure out the layout and the branding. We even got a few good reviews after that. It’s all about the first impressions. That’s what I always say. First impressions are everything. I mean, if the design is good, the food is good, and the service is friendly, people tend to leave happy. But if one thing goes wrong, it can ruin the whole experience.

I just made a new batch of raspberry jam. It’s delicious, and I think it’s going to be perfect with some chocolate ice cream. Have you tried it yet? I think I might have had a spoonful earlier. It was so sweet, and it reminded me of the time we went to the market and picked our own raspberries. I didn’t know they could be so good. Yeah, I remember that! Mom said we could pick them if we helped her with the garden. She said it was good luck to eat the first batch. Do you think that’s true? I don’t know, but I do know that the berries are better when you pick them fresh. I’ve been trying to grow some in my garden, but the birds always come and eat them before I can get them down. Oh, I had the same problem with the gerbils. I tried to keep them in a cage, but they’d always escape and dig up the vegetables. I thought I was being clever by putting the cage near the garden, but it only made things worse. I’ve been thinking about getting a bike. I heard that biking to school is a good way to stay fit. Plus, it’s better for the environment. But I’m a bit worried about the weather. What do you think? I think it’s a great idea. I did that when I was your age, and it helped me make friends. It’s also a good way to get exercise. But if it’s raining, a raincoat is a must. You can’t ride in the rain without one! I still ride my bike to school, even when it rains. It’s just part of the routine. But I always make sure I have a waterproof jacket. Maybe I should start wearing that too. I’m not sure I’ll ever be able to ride a bike. My toddler keeps me busy, and I’m not sure I have the time or energy. But I love the idea of being outside, even just taking a walk with the kids. Walking is a great alternative. I’ve been taking the kids on walks in the park, and it’s a good way to talk about birds and their eggs. I even found a nest the other day, and it was so exciting.

I just got back from the market. I picked up some fresh veggies and a nice selection of cheeses. Did you know they’re having a sale on local produce today? It’s a bit of a hassle, but I thought it’d be worth it for the quality. Oh, really? I haven’t been to the market in ages. I’ve been relying on the local shop for everything. But I guess I should start going more often. I’ve been too lazy, honestly. Oh, and I was just thinking—should we arrange to meet up for a meal out soon? I’ve been meaning to take you out for lunch to celebrate your promotion. That sounds lovely, love. But I’ve been feeling a bit under the weather lately. I’m not sure if I’m up for going out. I’d rather stay in and have a nice dinner. Though I did take a walk this morning, and it felt good. I’ve been trying to get back into some sort of routine. That’s understandable, especially with the weather being so unpredictable lately. I’ve been thinking about taking a break from work, maybe for a few days. I’ve been working too much, and it’s starting to take a toll. Have you considered going on a short trip or something? Maybe a weekend away? I’ve been thinking about that, actually. I’ve had this idea to go to the seaside for a few days. It’s been a while since I’ve had a proper holiday, and I could use a change of scenery. But I don’t know if I can afford it. I’ve been saving up, though. I’d say go for it, love. You deserve a break. I remember when I was younger, I used to travel all the time. We used to take trips every weekend. It was a different life, but I suppose I’ve grown too used to staying in. Though, I do miss the good old days. Speaking of old days, I’ve been meaning to ask you about your eyebrows. I’ve been trying to keep mine neat, but I’m not sure how I’m doing. Should I go to the hairdresser and ask about eyebrow maintenance? I’ve heard it’s a bit of a specialty. Oh, you should. I had them done a few months ago, and it was worth it.

I just thought I'd mention, I've been feeling a bit overwhelmed with the baby lately. It's been a whirlwind of feedings, naps, and then the constant chatter about weaning. I'm not sure I'm ready yet, but I know it's coming. I understand completely. I remember when I was your age, I was completely clueless about everything. But I think we both have this instinct, don't we? The baby's just so sweet, and it's hard to imagine moving on. But we have to be realistic, right? Yeah, I know. It's just the timing feels off. I've been talking to a few other mums, and they all say it's best to start around six months. But I feel like I'm not ready to cut out the milk yet, even if it's just for breakfast. Maybe you can start with just one meal, like lunch or dinner, and then gradually reduce. I mean, why rush it? The baby will adjust, and you'll get used to it too. I think that's what I did with my son. It took a while, but it worked out in the end. That does sound like a good plan. I was just worried it would be too hard. But I guess it's part of the journey. Speaking of which, have you heard about the sign language classes they're having this week? Yes! I signed up for those last week.
