I've been thinking about it too. I feel like we should both go. It might help us connect with the baby in a different way. I'd love that. Do you think you could meet me there? The sessions are on Tuesday and Thursday, and they're only an hour long. It's not too long, and it's a great way to spend some quality time together. That sounds perfect. I'll get the details from you. And maybe we can invite some of the other mums too. It could be a lovely group. I'll make sure to send you the flyers. We can also talk about our plans for the week.

I can’t believe how peaceful it is out here. You know, I’ve been lecturing for years, and yet every time I come out here, I’m reminded of how much I miss the simple things — like walking through a field with no one but the birds and the wind. I know what you mean. It’s like the countryside has this way of putting everything into perspective. You don’t get that in the city, do you? I mean, I grew up in London, and even though I love the city, there’s something about the silence and the space here that really grounds you. Exactly. I think it’s the hills. They’re so different from the flat landscapes in Norwich. You can see the whole village from up there, and it feels like you’re part of the landscape rather than just passing through it. Yeah, and the way the light changes as the sun moves. I remember when we first moved here, I was taken aback by how the light seems to dance on the fields, especially in the early morning. It’s almost like the countryside is alive with its own rhythm. I’ve been thinking about that a lot. It’s funny how the countryside can feel like a different world from the one we’re used to. When I walk through the village, I see people who’ve lived here their whole lives, and yet there’s a sort of timelessness about it. It doesn’t feel like it’s changing as fast as the city does. That’s true. I remember talking to an old man the other day who said that the village has been the same for generations. He even mentioned the same shop and the same church — it’s like they’re anchors in a world that’s constantly shifting. It’s comforting in a way. I suppose that’s why I always feel so at ease when I’m out here. Maybe it’s the fresh air, or maybe it’s just that there’s no rush. Everything moves at a slower pace, and that makes me feel more connected to myself. You’re right. We should come out here more often. It’s a chance to disconnect from the noise of the world and reconnect with something real. I think that’s what I’ve been trying to do with the lectures — bring that sense of simplicity and clarity into the classroom.

I just watched this new film called  The Quiet Divide —it’s got this really intense storyline about a family dealing with grief and secrets. You’ve got to see it. It’s not the usual Hollywood stuff, more like a slow burn. Yeah, I heard about that one. I haven’t gotten around to it yet, but I’m definitely going to. I’ve been so caught up with work lately. Speaking of which, have you heard about what’s going on with your cousin, Tom? Oh, you mean the guy who started his own bike maintenance business? Yeah, he’s doing pretty well, actually. I think he’s got a few customers now and even taken on a few apprentices. He said it’s a bit of a tough market, but he’s making it work. That’s impressive. I’ve been thinking about starting something like that myself, but I’m not sure. I mean, I’ve got this engineering job, which is stable, but sometimes I feel like I’m just going through the motions. You know? I get that. I’ve been feeling the same way lately. My job as a corpus administrator is a bit repetitive, but I tell myself it’s part of the process. Still, I sometimes wonder if I’d be happier doing something more hands-on. I know what you mean. It’s funny, right? We’re both in professional roles, and yet we’re both thinking about stepping out of our comfort zones. I mean, someone has to be the one to start a new business or try something different. Exactly. Also, have you seen the way the cyclists are acting lately? I swear, they’re like a different species on the road. One day you’re just trying to get to work, and the next thing you know, you’re dodging them like they’re trying to run a race. Yeah, I’ve had it with them. I had this one incident where I was trying to merge into a lane and this cyclist just swerved right in front of me. I almost hit him. It was ridiculous. I know, it’s so frustrating. I mean, I’ve got respect for cyclists, but you’ve got to follow the rules. I think the whole thing is about awareness on both sides. If we all just tried to be a little more considerate, things would go smoother.

I can’t believe how vibrant the wildflowers are today, even with the unpredictable weather. It’s like nature’s way of saying, “I’m still here, thank you.” Yeah, it's incredible. I remember when we first moved here, the fields were mostly just bare and a bit muddy. Now, every time I walk this path, it feels like a different story. Almost like the land is telling us something. That’s a poetic way to look at it. It makes me think of the old English countryside books I used to read when I was a student. There's a certain rhythm to the seasons here, even if it’s not always predictable. I know. It's like the land itself has a memory. I was thinking the other day about how much of the English landscape is shaped by centuries of farming and agriculture. You know, even with all the changes, there's still something ancient about it. Absolutely. I was in a lecture last week about the history of cash crops in England. It's so fascinating how the economy of the region has shifted over time, from traditional crops like barley and wheat to more modern ones like potatoes and even some exotic plants. That’s a good point. I’ve always been curious about how language and economics intersect. You can’t really separate them, can you? The way people talk about land, about farming, about money—it all connects. Exactly. And it’s not just about the land. Our own lives here have been shaped by these forces. I mean, we’ve both been lecturers, right? We’re part of that higher professional world, but we’re still grounded in the countryside in a way that most people aren’t. That’s the thing, isn’t it? We’re not just talking about research or academia—we’re talking about the real world. The real world that still has fields, farmers, and the kind of community that can’t be replicated in a city. It’s something I think about often. I’ve always been drawn to the idea of language being tied to place. How dialects and accents can tell you so much about where someone’s from. I mean, even our own speech here is a bit different from what we grew up with in London or Norwich. It’s like the land itself has made us into different people.

I just got a text from my cousin. She's coming to town next week and wants to stay with us. I need to check if we have enough space in the flat. That’s great news! She’s coming to visit? That’s been a while. How long is she staying? She’s staying for a week, I think. She said she wanted to see the city and maybe go to a football match or two. I’m not sure yet, but she mentioned the North East as a place she’d like to explore. The North East? You know, the Angel of the North is just a short drive from here. Maybe we could take her up there on the weekend. It’s one of those landmarks you just have to see. Oh yeah, I remember seeing it on the way up to the city last year. It’s massive. I guess if she’s coming from the South, she might not have seen it. Exactly. I think it’s kind of a tourist spot, but it’s still worth the visit. Plus, it’s a great way to get out of the city and see some beautiful scenery. I’ll ask her if she wants to go. She’s pretty into football, so maybe we can find a match that’s not too far. I heard there’s a good local team playing in the Championship. If she likes football, you’ll have to take her to a game. I know one of the local teams is playing at a stadium just outside the city. It’s not too far, and the atmosphere is always electric. I’ll make sure to set that up. Oh, and we need to talk about the flat again. She’s bringing her partner, so we might not have enough space. Some of them are quite expensive, but maybe we can find one with a parking space. It’s not like we can park on the street anymore. Yeah, parking is a nightmare here. I mean, I drive a car, and I’ve got a parking permit. But it’s not something I can just hand over to someone else.

I just saw a documentary about the trial of a famous celebrity, and it was absolutely fascinating. They were accused of... well, I don’t remember the full details, but it all came down to a misunderstanding with a minor character in their film. It seems like the entire media circus overblown it. That’s always how it goes, isn’t it? I mean, the whole thing could have been a minor issue, but once it’s in the news, it becomes a full-blown scandal. I remember someone once told me that the public has a very short attention span when it comes to celebrities. One day they’re the talk of the town, and the next, they’re forgotten. Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve seen it happen with so many people. But I’m not here to talk about that. I’ve been watching the geese all morning, and they’ve been coming in and out of the pond like they’re trying to decide which way to go. It’s almost like they’re having a meeting or something. That’s interesting. I’ve noticed them too, especially this time of year. They’re migrating, aren’t they? I’ve read that they travel thousands of miles, but I never really thought about how it works. Do they all just decide to go at the same time? I think it’s more about the changing seasons and the availability of food. They follow the weather patterns, I believe. And don’t get me wrong, I love watching them. There was this one time when a flock of geese landed on the roof of the local community center, and it turned into quite the scene. The kids were all excited, and the adults were just trying to get them off. Oh, I remember that. I had to climb up on the roof with a broom to shoo them off. It was a bit of a mess, but it was also funny. I always say that wild birds have more freedom than most of us. They don’t have to worry about deadlines or bills. They just follow the wind and the seasons. That’s true. It’s always nice to see wild birds in the garden, especially in the mornings. I think it’s a reminder of nature and how everything has its own rhythm. It’s something we can learn from.

I can’t believe it’s already April. I feel like we just had lunch last week. How’s your week going, Anne? Oh, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster! I had a job interview yesterday that left me absolutely drained. It was for a new teaching position in Manchester, and I had to do a lesson with a group of Year 7s on the spot. You mentioned you were expecting a baby last month. Oh, she’s doing so well! She’s already been babbling and smiling at us, and she loves the baby clothes I’ve been buying online. I’m so excited, but I’m also about to go through the most frustrating stage of the pregnancy – my cravings are out of control. I know that feeling. I’ve been trying to eat healthy, but I keep getting these random cravings for things like pickled eggs and pizza. It’s so weird. I think the baby is just trying to tell me something. I’m sure that’s it. You know, I’ve been thinking of making a baby shower soon. Would you like to come? It would be great to have some of the friends from our teaching days together again. That sounds fantastic! I’d love to come. Just don’t expect me to be the one bringing the food – I’ve already promised to make the cake.

I just can’t decide what I’m going to do next. I’ve got this job as a production controller, but honestly, I’m not sure if I’m meant to be in this role for the rest of my life. I know what you mean. I was thinking about taking a gap year, you know, just traveling or working somewhere different to see what I like. I feel like I need a break from the same routine. That sounds like a great idea. It’s so common, isn’t it? I mean, we’re both in the same age group, and we’re both unsure what we want. I think that’s part of growing up. You just have to keep trying things and not be afraid to change direction. I guess you’re right. I just don’t want to waste my time doing something I don’t love. I mean, I’m not in debt or anything, but I feel like I’m not contributing in a way that really matters to me. That’s a good point. I’ve been feeling that too. Maybe it’s time we both start looking into more options.

I swear, I don’t know what’s gotten into him lately. He’s been so distracted, like he’s got a secret or something. I’ve been trying to get him to talk, but he just keeps changing the subject. So, I just got a text from my sister saying her new flat has a  basement  and she's terrified of the stairs. She said it's like living in a haunted house. I told her, “You’ve moved from a  terraced house  to a  mausoleum .”      Yeah, I can imagine that. I mean, I’ve never even seen a basement before. I thought they were only in old houses, like in the movies. My dad says he used to have a basement when he was a kid. He said it was full of old bikes and stuff.      That’s what I used to think too. But I’ve actually been to a few places with basements. My parents used to live in a semi-detached in Manchester. The basement was an added-on room, and they turned it into a games room. It was a bit of a mess, honestly. But I used to love it.      Really? That sounds cool. I mean, I guess if you had a basement, you could have a room for your stuff. But I don’t think I’d ever want to live in one. I’d be too scared of the dark.      I think it’s just the natural fear of the unknown. You know, like the old “what’s down there?” myth. But honestly, I’ve been to some great places with basements. My cousin in Leeds has a basement that’s like a mini-wine bar. He puts on events there.      A  wine bar  in a basement? That’s amazing. I’d love to go to that. Although, I’d probably be too nervous to even walk down the stairs.      You’d be fine. It’s just like any other part of the house. Once you get used to it, it’s just another room. Speaking of rooms, have any of you guys been planning your holidays yet?      Yeah, me and my mate are thinking of going to Spain next year. My parents said they’d take us if we get a scholarship for the hockey camp. But I think it’s more about wanting to go to the beach than the hockey, honestly.      That sounds like a good plan. I’ve been meaning to go to Portugal for a while. The food there is amazing, and the beaches are just beautiful. I think I’m going to take the kids next summer.

I can't believe we've been on the road for six hours already. I was hoping for a bit more scenic drive, but I guess this is the best we can do between Redwood National Park and Eureka. I've never seen anything like it. It's wild, isn't it? I've got a nephew who just moved here from London, and he's been talking about how different it all is. He said he was so confused at first, thinking he was in a sci-fi movie. That's funny. I remember when I first came to the US for work. I was in New York, and I thought I'd seen everything, but nothing beats this. I mean, I never thought I'd see a tree that tall. It's like nature's own cathedral. Exactly! Though I have to admit, this drive has been a little more interesting than the last few trips. I think we’re both learning something. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, if nothing else, it’s giving us something to talk about. I think I’ll be the one telling the stories when we get back.

Aye, these are as good as they get. I got the recipe from my aunt in Dublin—she’s a real cook, that one. You know, it’s not just about the meat, it’s about the crust. I tried to do some research online, but there’s so much junk out there. Sometimes I wonder if I should go to a real doctor instead of just trying to figure it out myself. Yeah, I know. I just received the vintage cups and saucers I bought from eBay. They’re absolutely beautiful, aren’t they? I can’t believe they’re still in such good condition after all these years. Oh, they look amazing! I’ve been meaning to get a set like that for ages. You know how much I love collecting old things. It’s like time travel every time I use them. I know, right? I think they were from the 1950s. The pattern is so classic. I even found a few matching plates too. I’m going to set up a little display in the living room. That sounds like a great idea. I can help you sort them out. By the way, I saw a new stall at the local community market this week – they had some really unique vintage items. If you’re looking for more, maybe we could go together next weekend? That would be lovely. I’ve been meaning to check out the market again. I also saw some buckwheat bread at the shop. Mate, I swear I just got a text from my sis saying she’s ‘financed’ a weekend away with some mates. I’m like, ‘financed?’ What does that even mean? I thought you had to pay for it yourself. I can't believe it's already April. The weather’s been so inconsistent—it was snowing just last week, and now it's like midsummer. I’m so ready for spring to settle in properly. Sounds like a great plan. I’ll be looking forward to hearing about your progress. Oh, and I’ve got a baby shower coming up—do you want to come? It’s next weekend. That would be lovely. Right, so I’ve been meaning to ask—what exactly do you do at Cambridge University Press? I mean, I know it’s publishing, but how does it all actually work?      It’s a bit of a mix, honestly. I’m a publishing assistant, so I handle the day-to-day stuff—proofreading, formatting, tracking deadlines. It’s not too bad, but it’s a lot to juggle with all the different projects. I mean, I know what publishing is like, but I didn’t realize there was this kind of linguistic research happening here.      Actually, Cambridge’s a big hub for language studies. The whole place is steeped in academia, so it’s just natural for people to be into language and communication. I’m actually from Sweden, but I’ve been living in the UK for a few years now. I sort of fell into publishing by accident.      That’s the thing with temporary roles—sometimes you end up staying longer than you expected. I’ve been here for over a year now, even though I started as a temp.      It’s funny how these jobs can turn into something more. I started here as an assistant, and I’m still here, even though I was expecting to leave after a year.      Sounds like you’re all in the same boat. I feel like I’ve been here for ages too, even though I’m only temporary.

Alright, so I’ve been thinking about the passport photos again. I’ve got the form filled out, but I’m not sure if I should go to the local post office or one of those photo booths in town. I am so tired, I think I’ve been up all night. I had a nightmare about that trip to the hospital again. You remember, the one where I fell on my arm? Yeah, I remember. You remember that anniversary party we had last week? The one with all the relatives from York and the cousins from Huddersfield. Start with the basics, then build up. I used to do that with my own kids. You know, I used to be a maths examiner, so I can tell you, there’s a lot of logic in it. It just takes time. I guess I’ll have to ask you for help then. I mean, if you’re not busy with your exams and stuff. Always happy to help, lad. You’re one of the few people I can talk to about things like that. And besides, if you pass your exams, I’ll have one less thing to worry about. You’re a real lifesaver, Mrs. Whitaker. I owe you one. You’ll owe me more than one after next year.

Dad, I just put my water bottle in the cooler bag, and it’s like it’s got a life of its own now. It’s been bouncing around for the past twenty minutes!      You know, I had a water bottle once that did the same thing. I used to think it was haunted.      Yeah, but that was before I found out it was just too full. You can’t really tell when it’s full if it’s got a lid on.      That’s true. You know, I still have that old pen you gave me when I was learning to write. Still works, though it’s got that weird curve on the top.      Oh, that’s the one I used to write all my homework with in sixth form. I even used it for my Latin exam.      You were so nervous about that exam, weren’t you? I remember you getting a pen stuck in your ear trying to write the Latin for “rain.”      Yeah, and I still got an A. Or was it a B? I’m not sure.      You got an A. I was there. You even got a star on your report card.      You were there? You weren’t even in the room!      I was in the corridor. And I saw the teacher give you a wink.      That’s the kind of thing that makes you think you’re the smartest person in the world.      Well, you are. You just have to make sure you keep eating the chocolate. I heard the doctor said it helps with IBS.      IBS? I thought it was a new superhero.      No, it’s that thing you get when your tummy’s all messed up. I used to have it all the time when I was working in Manchester.      So you’re saying we should all be eating chocolate on the way to Cornwall?      Yeah, and maybe a bit of liquorice. It’s good for the tummy. Though I think it’s more like a medicine than a treat.      I don’t know, Dad. I think I’d rather just eat chocolate. It’s more fun.      Well, you’re right. But don’t forget to bring a pen. I’ve got this one here from Holland and Barrett that I use for everything.      Okay, but I’m keeping my water bottle. It’s got a personality.      Fair enough. Just make sure you don’t lose it.

So, I've been thinking about the new software we're supposed to be using for the transcription work. It's supposed to make things faster, but honestly, I’m not sure I like the way it's structured. It feels a bit too automated, and I worry it might miss some nuances in the speech. Has anyone else tried it yet?      Yeah, I did a few test runs last week. It actually caught a few things I might have missed, but then again, it also misinterpreted some phrases. For example, it turned "I’m going to the shops" into "I’m going to the shop," which is technically correct, but it lost the sense of plurality. It can be frustrating when you're working with dialects or regional speech patterns—it doesn't always account for that.      Ah, I’ve heard similar issues with automated systems before. I’ve worked with them in education when transcribing lectures or student interviews. One of the problems is that they often lack the contextual understanding required to distinguish between slang, idioms, and formal speech. I remember once a system misread "I’ve had enough" as "I have had enough," which completely changed the tone of the conversation.      I can imagine how that would confuse things. I’ve never really worked with transcription software, but I do deal with a lot of different voices in my work. I’ve got to listen to people from all over the place—different accents, different ways of speaking. There’s a lot of variation in how people express themselves, and it’s a bit of an art to catch the right meaning without judging the speaker.      That’s exactly it. It’s not just about accuracy—it’s about understanding the speaker’s intent. I mean, the job is to transcribe, not to edit or interpret. But when the software tries to "correct" things, it can sometimes do more harm than good. I’ve had to go back and fix a lot of errors that weren’t even mistakes, just misinterpretations.      I agree. I think we need to be careful not to over-rely on these tools. They're useful for the basics, but when it comes to more complex or nuanced speech, a human ear is still irreplaceable. Especially in our case, where we deal with a lot of regional dialects.      And don’t forget, we’re not just transcribing words—we’re preserving voices.

Okay, I've got a few things to do before Mother’s Day. I was thinking about taking the kids to Forest School today. It’s a nice way to get them out of the house and into nature.      Forest School? Is that the one near the woods? I remember hearing about it from my mum. It’s supposed to be really good for kids’ development, right?      Yeah, I think it’s where you learn to climb trees and stuff. But I don’t know, I’m a bit scared. What if I fall?      Oh, don’t worry, you’ll be fine. It’s all about learning to be safe and having fun. Just like when I was a kid. I remember this one joke about a tree and a squirrel. Let me tell you.      Okay, go on.      So, there’s a tree and a squirrel. The tree says, “What’s your name?” The squirrel says, “I’m a squirrel.” The tree says, “What’s your job?” The squirrel says, “I’m a nut gatherer.” The tree says, “Oh, I’m a nut…_picker.”      Wait, is that a pun?      Yes! It’s a play on the word “picker.” It’s one of those funny little idioms that people use. You know, like “spill the beans” or “hit the sack.”      Oh, I know that one! My teacher used to say, “Don’t spill the beans,” when we were in the classroom.      Exactly! It’s the kind of thing that makes language so much fun. Maybe I should start using more idioms when I’m talking to the kids. It’ll make things more interesting.      Can I use some idioms too?      Of course! Just don’t overdo it. You need to make sure you understand what they mean. Let’s go with something simple.      Okay, I can try. Like “the cat’s meow,” or “the ball is in your court.”      I like that! You’re getting the hang of it. Now, about the Forest School – are you both excited?      I guess. I just hope I don’t get stuck in a tree.      Not if I’m there to help. We’ll make sure you have a great time. And if you do get stuck, I’ll just call the fire brigade.      Wait, isn’t that for real emergencies?      Well, it’s a joke. But seriously, we’ll have a great day, and I’ll make sure you both learn something new.

I just got a call from my sister. She's been really down lately. She's been dealing with some health issues, and I think she's starting to lose hope. That’s really sad to hear. How bad is it? It's cancer, actually. She was diagnosed a few months ago. She's been through a lot, and I think it's taking a toll on her mentally. I’m so sorry. I hope she’s getting the support she needs. It's like she feels guilty about being a burden. That’s really tough. I remember when my dad was ill, he used to say the same thing. It's like he didn’t want to bother anyone. I’ve seen how even a small illness can change someone’s whole life. Have you considered getting her professional help? I have, but she’s resistant. She doesn’t want to be labeled or treated like she’s broken. I wish I knew how to reach her. I know it’s hard, but sometimes you just have to be there. Let her know you care, even if she doesn’t want to talk. Maybe she just needs someone to listen. That makes sense. I’ve been trying to be patient, but it’s really hard. I worry about her all the time. I get it. I’ve been there too. My mum was like that—always brushing off her problems. It wasn’t until she had a breakdown that she finally asked for help. I think it’s just about finding the right moment. I hope that’s what happens for my sister. I just want her to feel supported. And you’re doing the right thing by being there for her. That’s the best kind of support you can give. Thank you. It means a lot. I just hope I can be there for her in the way she needs, even if it's just being a shoulder to cry on. You will be.

So, I just got an email from the university about the new semester timetabling. They’ve moved a few of my language classes to different days. But you know, it’s all part of the experience, right? Especially if you’re studying something like linguistics.      Absolutely. I even go to a few vegan cafes in the city. They have these incredible fusion dishes that blend Korean and Chinese flavors.

Alright, so I just got this really weird present for Secret Santa. It was this box full of flavoured vodka... like, actual vodka with flavouring? I can’t believe we’re doing this. I thought we were going to the gig, not driving through the countryside like we’re on some kind of road trip. Relax, it’s not that long. I just wanted to stop and see the view. You know how I get when I’m in the car—need to take it all in. Yeah, I know. But honestly, I’ve been working non-stop this week. You don’t have to be the person who just manages the data—you can be the person who shapes it.

Well, I’ve been feeling a bit off lately. That cold I had last week hasn’t quite gone, and I’m starting to think it’s something more serious. You have to take care of yourselves more than ever. Yeah, the weather’s been so changeable lately. One minute it’s sunny, the next it’s pouring. I think it’s because of the jet stream or something. You’re not too late! I mean, I know we’re all just starting out, but it’s not like we’re in a rush. You’ll find someone, I’m sure. Yeah, and you’re still young. You know, I’ve been trying to get my head around this new tablet I got. It’s all about the apps, isn’t it? I can’t even remember what a ‘smartphone’ is anymore. I think it’s something to do with the internet?      Oh, it’s just a phone that's smarter than you, really. You can do so much more with it—like watch videos, listen to music, even play games. It’s made things so much easier. But I still find it a bit confusing. I remember when we used to have to write things out on paper. You couldn’t just tap a button and it did all the work for you.      I remember when we used to have to write letters by hand and wait for them to be delivered by post. Now, it’s all instant. I tell you, it’s like living in a different world.      And yet, we still have to deal with the same old problems. You know, money. I’ve been trying to get my head around the government benefits system. It’s a nightmare. I’ve got a friend who’s been in and out of the system for years, and it just gets more complicated every time.      I know what you mean. I’ve been out of work for about ten years now. I used to run a small shop, but it closed down. I’ve tried a few things, but nothing sticks. I mean, it’s not like I don’t want to work. I just can’t seem to find the right thing.      I know the feeling. I’ve tried a few things too. I did some part-time work as a teacher, but it wasn’t enough. I’ve got a mortgage to pay, and I’m not going to be getting any richer any time soon.      It’s so frustrating. I think the system is set up to leave people like us behind. I mean, we’re not asking for much. Just a chance to have a little bit of security, you know?      True. I sometimes wonder if the government even cares about people like us.

I just love teaching language, it's such a fascinating job. I get to meet so many different people and learn from them too. How about you, John? What do you enjoy doing these days? Oh, I used to love my job as a Managing Director. It was exciting, but now that I'm retired, I've found a new passion. I've started taking up painting. It's a bit of a challenge, but I enjoy the way it makes me feel when I finish a piece. That sounds wonderful. I bet it's a great way to pass the time. I've always been interested in languages, even as a child. I used to collect dictionaries and learn phrases from different countries. It's one of the reasons I became a language teacher. That's a real talent. I can see how that would make a difference in someone's life. I've always been more into practical things, like fixing things around the house. I've taken up gardening too. It's a calming activity, especially after a long day. That's great. I think gardening is amazing, especially in the spring when everything comes to life. I've been trying to grow some herbs in my kitchen window. It's not much, but it's a start. I've done some of that too, but I'm still learning. I find it really satisfying when something you've planted actually grows. It's like a little win each time. It's such a different kind of success. I also enjoy reading. I've been reading a lot of fiction lately. It's a great escape, especially after a long week of teaching. That's a good hobby. I do enjoy reading too, though not as much as I used to. I used to read a lot when I was younger. I think it's a great way to keep the mind active. Definitely. I've always found that reading helps me unwind. I also love traveling. I've been to some amazing places, and I always try to learn a little bit of the local language to make my trips more authentic. That's a great approach. I've been to a few places, but I never really got into learning languages. I think I would have enjoyed it more if I had started earlier. It's never too late to start.

So, did you get anything for Valentine’s Day? I mean, I know it’s not like it’s a big deal or anything, but I still like to do something for the people I care about. Yeah, honestly, I didn’t do anything super fancy. I just bought my mum a nice card and a bar of chocolate. She was like, “Oh, you’re such a good daughter.” I was like, “Yeah, yeah, I know.” Ha! Oh, that’s sweet. I think I’m going to try to do something more for my mum this year. Maybe take her out for dinner? But I’m not sure if she’d like that. She’s like, “I don’t need any more spoiling.” I get that. But isn’t it nice to do something for the people you love? I mean, I still have that movie we went to last year. It’s like,  Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind  or something. I can’t remember. Oh, that’s a good one. I remember we laughed so much. I think it was after that we started talking about trying to find a partner. Like, “Maybe we should start dating.” Yeah, I think that was the night we started looking into the dating scene. Though, honestly, I still think I’d rather just be with someone I already know. I know, right? I mean, it’s not like we’re not allowed to be with anyone else. It’s just that I like the people I already know. Definitely. Anyway, I was just thinking about this weekend. Are we going to the cinema or something? I saw a few movies on my list. I think there’s a new one out about a girl who goes on a road trip. Oh, I’ve heard of that! I’m thinking of going to that one. But I’m not sure if I’ll get a date. Oh, come on, you don’t need a date. Just come with me. We can laugh and eat popcorn. Deal! I’ll bring the snacks. I’ve got this bag of those candy canes I bought from the market.

So, do you think the housing crisis is really just a symptom of capitalism, or is it something deeper? I mean, I've been reading a lot about it lately and I'm starting to feel like it's not just about greed. It's more about the way power is structured in society. I get that. I think capitalism has a lot to answer for, especially when it comes to housing. But I also think there's a racial angle to it too. I’ve heard so many stories from friends in London—people of color can't afford to live here, even if they work hard. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. I mean, I grew up in Watford, which is pretty middle-class and stable, but even there, you see the divide. It’s not just about money; it’s about who gets the resources and who doesn't. And then you have the housing policies—like the Right to Buy—making it harder for people to access decent housing in the first place. Exactly, and the way property is treated as an asset rather than a human right is insane. My mum’s always talking about how she grew up in a council house and that was normal. Now, people are paying hundreds of thousands for a flat that's barely livable. It’s just not fair. I know. I’ve been thinking about this a lot as an architect. I mean, we design buildings, but we don’t get to shape the policies that make housing unaffordable. It’s like we’re part of the system but not in a position to change it. I wonder what the solution is. Are we just doomed to this cycle? I don’t know. I think we need more regulation, more social housing, and a better way of balancing capitalism with equity. But I also think the political climate is pretty hostile to that. People are scared to talk about it, and politicians don’t want to address it because it’s politically risky. That’s a good point. But I think it starts with awareness. If people start to question the status quo and demand change, then maybe something can shift. I mean, we're not all the same, but we're all affected by these issues in some way. Absolutely. That's why I write about it.

I just got a call from the nursery. They’re all set for the baby to start next week. I was wondering if you wanted to come with me to drop him off? It might be nice to have someone there to help. That would be great, Mum. I can help with the transition. I mean, I know how hard it is for you, especially with the baby weening. You don’t have to do it all on your own. Thank you, love. It’s not just the weening; it’s the whole adjustment. Going back to work too—it’s a big step. I’ve been thinking about how to manage it. Maybe you could help me plan the schedule? Definitely. And it’ll be a chance for us to enjoy some time together without the stress of daily life. You’re right. That would be good. I need to take a break too. Speaking of which, have you seen the new TV show I’m watching?

Well, I think that’s the last thing we’ll be discussing tonight. We’ve got more important matters to talk about. Did you hear about the incident at the shop last night?      Yeah, I did. The police were called, and they’re asking for statements. I don’t think it was that big of a deal, but I guess it’s better to be safe than sorry.      I heard about it too. I was out there that night. It was nothing, really. Just a misunderstanding with the customer. But I guess it’s going to be a pain in the neck to go through all this paperwork.      It’s ridiculous. I mean, I had to give a statement and I was already late for work. It’s one thing to be polite, but when does it become a problem? I mean, I was in a hurry and I said the wrong thing, and now I’m stuck with this.      I feel for you, mate. But maybe I can help. I’ve got some experience with giving statements. You’ll need to be clear and concise. They just want the facts, nothing more.      I appreciate that, but I don’t know if that’s necessary. It was just a small argument over a faulty phone. The customer was being unreasonable, and I just wanted to get out of there. Honestly, I don’t think it’s worth the hassle.      I don’t think it’s that big of a deal, but I still have to make sure I’m not in trouble. I mean, what if they think I did something wrong? I don’t know what they’ll think.      That’s the problem. You never know. I told them what happened, and they just said they would take it under consideration. I mean, I tried to be polite, but I was in a rush. I had to get to work.      Okay, well, let’s change the subject for a moment. I was just told that the EE phone bill is on the way. It’s going to be one of those expensive ones again, isn’t it?      Yeah, you know how it is. I’ve been trying to cut back, but those bills just keep coming. It’s a shame we can’t all get cheaper deals.      You’re telling me. I’ve got the same problem. I’ve started using less data, but it’s not helping.

So, how’s the new life treating you, mate? You’ve been married now for a few months, right? Yeah, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I mean, it’s great, but honestly, I didn’t think I’d be living in Bedford again. You know, after all that time in Cyprus? I can imagine. I’ve been thinking about going back to Cyprus myself, but I’m stuck here teaching English. Still, it’s not all bad. At least the weather’s better than the flat in Luton. You’re not wrong. Yeah, I moved into this flat a few months ago. It’s a bit old, but it’s got character. You know me, I like a bit of history in my walls. And it’s close to the library, which is a bonus for my job. Sounds great. I’ve been meaning to visit you. I’ve got a lot of catch-up to do. And I’ve got some souvenirs from Cyprus, you know – spices, herbs, even some olive oil. You should try some of the stuff, it’s amazing. Oh, I’d love that. I’ve been getting into cooking more lately. I’ve even picked up a mortar and pestle. It’s funny, I never used one before, but it’s actually oddly satisfying. You ever try making your own bread? I did once. It was a disaster. I burnt it and nearly set the kitchen on fire. But I’m getting better. I’ve been experimenting with chickpeas and nuts. You know, healthy stuff. I even started growing a few herbs in my window box. That’s brilliant. I’ve been thinking about starting a small garden too. I’ve got this idea for a little patch of land near the flat. Maybe I could grow some of the stuff you’ve got from Cyprus. You should. It’s a good way to relax and get back to basics. I’ve got this idea for a small business selling herbs and spices. I think it could work. That’s a solid plan. I’d love to help you with that. You know what they say – you can’t have too much of a good thing.

I can't believe we've got another English test next week. I'm so stressed about it. I just don't feel like I'm grasping the material at all. Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to read the textbook every night, but it’s just so dense. I feel like I’m going in circles with the essays. I think I need to start practicing more with the questions. No, I think everyone's feeling it. Especially with the school orchestra. I mean, I'm part of the wind-band, and it’s taking so much time to practice. Maybe we can study together after class? I mean, we could swap notes or something. That sounds like a good idea. I can help you with the French, and you can help me with the English. Then we’ll both be better. Yeah, that’s not a bad plan. I think we should try it. And maybe even go to the art lessons together? I heard there’s a new project coming up. You're on.

I just saw a lorry pulling in with a load of fish. You know, I used to take my kids to the market in Darlington when they were little. I miss those days.      Yeah, I remember when I used to go with my dad to the market. He’d always buy me a hot dog. Though I reckon that’s not what you’re thinking of now, is it?      No, not exactly. But I bet you’d get a better hot dog now than you did then. Though I’m not sure I’d go for the fish. I’d rather have some chips and a pie.      I’d say the fish is the way to go, but I’ve got a bit of a soft spot for the old school stuff. You know, the kind of food that makes you remember your grandma’s kitchen.      Exactly. I think that’s the thing about food—it brings back memories. Though I have to say, I’ve noticed the price of everything’s gone up. Even the chips.      Yeah, I’ve been meaning to talk about that. My brother works in a café near Hull, and he’s been having to raise prices just to keep the doors open. It’s not fair.      I know. I’ve got a friend who runs a takeaway. He’s been struggling too. I told him he should try selling burgers and fries instead of just chips and pies.      I’d say that’s a risky move. Burgers and fries are high in calories. Maybe he should sell some healthy options instead?      Oh, come on. Burgers and fries are part of British tradition. You can’t just start selling kale and quinoa.      I’m not saying replace them. Just add a few healthy choices to the menu. People are more health-conscious now.      That’s true. I’ve noticed more people asking for lighter meals. Though I still think fish and chips are a staple. Not just in my town, but across the whole country.      Yeah. It’s part of our identity. Even though the prices have gone up, I think people still love it.      I think I’ll go for a fish and chips then.      Better than a burger, don’t you think?      Yeah, and no disappointment. You can’t go wrong with that.      Yeah. I’ll take that as a compliment.      That’s what I like to hear.

So, I was telling my dad earlier that I think my genes are to blame for my weight. I mean, look at me—always eating cake, never gymming, and yet I’m still thin. He said it’s the other way around!      Yeah, I’ve heard that one before. I reckon it’s not genes, it’s just that you don’t eat as much as you think. I’ve seen plenty of people who eat like pigs and still look like they’ve been hit by a bus.      I’ve always said it’s the way you eat, not the food itself. I mean, I used to eat all the time, but I never got fat. I guess I just moved around a lot. And if I didn’t, I’d be the one crying about my weight, not the other way around.      You’re right, in a way. But I still think my dad’s got a point about genes. My mum’s always been like that—thin, even when she used to smoke and drink. I think we’re just built that way.      I reckon it’s a combination of everything. I mean, I’ve always been into health, but I still had to have surgery once because of my weight. It was a shock, honestly. You think you’re doing the right thing, but your body just doesn’t respond the way you want it to.      I can’t even imagine having surgery. I mean, I’ve had a lot of stuff done to my car, but that’s different. I mean, I’ve had a few operations on my hands over the years—mainly because I’m a mechanic and I bang stuff around.      Yeah, I’ve had a few operations myself. I had a appendectomy when I was a kid. My mum was beside herself, but I still ended up fine. You know, I think the key is to not let it get too bad.      I guess it’s about balance. You can’t just live off cake and chips, but you can’t go overboard on vegetables either. It’s all about moderation.      And don’t forget exercise. I’ve always told my students that if you don’t move, you’re going to end up with those issues. I mean, I still walk every day, even if it’s just around the block.

I just got an email from the department head about the Moodle upgrade. They’re saying it’s going to be a big shift and we’ll need to train the students more thoroughly. I’m worried about how we’ll manage it with the tight deadlines we’ve already got. Yeah, I heard about that too. I was thinking about how we can streamline the process. Maybe if we use some of the new features they’ve introduced, like the interactive quizzes and the automated grading, it might actually save us time in the long run. That sounds promising, but I’m still concerned about the learning curve for the students. Some of them are already struggling with the basics, and adding another layer of complexity could make things even harder. I get that. But maybe we can break it down into smaller steps. You know, start with the basics of navigating the platform, then move on to the more advanced features. And if we schedule a short orientation session before the semester starts, that might help a lot. That’s a good idea. I was also thinking about how we can use the discussion forums more effectively. We could encourage students to post their questions there instead of relying on emails. It might foster more engagement and reduce our workload. Exactly. And it’d be good if we set up some example threads to show them how to ask questions clearly and how to respond to each other. We could even award points for the most helpful responses to motivate participation. I like that. It could turn the forums into a more collaborative space. But I wonder how we’ll handle the technical support side of things. If students have issues with the software, they might not know where to turn. I was thinking about setting up a quick help guide in the Moodle course itself. We can link to FAQs and even include contact details for the IT support team. That way, students can find the information they need without burdening us directly. That sounds like a solid plan. I think if we approach this as a team, we’ll be able to make the transition smoother for both us and the students. Maybe we should schedule a meeting with the IT department to get their input on the new features too. Definitely. I’ll reach out to them tomorrow.

I can’t believe how much jetlag I’m still feeling. I swear, I think I’ve got a mini-time zone shift going on in my brain. It’s like I’m still in Edinburgh, even though I’ve been back in Norwich for three days now. Yeah, I know what you mean. I was so exhausted after the flight, I didn’t even remember to change my sleep cycle. I ended up waking up at 5 a.m. this morning, thinking it was still 10 p.m. in London. It’s ridiculous. I feel like I’m still in the middle of a conversation with my boss, just because I keep catching myself thinking the time is still 10 p.m. My brain is definitely not syncing with the real world yet. I hear you. I’ve been trying to get back into the groove of things, but it’s harder than I thought. I even tried to go for a run this morning, but I just sat on the couch and stared at the ceiling, thinking about how I was supposed to be running. I feel like I’ve got a baby inside me. I’m so tired all the time, and my brain is foggy. I think I need a nap, but I can’t even sleep without falling asleep in the middle of a sentence. I think it’s the jetlag. You know, the body’s still adjusting. I’ve been feeling the same way. I’m not even sure if I should be worrying about the baby’s sleep patterns yet. I mean, they’re not even here yet. Exactly. It’s like I’m being split in two – one part of me is fully aware of what’s going on, and the other part is just trying to catch up on sleep. I can’t wait for the baby to be here so I can get some real rest. I know. I’ve been reading up on baby sleep patterns, just in case. I think I’ve got a plan. I’ll be the one who stays up with them, and you can get the rest. It’s the only way we’re going to make it through this. That sounds fair. I’ll take the night shifts, you take the day. I owe you one for the jetlag. I know you were up all night waiting for me to get home.

I've been thinking a lot about friends lately. It's strange how some of them have moved around so much. I remember when I was in Liverpool, I had a friend from Kurdistan who used to come over for a drink every Friday. He'd talk about the politics in his country like it was the biggest thing in the world. Yeah, I know what you mean. I still keep in touch with a few people from back home, but it's not the same. The political situation there is so unstable, especially with the oil politics. It's like everything is connected to the oil, isn't it? It is, isn't it? I mean, the way the oil supply affects everything. It's like a giant machine, and if one part breaks down, the whole thing starts to rumble. I've heard some people say that the Wahabi influence is playing a role in some of the conflicts too. It's complicated. Definitely. I've seen it firsthand. When I was working as an interpreter, I was in some meetings where people were talking about how the Wahabi ideology is spreading, and how it's affecting the younger generation. I think young people are really struggling with the choices they're being presented with. That's heartbreaking. I remember when I was younger, I used to think that having freedom of choice was the most important thing. But now I'm not so sure. I've seen how the whole political climate can shape people's lives in ways they never expect. Exactly. And it's not just politics—it's also about migration. I've been helping a few people get their visas, and it's frustrating how the process is so complicated. People are trying to move for better opportunities, but the system is so slow and broken. I can only imagine. I've been thinking about moving house myself. It's not just about the property; it's about where you put your roots. I've been in Liverpool for years, and I feel like the city is changing. It's like the old friendships are fading, and new ones are forming. That's a hard thing to deal with. I've had a few friends from abroad who have moved away, and it's been heartbreaking. I guess it's just the nature of life.

So, I just got the last of the lamb out of the oven. It’s practically falling apart. I think we’re in for a real treat tonight.      That does look delicious, honestly. I’ve been craving roast lamb all week. But you know, I still can’t believe we’re having it at  this  time of year. It’s like something out of a Scottish Highlands scene.      Oh, don’t be so dramatic, love. It’s not that unusual. We’ve had it in the summer too, when the weather’s just too hot for anything else. And besides, it’s not like we’re not used to it. I’ve been cooking it for decades.      You’ve definitely got the technique down, Mrs. MacAllister. I still can’t get the seasoning right. I think I’ve tried every recipe in the book.      Maybe it’s just a matter of time. I’ve been thinking about taking the family on a cruise, you know. Something to break the monotony. I’ve tried to work out more recently, but with the workload, it’s hard to find time.      I’ve been trying too, actually. I even joined a gym a few months back. It’s been challenging, but I’m starting to see some results. Though I still can’t beat the old dogs at the park.      Oh, you’d be surprised how much energy those old dogs have. I used to take them for walks every morning, and they’d always race ahead like they were on a mission.      That’s what I always thought. I’ve been meaning to get a dog myself, but with the rented accommodation and everything, it’s not really feasible.      I know what you mean. I’ve been talking to the landlord about maybe getting a pet, but he’s been pretty strict about it. Though I’m not sure how much he’s actually heard about it.

You know, I’ve been thinking about moving out of this flat. It’s getting too small for all of us. I mean, it’s not like we’re all sleeping in the same room or anything.      Oh come on, it’s not that bad. I mean, we’ve all got our own space. Plus, it’s not like you’ve got anywhere else to go, right? You’re unemployed, remember?      Yeah, I know, but I’m not feeling like I’m being taken seriously. I’ve got a degree, and I’m still stuck here. What’s the point of working hard if you end up in the same situation as your mates?      You’re not the only one who feels that way. I’ve been thinking about applying for a place in Manchester. I heard there are more opportunities there.      You know, I’ve been working part-time as a teaching assistant. It’s not much, but it’s a start. I’m trying to get into a proper course, maybe something in education.      That’s cool. I mean, you’ve got more going for you than me. I’ve been trying to get into work for months, and I just keep getting rejected.      I know, I know. It’s tough. But you’re not alone. We’re all trying to make it work. Plus, you’ve got your friends here, right?      Yeah, I guess. But sometimes I feel like I’m just waiting for something to happen. Like, I’m stuck in a loop.      I get it. I’ve been to university, and I realized it’s not always about the degree. It’s about experience and connections. I’ve been meeting people through my courses, and it’s helping.      Exactly. I’m trying to build those connections. I’ve got a couple of internships lined up, and I’m hoping it’ll lead somewhere.      You know what? Maybe I should try applying for some courses. I’ve been putting it off because I didn’t know where to start.      That’s the spirit! We’ll help you with that. And don’t forget, we’re all in this together.      To moving forward and not giving up.      And to not letting unemployment define us.      Cheers to that. I feel a bit better already.      Good. Now, let’s talk about food. So, do you ever just sit down and scroll through Facebook for ages like I do? I mean, it's not like I’m doing anything useful, but it's somehow comforting. Honestly, I can relate. It's like our brains are trained to process information through screens and documents, not face-to-face. It's a bit strange, isn't it? Exactly. I swear, I’ve never seen a film so full of meatballs. I mean, it’s like the whole plot revolves around a giant meatball. I’m more confused than ever. Yeah, but it’s a kids’ film, right? So, do you watch the Euros? I’ve been trying to keep up with the matches, but with work and all, it’s tough to find the time. Oh, you know, I’ve been doing a lot of watching lately. I was reading up on New Labour—Tony Blair’s time, you know. It’s interesting how people look back on it now. Some say it was the era of stability, others say it was too much of a leftward shift. What do you think? Well, I’m not a big politics guy, but I’ve seen how it affects people’s lives. You know, when I first started driving, everything was more straightforward. There weren’t as many rules, and people weren’t as worried about the government. Now, it’s a different story. They’re always talking about the economy, and it’s hard to know where you stand. I suppose that’s the trouble with the government these days. They’re always trying to balance one thing with another. I mean, I’m a lecturer, so I get a lot of time to think about these things. But I still find it hard to keep up with all the changes. Yeah, it’s all a bit overwhelming, isn’t it? You hear about new policies, and you wonder how they’ll affect things. But then again, people like me—working with my own hands—have to deal with it day in, day out. I can see that. I think it’s important to keep up with what’s going on, even if it’s not always easy.

So, I've been listening to these BNC recordings again. They’re fascinating, honestly. You know, those corpus of spoken English from the British National Corpus. I can't believe how much variation there is in pronunciation and vocabulary even within the same region. I mean, I follow a lot of people from different countries, and it's like they're using English in such different ways. Sometimes it feels like a whole new language.      I've noticed that too. Like, some people use so much slang or emojis that it's almost like they're speaking a different language. I’m trying to keep up with all the new terms, especially on LinkedIn. You know, it's like a whole new dialect just for professional networking.      That's true. I've had to learn a whole new set of phrases and expressions for being an editor. Like, “disrupt the status quo,” “scaling the business,” “leveraging opportunities.” It's insane. I keep thinking, “Is this even English anymore?”      Ha! It’s like a refreshing break from the constant changes in English. But I still get confused sometimes when people talk in such fast Spanish.      Oh, I get it. I’m scared of flying too, though. I’ve been meaning to visit the Maldives for years, but every time I think about it, I start panicking over the flight.

Alright, I’ve got the pesto sauce ready, and the pasta’s about to be done. Should I finish up the salad while I’m at it? It’s been a while since we had a proper meal together. Yeah, go for it. I can’t believe we’ve got everything ready. That was a mad rush getting all the ingredients out before the oven got too hot. But look at this—our dinner is looking amazing! I still can’t believe I managed to get it right the first time. But honestly, the taste was worth it. Definitely. It’s one of those dishes that really brings people together, don’t you think? I’ve always thought that cooking is a great way to connect with others, especially when you’re in a new place. Like, have you ever thought about moving somewhere else? I’ve actually thought about it, but I’m not sure yet. I’ve been considering doing a short trip to Spain for a few weeks. I’ve heard that the food is incredible there, and I could use a break from the constant news cycle. It might be good for my mental health. That sounds like a good idea. I’ve been thinking about taking a cooking class abroad too. I heard there’s a new one in Barcelona that focuses on Mediterranean cuisine. I can't believe we've been teaching at the same university for three years and we still haven't managed to get a proper dinner together. It's ridiculous, really. I know, I know! It's always some excuse or another—either I'm grading papers or you're in a meeting. But I think we need to make a conscious effort to actually meet up and not just talk about work over coffee. Exactly. I was thinking this weekend, maybe we could meet up with the others. You know, the whole group. I feel like we’ve all drifted apart a bit lately. I can’t believe it’s been a year since we last saw each other. You’ve changed so much, Rob. And you’ve got that same energy as ever, Jane. Still teaching languages, I see. Still doing it, yes. I’ve actually been thinking about doing a postgraduate course in linguistics. It’s been on my mind for ages. That’s fantastic. A postgrad? I’ve been thinking about getting back into photography too.

I just saw a really weird sign on the side of the road. It said “Jamaica Inn” and I got all confused. Is that a real place or are we going somewhere else? It is a real place, love. It's a famous novel by Robert Louis Stevenson, actually. But there’s also a real Jamaica Inn in Cornwall, which is where we're heading. It’s like a haunted house in the stories, but I think it's just a regular inn now. Oh, that’s cool! I’ve read the book before. It was really spooky. But I thought it was set in the moors, not Cornwall. Wait, isn’t the real Jamaica Inn in Devon? You're right, it's in Devon. But the book is set in the real Cornwall, so it’s a bit of a mix. Anyway, we're heading for a different kind of adventure. I just thought of something—do you remember when we used to send telegrams when you were little? Yeah! We used to write messages in Morse code and send them over the telegraph. I loved that. Do you still remember how to do it? I do, actually. You know, I used to work in customer services and we had to handle a lot of old-style communications. But I think it’s more fun to talk about the books we’ve read. What about  The Wizard of Oz ? I still remember the scarecrow and the tin man. Oh, definitely! I used to read  Alice in Wonderland  when I was younger. I still love the way Lewis Carroll uses words and logic. It’s like a puzzle. That’s what makes it so special. And you know, talking about books makes this drive more interesting. We can even talk about how technology has changed the way we read. I remember when we had to use braille for the blind. It was so different from now. Yeah, and it’s amazing how we can access so much information now, even on the road. But I still think there’s something magical about being in a caravan, like the ones we saw on the way here. I love the way the wind turbines look against the sky. They do look like giants walking on the hills. And don’t get me started on the scenery. I’ve never seen so many flowers in one place.

So, I was just thinking about that time I tried to cheat at Monopoly. I got so obsessed with buying properties, I ended up owing my dad a fortune in plastic money.      You think that's bad? She always caught me, but I’d just laugh and say, “It’s called strategy, love.”      That’s nothing. I once tried cheating at chess by moving my queen twice in one turn. My dad nearly had a heart attack. He still won, though.      You know, I was telling my mum about that. I’d be the first to sign up.

Right, so I was at the pub last night and this bloke was like, “You got to be joking, you’re not smoking anymore?” I said, “Nah, I’ve given it up. Not since uni, honestly.” Oh no, really? I’m trying to save up for a deposit on a place near uni, and every time I think about buying a pack of fags, I just think, “This is not helping.” I’ve been thinking about it too. Maybe I should try again.

Hey, I've been meaning to ask you—what's been going on with you lately? I feel like we haven't had a proper catch-up in ages. Oh, I know, I've been so busy with my exhibitions and trying to get some time to myself. I've been working on a new series of paintings inspired by my time in Vienna. So, I just had a really weird moment at the supermarket. I was trying to buy some protein powder for my gym session, and this guy came up to me and said, “You sure you’re not a woman?” Like, what? I didn’t even know what he was talking about. I was just looking at the label.      Oh no, that’s so frustrating. It’s like people still think that men are the only ones who go to the gym. I mean, I was in a gym once and a guy walked up to me and asked me if I was a  girl  because I was lifting weights. It’s just  everywhere .      Exactly. And it’s not just the gym, it’s everywhere. The other day I was driving and there was this guy in the car next to me, and he just turned around and started making comments about my driving. Like, “You’re not even trying, are you?” I didn’t even know what he was talking about.      I’ve had that happen too. I mean, I was driving with my friend and we were both in the car, and two guys in a van just started shouting at me for  driving too fast . It was so rude. But it’s not like I was doing anything wrong – I was just driving the speed limit.      It’s so tiresome. I mean, I’m not trying to be dramatic, but it’s like we live in a world where someone has to always be looking over their shoulder. I don’t even know how to respond sometimes. I just want to say, “Yes, I  am  a woman, and I  am  driving, and I  am  lifting weights, and I  am   English .” But they just don’t get it.      I think it’s part of the whole gender issue, you know? Like, women are always being judged for what they do. I remember when I first started teaching, I was told I’d never be taken seriously because I was a woman. And now, even when I’m being  professional , people still act like I don’t know what I’m doing.      I get that. I was in the classroom once and the principal said I wasn’t  qualified  to teach because I was “too old.” Like, I was 35, and he said I looked like I was  retiring  or something.

I’ve been meaning to show you these mugs I made last summer. Hand-thrown, you know. I think they’re quite nice, don’t you? Oh, they’re beautiful! I can see the care in every one of them. You’re getting more creative with age, aren’t you? Well, I suppose gardening has given me a bit of a creative streak. Not that I’m suggesting you’ve not been creative, of course. You’ve always had a green thumb, even when you were teaching. I like to think so. Though I’ll admit, I’ve had my share of accidents in the garden. Last week, I accidentally knocked over a bucket of milk and it splattered all over the new shrubs. Oh no! That’s not good. But I’m sure the shrubs will recover. You know, I had a power cut last week too. It was the middle of the night and we had to use flashlights. I was reading, and the dog was barking like it was the end of the world. You don’t say! I once had a power cut and my bird flew out of the window. I spent hours trying to find it. It landed on a neighbor’s roof and wouldn’t come down. I had to call the fire brigade! That’s something else. I still remember the time when we were at that local festival and the weather was just perfect. It rained so much that everyone was dancing in the puddles. It was funny, but also a bit chaotic. Yes, that was a good festival. I still remember the milk man who brought the milk each day. He had this old van and a terrible habit of knocking over the milk bottles. One day, it was a real mess. I remember. I used to tell him he should be a professional spiller. Anyway, I was thinking about decorating the garden room. I’ve been waiting for a nice day to paint the walls. That’s a good idea. I’ve been thinking about putting up some shelves for my books and maybe some plants. I’ve even thought about the spiders. They go in and out of the window sometimes. I’ve seen that. They always seem to know when it’s time to move. I think they have their own lives, really. You never know what they’re up to.

I just got the email from the travel agent about our holiday. We’re going to Spain again this year, like last time. I’m so excited, I can’t wait to see the beaches and try all the tapas. Plus, it’s a chance to celebrate the summer and have some fun. I think I’m ready to go with that idea. I’ll check with the travel agent and see what options they have for a group trip with some of my friends. If we do go to Spain, maybe we can all meet up in Barcelona and have a night out together. That sounds like a perfect plan. Just don’t forget to pack your camera—you’re going to need it for all the beautiful places we’ll see.

I just watched  10 Things I Hate About You  again, and I was like, "Oh my god, this movie is so good!" It’s like,  why  haven’t I seen it before? Yeah, I know, right? It’s one of those classic rom-coms that just never gets old. I mean, the chemistry between Katie and Patrick is  so  on point. I remember when we watched it in class, and the teacher got so distracted by the romantic scenes that she totally missed the whole plot! Oh no, really? That’s the worst. I think I was actually laughing so hard during the balcony scene that I almost wet my pants. But seriously, it’s like the best movie ever. I wish we could just rewatch it every single day. I agree! But I think we should plan a trip to London soon, like, really soon. I mean, we’re both going to be in secondary school for a while, and we’re not going to have time to go out and explore the city. What do you think? Yeah, I mean, I’ve always wanted to go to London. I’ve heard so many stories about it, like the Tower Bridge, and the museums, and the places where all the famous authors lived. I just imagine walking around with a map, and figuring out all the best spots to visit. That would be amazing! I was thinking we could go during the summer. Like, maybe in June or July. We could even plan a whole itinerary. Maybe even stay in a hostel or something. I heard that the student discounts in London are super good. And we could take the tube everywhere—it’s like, so much easier than trying to figure out how to get around on foot. Exactly! And we could also see the West End plays. I mean, we’re young, we’ve got the energy, and we’ve got the time. I just think it’s a once-in-a-lifetime thing. Plus, it’s gonna be so much fun, like,  I can’t wait . I know, right? I’m already imagining it. London, with you by my side.

You know, I was just looking at Facebook this morning. It's all got so complicated now, with all these groups and pages. I can't even remember where I started.      I know, I've been trying to get back on for ages. But every time I try, I get lost in some weird group about chicken pox. I mean, I had it when I was a kid, but now it's like people are obsessed with it.      Didn’t you say your daughter had it last year? I remember her telling me how it was so awful, but then she was fine. Still, I think it’s one of those things that people just get overly excited about on social media.      Yeah, but it’s not just chicken pox. I’ve seen people arguing about breakfast, or even about the best way to wash a car. It’s like everyone’s got an opinion on everything, even if it's not relevant.      I get that, but it’s funny how it’s different for us. We don’t have the time or the energy to go on like that. I mean, I’ve got OCD now, which is more of a problem than any of that stuff.      Oh, really? Is it bad?      Not bad, just… persistent. I can’t stand clutter. I had a drawer full of oddly shaped socks, and I had to throw them all out. It was a relief, but I still feel like I’m not in control.      That’s tough. I’ve heard about OCD before, but I never really understood it. I mean, it’s not like you’re doing something dangerous, right?      It’s not just about cleaning. It can be about thoughts too. Like, you might have a compulsion to check your phone a certain number of times. It’s not something you can just ignore.      Exactly. I’ve had to get help, but it’s hard to explain to people. Most of my friends are long gone or too busy to talk about it. Still, I’m trying to cope.      I understand. It’s not easy, but I think you’re doing okay. And you know what? You don’t have to do it alone. We’re all here.      And if you ever want to talk, we’re always here. Even if it’s about chicken pox or Facebook.      Yeah, or even about religion.

So, I was just telling my niece about the time I tried to teach my cat to fetch. It ran off with the ball and got stuck in the garden shed.      That’s not the first time I’ve seen that happen. My dog once chased a butterfly into the pond and got stuck there for hours.      A lot has changed since the old days. I remember when we had to go to the shop for bread and eggs, and now we just order online.      Yeah, I guess it’s all about convenience. I used to love the way things were before everything was delivered to your door.      I miss the old days, but I suppose it was just the way things were. I remember when we used to take our holidays to Germany, and we’d always get lost.      You didn’t get lost, you got turned around in a foreign country and ended up in a village that didn’t speak English.      That must’ve been terrifying. I’ve only been there once, and I didn’t speak a word of German. I just pointed at the map and asked for directions.      I remember the first time I went there as a boy. I was so nervous, I couldn’t even say “Good morning.”      I wish I could go back and talk to my younger self. I would have told them to be brave and try speaking the language.      It’s all about taking the plunge. I remember once I tried to speak French in Paris, and it was the most embarrassing thing I’ve ever done.      I once tried to order a coffee in Spain and said “café,” which turned out to be the wrong word. The barista just stared at me.      That’s probably the same barista who told me I was “too polite” when I asked for a hair cut.      I bet you got a good cut though.      I think we all have our moments. But what’s important is that we’re here, together, and we’ve got each other.      Yeah, that’s what matters. And I think we should all try to go on holiday together sometime. Maybe to Germany again?      Only if we take someone who speaks the language.      I’ll bring my German textbook. I promise I’ll study hard.      That’s the spirit. I think you’re just being modest.      Well, it’s about time we all started planning.

Hey, mate, how’ve you been? It’s been ages since we last saw each other. I’ve got to say, I’m thrilled to see you here in my new flat in Sussex. I go out of my way to use colloquialisms and regional phrases when I can. It’s funny how people from different areas have such different ways of speaking.      Absolutely. I think that’s one of the things I love most about linguistics.

I just got a call from my sister. She's been really down lately. She's been dealing with some health issues, and I think she's starting to lose hope. I don’t know how to help her without making it worse. That sounds awful. I’m so sorry to hear that. She’s been through a lot, hasn’t she? I remember when we were kids, she was always the strong one. I wonder if she’s feeling like she’s letting everyone down now. She’s been battling cancer for over two years. It’s in remission, but the side effects have been brutal. She’s had to stop working, and she’s been so isolated. I don’t think she’s talking to anyone about it, not even our parents. That’s really sad. I know how hard it is to be in that situation. I had a friend who was diagnosed with breast cancer last year, and it changed everything for her. She had to give up her job, move out of her own home, and deal with the emotional toll. It was heartbreaking to watch. I know. I can’t imagine what she’s going through. But I feel like I should say something, even though I don’t know what. I don’t want to make her feel worse. How do you know when to push and when to leave her alone? That’s the tough part, isn’t it? I think the key is to show up consistently and let her know you’re there. Let her talk, even if it’s not about the illness. Small conversation can make a big difference. Also, remind her of the good times. She’s still the same person she was, even if she’s going through something hard. You’re right. She’s had so many good memories, and I think she needs to remember that. I was thinking about sending her some old photographs of our childhood. Maybe that could help her feel connected to the person she used to be. That sounds like a great idea. I think it’s important to focus on the positives while still being honest about the situation. Also, maybe you could take her out for a walk or something. It’s not about solving her problems, but just being with her. Yeah, that’s what I was thinking.

So, what’s the deal with you two and your obsession with tennis? I swear, every weekend you’re either hitting a ball or talking about coaching!      Yeah, we’re thinking about taking up coaching after school. Dad says it’s a good way to earn some extra cash and get some experience.      I remember when I was your age, I used to play a lot too. My dad was a local coach, so I had the advantage. But I never really took it seriously, I guess.      Wait, so you actually used to play? I mean, like professionally?      No, not professionally. Just for fun, mostly. I was pretty good, though. I think I could have made it if I’d stuck with it.      Maybe we should ask you to coach us! We’re not that bad, are we?      You’re not bad, but you’re not ready for me. You need more discipline. And you need to understand the fundamentals.      Well, if you’re going to be a coach, you better start by getting your own act together first!      Hey, I’ve got a plan! I’m thinking about apprenticeships after school. Maybe in sports coaching or something.      Yeah, I’m thinking the same. My mates and I are trying to figure out what we want to do. I’ve been looking into importing and exporting, but it’s a big move. I need to be careful with the money.      So, is it better to get an apprenticeship or just go straight into something like that? I mean, I’ve heard mixed things about apprenticeships.      It depends on the person. Some people learn best by doing, while others need the structure of a college course. But I’d say an apprenticeship can be a great way to get hands-on experience.      So, maybe we can look into that? Like, do an apprenticeship in sports coaching?

I can’t believe we’re actually on the train to Lancaster. I’ve been waiting for this trip for ages. It’s the first time I’ve been to the north of England, and I’m excited to see the coast. I know, right? It’s going to be a great trip. I’ve heard the coast there is absolutely beautiful. I was thinking about visiting the seaside when I was younger, but I never got around to it. Maybe this will be the time. That would be amazing. I’ve always wanted to go to the coast. Do you remember that time we talked about visiting the coast during university? You even mentioned the cockle disaster in the south of England. It was a funny story, but it really highlighted how regional dialects can vary so much. Exactly! I’ve been reading about how the language industry is evolving, and it’s always interesting to hear what people like you think. Yeah, it’s a bit of a buzzword these days, isn’t it? But I think it’s about more than just buzzwords.

So, I was thinking, do you remember that time we tried to see The Vaccines in Manchester? I think it was like 2013 or something. Oh, I remember! We got there like an hour early, and there was this massive queue. I swear, we were like the third people in line. Oh, I can’t wait to see them. To great music, and great friends. To the best times. Always. You know, I was thinking, maybe we should start a music group. Like, a small band or something. Yeah?
