So, I think we’ve all agreed that the way we’re playing Pandemic is a bit too chaotic. I mean, I’m not even sure who’s in charge of what anymore.      Hey, don’t knock it! We’ve got a unique dynamic here. You know, it’s like we’re all playing the roles of the different countries, and it's actually kind of fun.      Yeah, but I’m not sure we’re even following the rules properly. I mean, we’ve got the flu and the smallpox, but we’re all just passing out cards like it’s a game of chance.      Honestly, I think we should just set some ground rules. Like, who’s responsible for which disease? Maybe we can assign roles based on our skills.      Oooh, that’s an interesting idea. I mean, I’ve always been good at organizing things. Maybe I could take on the smallpox one, you know, since I’ve got the experience from my charity work.      Wait, hold on. I think I’ve got a different perspective. You know, sometimes, when you’re playing with a group, the chaos is part of the fun. It keeps things interesting.      But I think the chaos is getting out of control. We had someone trying to cure the black plague with the wrong vaccine, and then we ended up losing the game because someone got confused about the board.      Hey, that was  you  who got confused about the board, remember?      Oh come on! I was trying to make sure we didn’t all die. I mean, we had three diseases going at once. It was like a real life pandemic.      Honestly, I think the key is to slow down. Pandemic is a game that requires strategy, not just luck. You know, I was a chef, and I learned that timing is everything. Maybe we could all take turns leading the game.      That’s a great idea. If we rotate who leads the game, it might help us all get more involved. I mean, I’ve been watching a lot of strategy games lately, and it really helps to have a clear leader.      I think we should also make sure we’re all playing to the best of our abilities. You know, I’ve seen some really strange moves in this game. Like, someone once tried to build a research station on a city that didn’t even exist.

Alright, let’s get this started. I’ve been dying to tell you all about my recent trip to the Lake District. It was absolutely magical, and I’m still reeling from it. Oh, I’d love to hear about it! I just can’t get over how different my accent is from my parents. I was raised in Gillingham, and I still sound like I’m from the south, but I can’t even tell if I’m from Kent or somewhere else. Alright, I think I've got this sorted, but I just want to make sure I haven't missed anything. I got the form from the uni email this morning, and I’ve been going through it all afternoon. So, I was just thinking about my dream last night. I had this crazy idea that I was running a little café in the countryside, with a big garden and a dog that barked at the mailman. I can't believe we ended up in A&E again. It's like we're playing some kind of sick game. I know, I’m still reeling from the fact that I ended up with a broken arm. I've been thinking a lot lately about starting a small business. I've been meaning to ask you lads, what's the best way to make a proper cup of tea? I got the electric kettle out the other day, but it's not like the old days when we used to boil it on the stove. So, I just got an email about a CRB check for a new job. You know, that police background check thing. I’m starting to feel like I’m applying for something that’s more about my past than my skills. Or at least, not in the way that would show up on a CRB check.      True, but I guess it’s just part of the system. I mean, I’m in a managerial role, and I had to go through the entire process. It was a bit of a hassle, but I guess it’s a requirement. Maybe they’ve been keeping in touch more than we have. It feels like the cancer has taken a lot out of her, but she’s still trying to be there for everyone else. I know. She’s always been the most selfless person. I think that’s part of why it’s so hard on her. She doesn’t want to burden anyone with her problems. That’s why it’s so important for us to be there for her. She needs support, not just from her family, but from her friends too. We should make time for her, even if it’s just a quick call. I agree. And maybe we should also look into the house for sale in the village. It’s been on my mind, and I think it could be a good opportunity. We’ve been talking about moving for a while, and this could be the one.

I swear, I don't know how people do it. Every time I try to take a break, there's someone needing something. It's like the whole building's on fire, and I'm the only fireman. Yeah, I feel you. It's like the minute you get a second to breathe, someone pops up with a problem. I was just sitting there, eating my lunch, and this guy came in screaming about a flat tyre. What's next, a broken toaster? Honestly, it's exhausting. I was doing my shift yesterday, and when I finally got a moment to relax, the head of the building comes in and says there's a leak in the supply room. You know what that means? A whole afternoon of cleaning up after someone else’s mess. I know, I know! I was just trying to read a book last night, and this girl comes in saying her fridge is broken. You think I’m going to help her fix it? I’m not a fridge repair guy, you know! And don’t even get me started on the noise. One of the flats is always playing music at 11 p.m. like it's a party. You think I want to hear that when I'm trying to get some sleep? Yeah, I swear, I could sleep in a tomb. I was trying to catch up on some work last night, and next thing I know, the building is like a nightclub. What's up with people these days? I don’t know, maybe they just don’t care. You think about the ones who have to deal with all this? We’re not even paid enough to handle it properly, and we’re expected to be everywhere at once. Exactly! I mean, I get what we do, but it’s not fair. I’m trying to do a decent job, and I’m still getting yelled at for things that aren’t even my fault. Sometimes I just want to go home and not have to think about it. I hear you. I just hope things get better soon. I feel like I’m always trying to catch up, and it's like the moment I slow down, something else happens. Yeah, man. I can go on forever about this stuff. It's not like I don't have my own problems, but I can't even take a moment to myself.

So, I was in Antwerp last week, and I bumped into this guy I went to university with. We hadn’t seen each other in years, and he was there with his family, doing the Christmas market. It was like a dream come true — well, except for the fact that I had to explain  why  I was in Belgium in the first place.      That’s the best part about being British, isn’t it? We end up everywhere, and we can always find someone from home. Didn’t you say you were in Herne Bay for the shopping?      Yeah, I went to Herne Bay with my sister and her kids. It was chaos, but the seafood was worth it. I swear, if I had known the seafront was this good, I’d have moved there years ago.      I’ve always said Herne Bay is one of the best places for a weekend trip. I used to go there with my mum when I was a kid. She’d take me to the market and buy me sweets.      That sounds like a good memory. I wish I could remember my mum taking me to the market. But I’m sure she did. I just can’t recall it.      Memory’s a funny thing. It fades, but some things stick. Like the time I lost my sister. That’s one I’ll never forget — the way the world seemed to stop.      I’m sorry to hear that. Losing family is the hardest thing. But you know, I’ve been thinking about starting to learn a second language. I’m finally feeling like I can do it, especially with the job I’m doing now.      That’s a great idea. I’ve always wanted to learn French, but I never got around to it. My kids are growing up, and I want to speak to them better.      You know, I used to talk about learning languages all the time. Even when I was working. But retirement hit, and I just… stopped.      You know, it’s funny — I was in a package tour in Dorset last summer. I got so tired of the same line of sight, I started thinking about the box I had on the caravanning trip. You know, the one that broke down and we had to push it for miles?      Oh, I remember that! You were so angry, and I was so tired.

I just saw the news about the equality vote in Ireland — it’s going to be a big deal, right? I mean, I don’t know much about politics, but I know it’s about equal rights for LGBTQ+ people. Yeah, I saw that too. It’s a huge moment for the country. I think it’s going to be one of those things that people are really passionate about. It’s not just about the vote; it's about equality and acceptance. I get it, but it’s still so strange to me. I mean, aren’t people in the UK more progressive? I thought we were ahead of the game when it came to equality. What’s going on with Ireland? It’s not that they’re behind, it’s just that things happen at different times in different places. Ireland is very Catholic in some ways, and even though they’ve made a lot of progress, there’s still a lot of traditional values. This vote is a big shift for them. I can see that. My mum always talks about how things were in the past — like, you couldn’t even say the word “divorce” without getting a lecture. But she’s also one of the more open-minded people I know. I sometimes wonder if she’d be proud of what’s happening now? I think she would. She’s always been a big supporter of equality. But I know she gets a bit embarrassed when I bring up things like that — like, she thinks she’s too old to be part of the “progressive” crowd. Oh, you know her! She’s always trying to convince me that she’s not a “political person,” but she’s got opinions on everything. She even joked about wanting to run for office — “just to teach them what real leadership looks like.” I love it. She’s got such a way with words. And she’s not wrong — sometimes you have to be a bit loud to make a point. Speaking of which, I was just talking to my friend about how when I was a kid, my parents used to vote for every candidate, even if they were weird. That’s not weird — that’s just you. I mean, you were like a walking political debate in the family. I remember you telling me about that time you tried to convince my dad that the election was between two people who were both bad, but one was better.

I've been thinking about the lathe tools I used when I was working in the workshop. They were a bit rough, but I could tell when something was wrong just by looking at it. Oh, I remember you used to do that, Bob. You had a real eye for machinery. I always found it fascinating, though I never had the knack for it myself. Yeah, I used to work with lathe tools too, but more in a management role. I used to review the curriculum for engineering courses. It's funny how the skills can change, but the tools remain the same. That's true, Dave. I still get a bit nostalgic when I see a lathe in a shop. It brings back memories of working with my hands. It's a different kind of satisfaction than what I get these days. I know what you mean, Frank. I used to look after the children and then I retired. Now I just have the hamster. I've been trying to figure out what to do with it. I thought maybe I could put it in the microwave for a few minutes to see what happens—just for fun. Oh, you wouldn't do that! That's dangerous. The hamster would get burned. I remember once I left the microwave door open and it started to heat up, and I had to rush in and turn it off. That sounds like a close call. I once had a situation where the microwave started sparking, and someone had to unplug it. I think it was a faulty circuit board. Well, I don't want to risk anything with my hamster. I just wanted to see if it would move around, you know, like a small animal in the microwave. It's not like it's cooking or anything. I know, but even if it didn't cook, it could be stressed. Animals don't like being put in confined spaces, especially with heat. I remember when I had a small dog, and I once left it in a room for too long, and it got really anxious. That's right. Animals have very sensitive nervous systems. It's amazing how they can sense things we don't. I've read that some animals can detect changes in temperature or even electromagnetic fields. That's interesting, Dave. I'll just stick to feeding it and making sure it has a comfortable place to live.

I just finished transcribing that old letter from the 1950s, and it made me think—what if the whole mirror-writing thing is a sign of some hidden genius? I mean, you know those cryptic crossword puzzles we used to do, right? It’s like the mind is just working in reverse. I don’t know, I think mirror-writing is just a symptom of being too tired. I remember my grandmother used to write in reverse when she was feeling unwell. It was quite a puzzle to figure out. But anyway, I was just talking to the bank about the new interest rates. They’re still keeping it low, which is good for us, but the debt crisis still feels like it’s hovering over the country like a storm cloud. Oh, I agree, the debt situation is worrying. But I think the real issue is house prices. It’s like they’ve gone up so fast, it’s almost irresponsible. I mean, how can people afford to live in the UK anymore? Exactly, I’ve been thinking about that. My cousin just bought a place in London, and it’s like he’s paying three times what it cost a few years ago. I tell him, “You might as well live in a mansion and work from a tent!” Ha! I know someone who’s trying to sell their house for a third of what they paid. He’s been trying to get it off the market for years. The real estate market is like a never-ending joke. I remember reading a story in the paper about a cat that got into a fight with a drone. It was the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever seen. I don’t know how you can have a cat that’s smart enough to chase a drone, but also stupid enough to get hurt. Yeah, that was the highlight of the day. I mean, I still have that story bookmarked on my phone. It’s like the cat was trying to make a statement. Or maybe it was just being reckless. I think it was just a case of the cat being confused. I mean, drones are moving so fast, how would a cat even know what it was? It’s like the cat was trying to run from a ghost. I still think it’s a sign that our pets are becoming more aware of the modern world.

I can't believe the amount of time they're spending on LEGO Ninjago and Minecraft. They've been glued to the screen for hours, and I haven’t even managed to get them to read a single book. I know, Mummy! I tried to read them a story, but they just kept asking if there was more action in the game. It's like they're not even listening. I prefer Minecraft. I think it helps me build things. I built a whole castle in my world today. It's got towers and everything. That's great, but isn’t it just a game? I mean, I can see the value in creativity, but I worry about them getting too caught up in virtual worlds instead of real-life activities. I hear you, Mummy, but they seem happy. And it's not like they're doing anything harmful. They’re just playing. Besides, I think it helps them relax after a long day at school. Yeah, I get stressed sometimes when I can't figure out how to build something in Minecraft. But when I play, I feel better. I guess it’s a different way of relaxing for them. But I still feel like there's a balance to be struck. I worry about them not developing the habit of reading, especially with so many stories out there. I know, Mummy. Maybe next time we can read together. I like stories too. And I can help them make a story in Minecraft. Maybe we can combine both worlds? That sounds fun! I can build the setting and you can tell the story. I can even make the characters come to life in the game! That's a brilliant idea! Maybe we can do that. It might be a good way to encourage them to use their imagination in both worlds. But for now, I just want them to have fun. I guess it's okay as long as they're not neglecting their schoolwork. Yeah, I think they're doing well at school. They just need a bit more time to unwind. And I think playing with LEGO and Minecraft helps them do that. I agree! I feel more focused after playing. I can even solve problems in the game, like building bridges or figuring out how to get through a level. I’ll admit, I’m not entirely sure what they're doing half the time, but I suppose it's better than nothing.

So, how was your trip to the Lake District? I’ve been meaning to go for ages, and I got to see some of the places you mentioned in your blog.      It was amazing, honestly! We stayed in this little cabin by Windermere, and it was so peaceful. The only downside was the weather – it rained most of the time, but that only made the views more dramatic. You’d have loved the way the mist rolled in over the hills in the morning.      Oh, I’d love to go there when it’s not raining! I’ve heard the lakes are absolutely stunning, especially in the fall. Have you seen the fall colors around there? I’m hoping to visit next October when the leaves are changing.      Yes, I’ve heard the colors are incredible. If you’re planning a trip, let me know – I’d love to tag along. I’ve been thinking about doing some hiking and getting back in shape, so it would be a good excuse to get out of the city for a few days.      That’s a great idea! I’ll check the dates and get back to you. By the way, did you hear about the new local café that opened up in Lichfield? It’s supposed to be really good. I got the chance to try it last week, and the coffee was amazing.      I have heard about it! I’m going to check it out this weekend. I’ve been meaning to support local businesses more. I just need to make sure I can get there before the weekend rush. I have a group of friends meeting me there for brunch.      That sounds like a good plan. I’ll be there too – I’m meeting a few friends for a coffee and a catch-up. I was just telling them how much I’ve missed our chats lately. It’s been a while since we all got together properly.      I know, it’s been too long. I’ve been so busy with work, and I haven’t had the chance to catch up. I feel like I’ve been trying to catch up on everything – work, study, and now my social life.      Same here! Between classes and part-time work, it’s been a bit of a balancing act. But I really miss our usual hangouts. I think it’s time we plan a proper get-together.

So, I just got this sandwich from the café, and it’s the best thing since sliced bread. They have this special thing with tomato and something else—wait, what was it again?      Oh, you mean the “war hero” sandwich? The one with the military-themed sauce? I saw the menu, and it said something about 'honour and glory.'      That’s the one. I think the sauce is supposed to taste like victory, but honestly, it’s just spicy. You can tell it’s trying too hard.      Yeah, I get it. It’s like they’re trying to make a statement about the army, right? But I still like it. It’s got that bold flavor.      I told my brother about it, and he said it reminded him of the time he had to eat a military ration during a school trip. He said it was the worst thing he’d ever tasted.      That’s rough. I remember when we had to do that field trip to the museum—had to eat those sandwiches and drink from plastic bottles. I still don’t like the idea of military stuff.      Yeah, I get that. My cousin’s in the army, and I’ve seen how it works. But I still think it’s cool, you know? It’s like a badge of honor.      I guess it depends on your perspective. For some people, it’s all about discipline and courage. But for others, it’s just another part of the system.      Exactly. I mean, it’s not like we all get to choose, right? Some people are forced into it. I think about the school prefects too. You know, they’re like mini leaders, but it’s not always fair.      True. I had a prefect last year who treated everyone like they were enemies. It was exhausting. I mean, the whole point of it is to help, not to make people feel worse.      Yeah, and then there’s the racism angle. Sometimes the lunches we bring in are better than the ones they serve. I mean, I know it’s not the school’s fault, but it still feels unfair.      That’s one of the reasons I started bringing my own food. I don’t want to feel like I’m being treated differently. It’s about respect, right?      Totally. And I’ll admit, I’ve been watching a lot of documentaries lately—about the Vietnam War, and the military.

I just can’t believe how much we’ve changed since we were 13. I mean, it feels like yesterday we were trying to sneak out of English lessons to go to the canteen. Now we’re both doing A-levels and complaining about physics teachers like it’s the end of the world. Yeah, I remember we used to sit in the back of the classroom and try to read  17 Again  in our English lessons. The teacher never noticed, but we’d get into so much trouble if she did. It was the best way to pass the time when we were bored out of our minds. Still, I’ll never forget how much we used to talk about our form tutor. Mr. Harrow was such a nightmare. He thought he was the smartest person in the school, but honestly, he barely passed his own A-levels. I remember one time he got confused between Newton’s laws and Einstein’s theory of relativity. It was hilarious in hindsight. Oh, we used to laugh so hard when he tried to explain physics to us. I mean, he had the textbook open, and he was reading from it like it was a novel. He didn’t even know how to use a calculator properly. I reckon he got a D in his physics A-level. And don’t even get me started on our English teacher, Mrs. Thompson. She was so strict, but she had the best way of making us read books we’d never normally pick up. I mean, she made us read  17 Again  in the same week we had a school play about Shakespeare. It was a nightmare, but I still think it helped us appreciate literature more. I know, right? She even made us write essays about the film and then compare it to a classic novel. I think it was the most creative thing she ever did. At least she wasn’t as boring as Mr. Harrow. I miss those days. It feels like the school years are flying by, and we’re already halfway through our A-levels. I wonder what we’ll be like in ten years. I mean, will we still be best friends? Definitely. We’ve been through too much together. Even if we end up in completely different careers, I know we’ll still find a way to stay in touch.

So, what’s the word on the street? You lot haven’t mentioned Transylvania yet. I’ve been dying to go there for ages. I’ve got this friend who’s been there twice, and he swore the forests are like something out of a horror movie.      Oh, I’ve heard enough about Transylvania from you! You’ve been talking about it since we were in university. But seriously, I’m thinking about going this summer. I’ve got a few weeks off, and I heard the villages are super quaint, like the ones in the movies.      That sounds cool. I’ve only been to Romania once, and it was a bit of a mess. I got lost in the countryside and ended up at this café in a village that was basically in the middle of nowhere. But the food was amazing—like, seriously, the cheese was out of this world.      You lot are obsessed with Eastern Europe. I mean, why not just go to Budapest? It’s got the same vibe, and it’s way more accessible. Plus, I’ve been meaning to visit the thermal baths.      Budapest’s nice, but Transylvania has that old-world charm. Plus, I’ve read that there are these underground caves near the city. I want to go spelunking!      Spelunking? You’re not scared of the dark, are you? I’ve heard that some of the caves are like walking through a prehistoric forest. It’s seriously eerie.      I’d do it. I’ve got a fear of the dark, but I’m not a coward. If you need someone to accompany you, I’m up for it. Maybe we can do it together.      I’m more into the scenic routes. I was thinking about taking a road trip this summer. I’ve got a friend who’s from Australia, and he’s suggesting we head to the outback.      Wait, you said you’re an Aussie? You’ve got that accent—wait, no, you’re Australian but you speak like a Brit? That’s confusing.      Yeah, I grew up in Australia, but I’ve been in the UK so long that I’ve kind of lost my accent. Plus, I’ve been working as a barista in London, so the lingo has shifted.      That explains a lot. I’ve been trying to learn some Australian expressions. Like “arvo” or “barbie.” It’s fun, but I still get confused when people say “g’day” when they mean “hello.”

I just got a call from the photographer. He's going to do the family photos tomorrow at the park. We need to make sure everyone's dressed nicely and ready by 10 a.m. Are we doing the aerial hoop and the muddy obstacle course as well? I heard the photoshoot includes some fun activities. Yeah, I think that's part of the package. It's supposed to be a family day out. Dad said it's all included. It's a great idea. It’ll give the photographer some interesting shots. I wonder if Alice in Wonderland is going to be part of the theme. I've been listening to that album a lot lately. Alice in Wonderland? My teacher said it's one of the most interesting stories ever written. I think the music is really catchy too. I like the music. It reminds me of the party we had last weekend. We even had a dance floor. Mum said it was the best party she's ever been to. I had a great time. I think we should invite some friends for the photoshoot. Maybe even some of the people who came to the party. It would be nice to have a bigger group. But what if we don’t have enough space? The park isn’t that big. I think it's manageable. The photographer said he can set up in a corner and still have space for the activities. Maybe we can have the photoshoot in the morning and the activities in the afternoon. That sounds like a plan. I can help set up the obstacle course. I think I remember how to do it from the party. Great, I’ll help you. I’ve been wanting to try the aerial hoop again. I think I’ve gotten a bit better since the last time. You're not going to do that, are you? I heard it's really high. Are you sure you're ready? I think I am. It's just a little bit scary, but I’m determined. Besides, if I don’t try, I’ll always wonder what it’s like. I’m going to try it too. I think I can do it. Maybe we can even go together. That sounds like a good idea. We’ll have to make sure we’re both wearing the right gear. Also, what about the muddy obstacle course?

Well, I suppose we should start by talking about the exams. I heard they’re coming up next month. I’m not sure how they’ll go, but I do know the kids are under a lot of pressure. Yeah, I heard about that too. My daughter’s been practicing like mad. She’s doing her GCSEs next year. I don’t know how she’ll manage with all the stress. I used to be a childminder, so I know how much it can affect the kids. You’re not the only one who knows that. I’ve been a teacher for years, and I can tell you, pressure points are everywhere. I even had a student who got so nervous before exams he started biting his nails. Yeah, I’ve heard about that. I mean, I’m still at school, but I can tell you, even the teachers are stressed. I was supposed to do a mock exam last week, and I just sat there like a complete doofus. Hey, did you see the latest tweets about the football match? It was crazy watching the highlights. My cousin was in the crowd, and he said the fans were going wild. Football, eh? I used to love it when I was younger. I still go to a few matches if I can. Our local team’s not doing too well, though. I think the pressure’s getting to them. I can imagine. Still, it’s good to have something to look forward to. I mean, I’ve been trying to get the kids to take up some sport. It’s good for them, you know. I agree. My sister’s got her daughter playing netball. It’s amazing to see how much it helps them focus. It’s something they can do without all the pressure of exams. Yeah, I think I might try netball next term. I mean, I’m not the best, but it’s fun. I’ve got this new friend who’s into it, and she’s been trying to drag me along. I’d say you’re a big fan already. Anyway, what about you two? Are you doing anything special this weekend? I was thinking of going on a picnic with the lads. We haven’t done that in a while. I’ve been feeling a bit down lately, so it’s good to get out.

I just finished a game of Chinese chess with Dad. He’s getting pretty good at it, actually. I think he’s been studying the rules more seriously now. That’s impressive. I remember when I first tried it with him, he kept moving his pieces around like he was trying to make a point. Now he’s actually strategizing. It’s like he’s got a new hobby. I’ve only played a couple of times, but I find it intriguing. The way the pieces move is so different from Western chess. I mean, the rook can’t just move straight—it has to jump over the others. It’s like a different kind of logic. Exactly. You have to think differently. It’s not just about capturing pieces—it’s about controlling the board. I think Dad mentioned something about it being a game of patience, too. That’s true. I’ve been reading about it a bit. I mean, I’m an English language instructor, so I like to understand different cultures, even through games. I even tried to explain the rules to a few students last week, but they were more interested in the history of the game. Did you tell them about how it’s played in China? I read that it’s been around for centuries. They call it Xiangqi, right? Yes, that’s right. And it’s got quite a rich history. I think it was mentioned in some old books I read about Chinese literature. It’s funny how something so simple can have such a deep cultural significance. I wonder what my grandfather would have thought if he saw me playing it now. He used to talk about how he learned it as a boy in China during the war. He always said it helped him keep his mind sharp during tough times. That’s amazing. I bet it helped him survive. I mean, he was in the army, right? It’s like having a mental escape. Exactly. It’s something you can take anywhere. I think that’s why it’s still popular in many parts of the world. Even in South Korea and New Zealand, people play it. I’ve seen some videos online where they compare it to Western chess. It’s interesting how different the strategies are. But it’s also pretty satisfying when you finally win. I’m still figuring out the best moves.

I can't believe we're still in this bistro, talking about everything from MOTs to Netflix. It feels like we’ve been here forever. I know, it's like we're stuck in a time loop. But honestly, I like it. It's nice to chat without worrying about deadlines or students for once. It’s strange, isn't it? I used to think I’d never be in a place like this, doing this. I mean, I'm 46, unemployed, and yet here we are, having a chat over coffee in a Polish bistro. Yeah, I guess life does have a funny way of throwing you curves. I still can't believe I’m a teacher, let alone one who teaches English as a foreign language. Ten years ago, I would never have thought I’d be doing this. It must be a good move for you. I envy you in a way. I’ve been thinking about getting back into teaching, but the idea of working abroad, even for a while, feels impossible. I don’t even know where to start. I know, it’s daunting. But honestly, it’s not as bad as you think. I did a few months in Germany, and it was a great experience. You learn so much – about yourself, about the world, and sometimes even about your students. I don’t know if I’m ready for that. I’ve been out of work for so long. I just feel like I’m not useful anymore. Like my past career is just a memory. You're not a memory, you're still here, talking to me, right? And you’re still trying to find your way. That’s not useless. That’s just... waiting for the right moment. You know what I’ve been thinking? I’ve been thinking about pensions. I mean, I’m not even close to being eligible, but I feel like I’m already planning for the worst. I know, it's something we all have to think about. But you know, I’m not sure I want to wait until I’m 60 to enjoy my time. I’d rather work part-time, maybe even teach again, if it feels right. I think I might try that. Just something to keep me busy and not feel so lost. It’s funny, I used to be the one telling other people to plan ahead, and now I’m the one who needs to start.

So, do you know what you're going to study at university yet? I heard you're thinking about Human Sciences or Maths? Yeah, I'm still trying to decide. I like Maths, but I also enjoy the idea of studying human behavior and psychology. It's a bit of a toss-up. That makes sense. I'm going for Human Sciences too. I wanted to focus on something that combines both social sciences and biology, you know? Cool. It's a bit of a journey, though. You have to decide what you're passionate about. Do you think you'll study in London or go somewhere else? I'm leaning towards staying in London. It's closer to home, and I figure I can get some work experience while I'm there. Plus, I've got a few friends here I'd like to keep in touch with. That sounds smart. I was actually thinking about going to Manchester for Maths. My cousin studies there, and he says it's a great place for math and engineering. Manchester's a good choice. Have you thought about drinking or anything like that? I heard the bars there are pretty lively. Honestly, I’ve been trying to cut back. I’m not sure how much alcohol I’ll be able to handle at university. I’ve had some bad experiences before. Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to drink more responsibly too. I’m not a big fan of alcohol, but I know it's part of the social scene. Right, and I’d rather not be the odd one out. Still, I think I’d like to try some of the local beers. I heard there are some great ones in the Westfield area. Definitely. I’ve been into cooking too. I’ve been trying out a few new recipes lately. My mum’s got this old cookbook from her childhood that I’ve been going through. Oh, I’ve got one of those too. My nan gave it to me. I’ve been making some of the traditional English dishes. It’s always fun to cook with a family recipe. That’s cool. I think I’m going to try making some of the dishes from the cookbook. I might even throw a little cookout for my mates. So, I've been thinking about the new tax changes they've announced, and I wanted to go over it with you. I know you're studying economics, so I thought you'd appreciate the details. I just had the most frustrating meeting today. You know how it is—when you think you’ve got everything sorted, and then someone throws a curveball. I can't believe the conference is just a week away. I’ve been trying to get my head around the presentation I need to do, but honestly, I’m more nervous than excited. I know, it’s the same for me. I can't believe we've been on the road for six hours already. I thought it would take less time. I got lost twice, and now I'm more confused than I was at the start. So, I've been reading up on gerontology lately. It's fascinating how telomeres play a role in aging. I mean, if we can slow down or even reverse their shortening, that could really change things. But even if we do figure out a way to slow aging, there are still so many other things to consider. Like, how does that affect population growth, resource allocation, and the environment? Mum, you’d think with all that coffee you drink, you’d have a proper coffee maker, not that thing you call a coffee machine! Oh, come on, Elise, it’s not that bad. I can't believe it's been almost two years since we last met! I was just thinking about that trip to Cornwall last summer. Remember when we got lost trying to find that seaside café? Grandma, I’ve brought you some sweets from the shop. I got the ones with the funny faces on them. You remember those, don’t you? Oh, I do, love. They were all the rage when I was your age. So, what do you think about that blood moon last night? I swear it looked like a giant red apple in the sky. It was pretty spooky, wasn’t it?      Yeah, it was weird. I didn’t get to see it because I was out with my mates, but I heard it was really bright. My dad said it’s not a bad omen, though. He’s always talking about old superstitions.      My grandfather used to say that a blood moon means something big is about to happen. I don’t know if I believe that, but I do like how it looks. It’s like the sky is on fire.      Oh, you know what I think? I think it’s just the way the moon lights up the night. But I’ll admit, it’s a beautiful sight, especially when you’re out in the countryside.      Yeah, especially in Fitzgeralds Park. We used to go there all the time when I was a kid. You know, that’s where I met your mom, Aunty Mary. She used to take us for walks and tell stories about the stars.      Yeah, I remember hearing those stories. I didn’t think much of them back then, but now I’m starting to appreciate them. So, I've been meaning to ask you, how did you find the job interview for that new venture you're looking into? I heard it was a bit of a gamble, given the market these days. So, what do you think about that cow we passed just now? I swear it was staring right at me like it knew I was going to miss the turn.      You know, I had a cow once—well, not a cow, but a bull. That’s wild. I’ve never seen anything like that. I mean, I’ve heard stories, but I didn’t think it was real.      Oh, it was real alright. It was a big black bull, and he came charging at me like he was going to take me down. I had to swerve just in time. I still remember the smell of hay and manure that followed me for days.      I think it’s amazing how animals can be so unpredictable. I mean, I’ve always liked animals, but I’ve never been that close to a farm. I live in the city, and the only time I see cows is when I’m driving through the countryside, like on the way to work.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I grew up in Sunderland, so I was always around farms. My granddad used to have a few sheep, and I used to help out when I was kid. It was always fun, even though I got covered in dirt.      You’re from Sunderland? That’s where I used to live too, in Timperley. I used to know your granddad, actually. He was quite a character. Always had that little lamb that followed him everywhere.      Wait, really? That’s crazy. I didn’t even know he had a nickname. I think he called it “Lamb Chops.” He used to brag about how it was the smartest sheep he ever saw.      That’s classic. My dad used to tell stories like that too. He said he had a cat that would sit on his keyboard and demand food every morning. I still can’t believe that.      That’s the thing about animals. They have their own way of doing things. You learn to respect them, even if they don’t respect you back.      Definitely. They’re wild, but in their own way, they’re just like us.

So, I've been thinking about the school anniversary dinner next week. You know, it's been years since I was a teacher, but I still get a bit nostalgic when I hear about the old days. We’ve got this great group of people here, and we should make the most of it. Speaking of which, have you thought about the family trip next summer?

I just got the Parent’s Evening feedback, and I needed to talk to someone about it. It’s been a bit of a shock, honestly. Is it bad? I heard you were worried about the Maths results. The acrobats were amazing! Did you like the animals too? I loved the elephants. Of course! They were so big and gentle. But I guess not everyone is into the circus. Some people prefer books. Have you read any good ones lately? I read a book about a boy who goes to a circus and saves the day. It was really exciting! That sounds like a good one. I think it’s important to encourage creativity and curiosity. Maybe we can make a plan for after school. I was thinking about doing some fun activities to help the kids with their learning. Like what? Maybe we can do some hands-on projects, like making pizzas or baking, to teach basic math concepts. It’s more engaging than just sitting at a table with a worksheet. Pizza sounds fun! I like pizza. Exactly! And maybe we can combine that with some reading. World Book Day is coming up, and I think we could have a themed evening. We could set up a little book corner and even have a small show or something. That sounds like a great idea! I love reading, and I’d love to be part of that. Good. Now, I have to say, I also had a weird conversation with the teacher about what cooked human flesh smells like.

So, I was just telling Oisin that he's got the voice of a politician already. I remember when I was teaching, I had a student who used to say things like, “I don’t think that’s the best option, but I’ll still support it.” It was like watching a future leader in the making.      Speaking of politics, have you thought about the birthday party yet? Not that I’d say no anyway.      Wait, can I help? I’m not doing anything else today. I just want to be part of the fun.      That’s the spirit. You can help with the invitations. And maybe you can tell the story about the time we tried to set up a birthday bash in the garden and ended up with a flood because of the sprinklers.      Oh, that was a disaster. We had mud, rain, and a very confused toddler. It was like something out of a comedy show.      You know, I’ve been thinking about the rugby match this weekend. We should all go together. It’s a chance to bond, and maybe get some fresh air. Oisin’s always talking about it anyway.

So, do you know what’s the definition of a word that’s spelled the same forwards and backwards? Hmm, not off the top of my head. Is it something like a palindrome? Yeah, that’s it! Palindromes. They’re words that read the same forwards and backwards, like “madam” or “level.” Oh, I love that! I used to play with those a lot when I was younger. I even had a game where I’d write down random words and check if they were palindromes. But I think I’ve gotten a bit rusty. That sounds fun. I’ve never really played with word games like that before. I mean, I know about anagrams, but palindromes are something new to me. Yeah, I’ve heard of them, but I never really tried to create my own. I guess it’s like a challenge—trying to think of words that fit the pattern. Exactly! It’s like a puzzle. Sometimes you get stuck, and then you just have to think creatively. I remember once trying to make a palindrome with a six-letter word. I ended up with something like “deified.” “Deified” – that’s a good one! I like that because it’s not just a simple word; it’s got that extra layer of meaning. And it’s got a nice ring to it. I think I could use that in a presentation I’m preparing. Maybe I can make a slide about palindromes and how they’re used in language. That’s a great idea! I mean, they’re not just fun—they can also be used to show how language works in a clever way. Like, they’re symmetrical in structure, which is kind of fascinating. I never thought of it like that. I mean, symmetry is all around us, right? In architecture, in art, even in nature. It’s interesting how that same concept applies to words. Yeah, it’s like a mirror image. It makes me think of how the brain processes language—it’s got to be pretty complex to recognize the symmetry in words. I guess it does. Maybe that’s why I like it so much. It’s like a small peek into the mechanics of language. I can see how that would be a great topic for a discussion, or even a little competition. Do you think we could turn this into a game?

So, remember when we used to nap in the back of the bus on the way to uni? I swear one time I woke up to find my shoe had somehow ended up in the glove compartment.      Oh, you were  so  dramatic about it. You cried like a baby, and I just laughed and said, “You’re not even wearing that shoe!”      Oh, don’t act like you weren’t the one who fell asleep with your head on my shoulder. You were the one who snored so loud the whole bus heard you.      Yeah, but you were the one who kept saying “I’m not dreaming, I’m not dreaming” every time you woke up. It was like a horror movie.      I still get flashbacks of that. I mean, we were 19 and barely out of our teens. What else were we supposed to be doing?      Yeah, and we were so caught up in our music obsession that we’d just sit and listen to records for hours. I think we even got a few people to join us in the back of the pub once.      That’s when we started the “the music of our youth” thing. Silly, right? But we were so into it.      I still miss those days. It feels like we’re always on the move now—uni, then jobs, then… well, you know.      Yeah, I know. But you know what? I still listen to those old records every now and then. Sometimes I’ll pull out that old mixtape we made together. It’s got every song we ever liked.      I remember that. We called it “The Lost Sounds of Warrington.” I think we even included a copy of that one picture we took of us in front of the old town hall.      That’s the one where you’re trying to pose like a rockstar and I’m just holding your guitar.      Oh, that was  so  you! You were the one who told me I looked like a “toddling rock legend.”      It was a  masterpiece .      To the lost sounds of Warrington.      And to napping, music, and all the weird things we used to do.      And to arguing about whose DJ mix was better.      That was always the worst. You know, I still can’t hear that one song without thinking of your face.      What song?      “Do You Remember?” by The Smiths. It was the one you insisted we play at every party.

I just got the email from the council. They've confirmed the meeting is on Thursday next week, and it's going to be a full committee. I can't believe it's already Friday. I feel like we've been talking all week, and yet it's still got to go on. Have you seen the latest news about the council? Did you go to that old school friend’s birthday last weekend? I heard it was a disaster. Oh, that was a nightmare. I kept thinking, “Is that really Jane?” But they were all so different. Some of them are doing well, others have gone off the rails. It’s wild. Yeah, it’s like they’re all living different lives now. I’m going to try to catch it this weekend though. I go to the cinema every Friday if I can. You should come with me sometime. I might just do that. Although I’m not sure if I’ll be up for it after a long shift.

Mate, I swear I just saw an ad for a car boot sale that said "Everything you need to start a new life—except a passport and a credit card." That’s just ridiculous. Oh, I bet you’re not the only one who’s seen that. I saw it on my mom’s phone yesterday. She was like, “This is just a scam, obviously.” But I think it’s more about the nostalgia, you know? Like, what if you could go back and buy all the stuff you never needed? Yeah, but isn’t that the whole point of car boot sales? You go in with no idea what you’re going to find and come out with a bunch of random junk you’ll never use. I once bought a lamp that looked like a giant teapot. It’s been sitting in my hallway for three years now. Wait, really? I’ve got this weird lamp that looks like a giant teapot, too. I keep telling myself I’ll use it for a party, but I never do. I think it’s just a way for people to feel like they’re getting a bargain, even if it’s not worth the price. Exactly! And it’s not just stuff. I think the real point is the experience. You get to chat with people, see what they’re selling, and maybe even pick up a few useful things. Like that time I bought a vintage radio for a fiver. It worked, too. Until the batteries died. That sounds like a classic car boot story. I think I’d rather just go to an online store and get what I want without the hassle. But then again, I do miss the chaos of it all. Especially the people who sell things they don’t really need. It’s like a little bit of retail therapy, but for the seller. I get that. I mean, if you’re not into it, you can just walk away. No pressure. And if you do buy something, it’s like you’ve got a little adventure every time you go. Yeah, and it’s not like you can just buy that same lamp online without the whole…  shudder … customer service experience. I mean, I’ve tried. It’s just not the same. True. I think I’ll stick with the car boot sales, even if I end up with a teapot lamp.

So, I've been thinking about this new music app I downloaded last week. It’s called  SoundFlow , and it’s supposed to mix genres like never before. I mean, it’s got everything from classical to hip-hop, all in one place. Have any of you tried it?      I tried it last weekend. It was pretty good, honestly. I found a playlist that mixed a Beethoven symphony with some modern trap beats. It was odd, but kind of interesting. I couldn’t stop listening. You should give it a go.      That sounds bizarre, but maybe that’s the point? I mean, I love experimental stuff. I’ve been thinking about trying to produce my own music, you know? I’ve got a bit of a setup at home. I just need to get the right software.      Oh, that’s brilliant! I’ve been meaning to get into music production too. I’m a journalist, so I do a lot of interviews with musicians, and I’m always fascinated by how they create their sound. It’s like a whole different world.      Speaking of music, did you hear about the new album from that band  Echoes of the Past ? They’re doing something really unique with sampling old folk songs and blending them with electronic beats. I think I’ll join in too. I’ve been working on some ideas for a new project at work. Maybe we could even set up a little group podcast or something. It’d be a great way to combine our interests in music and media.      I’m in! I’ve been thinking about starting a podcast for a while now, and this seems like the perfect opportunity.

So, I was just thinking about the old days, you know, when we first moved into the area in the 1960s. It was such a different time, wasn’t it?      Oh yes, it was. I remember when I came here for my first interview as a teacher. I had just finished my training and was desperate to get out of the town I grew up in. I had no idea what to expect.      And you were in a place that was still quite run-down, weren’t you? I remember when I moved here for my postgrad in dentistry. I had to find a place to live, and I ended up renting a flat in a bit of a gritty area. Still, it was a good move for me.      That sounds like a lot of work. I came here for my dentist training, and I had to travel all the way from Birmingham to Manchester. I ended up in a place that was more like a boarding house, you know, shared rooms and all that. It was quite an adjustment.      I can imagine. I moved here in the 60s as well, and I remember having to rent a small cottage on the edge of town. The first few months were tough, but the view from the window was beautiful, and I made some great friends.      And did you ever meet your wife there?      Yes, I did. She came to visit one day and got lost trying to find the place. We ended up meeting at the local pub, and it was love at first sight. Still is, I suppose.      That’s romantic. I met my wife when I was teaching at the local college. She was a student, and I was giving a lecture on dental hygiene. She asked a question, and I was so flustered I stumbled over my words. She laughed, and that was the start of our relationship.      I met mine in a different way. I was doing a postgrad course in Athens. You remember the time we had to take that trip? It was the first day of the military dictatorship, and we were all caught in the middle of it. That was one of the most stressful times of my life.      Oh my goodness, that must have been a nightmare. I can only imagine what your time was like. I had to travel for a few months when I first started my teaching career, but nothing like that.

I just love this place, Marion. It’s so peaceful here. I’ve had my own gallery in Taunton for years, though I’m officially retired now. But I still take on a few custom pieces and host little art shows when I can. It’s a quiet life, but I wouldn’t trade it for anything. That sounds fascinating. I used to work as a speech and language therapist, but I’ve been retired for a while now too. I used to work with kids, which was rewarding, but it’s nice to have the time to do what I want. Did you always want to be an artist? Oh, I did. I grew up in Somerset, near Wells. My father was a blacksmith, and my mother was a painter. I spent a lot of time in the countryside, surrounded by nature, and I think that shaped my love for art. I studied at the University of Bath, actually—graduated with a degree in fine arts. But after university, I ended up working in antiques, which led me to starting my own gallery. It was a bit of a twist, but I loved every minute of it. That’s quite the journey. I was born in Sydney, but my parents were both English. I spent my childhood moving around a lot. I remember my father would take us to the beach every weekend, and I used to sketch the ocean and the waves. I never thought I’d end up back in England, but here I am, retired and living in Taunton. That’s lovely. It’s amazing how the places we grow up in shape who we become. I sometimes think about my childhood—those long afternoons spent sketching in the garden with my mother. I still have some of those old drawings, they’re tucked away in a box in my attic. I’d love to find them again sometime. That’s a beautiful thought. I still have a few things from my childhood too. I have a little notebook I used to write in as a kid, full of poems and drawings. I always thought I’d become a writer, but life had other plans. Still, I find comfort in the memories. It’s amazing how memories stay with you, even when you think they’ve faded away. I think it’s what keeps us connected to who we were, even as we grow older.

Hey, I was just thinking—do you ever get that weird feeling when you're about to open a Christmas box and you're like, "I wonder what's inside?"      Oh, totally. I mean, I’ve got that  exact  same feeling every time. I think it’s the way the decorations are piled up and the smell of cinnamon and ginger in the air. It’s like a countdown. Oh, you mean the ones that taste like Christmas? I’ve got a bag of them in the fridge. Wait, I think I saw your sister take some earlier.      Yeah, she was being extra festive. She even put one in my coffee. I didn’t know what it was, and then I had to explain it to my roommate. He thought I was trying to poison him.      You’re lucky he didn’t throw the coffee out.      What’s going on here? You two are talking about candy like it’s a conspiracy.      Oh, don’t worry, we’re just trying to survive the Christmas season.      Oh, I get it. I’ve been baking all morning. I had a customer come in who said she wanted a gingerbread house and a ‘sleigh’ cookie. I thought she was joking, but I made both.      That sounds amazing. You’re going to be doing all the holiday baking this year, right?      Maybe. I do have a lot of flour and sugar. I’ll even make sure the café is open for a little Christmas party.      Deal. I’ll bring the candy. You know, the kind that tastes like Christmas.      I’ll bring the decorations. Let’s be honest, the only thing that makes this house feel like Christmas is the mess.      Right. Let’s get this dinner going and then we’ll talk about how to make this place look like a holiday wonderland.      Sounds like a strategy.

I can't believe it's Alumni Day again. It’s always such a great chance to catch up with old colleagues and see what everyone's been up to. I run a café, and I’ve seen so many young people come in who are talented but don’t feel like they’ve got the right opportunities. I often tell them that if they’re passionate about something, they should chase it — no matter what labels people try to put on them.      Exactly. I’ve got this idea for a documentary about young people and their struggle with class and education – it’s been on my mind for a while. I was thinking of making it a viral video, like that chef one. Maybe something that could go big online.      That sounds like a cool project. I’m a film producer, so if you need help with the production side, just let me know. I think stories like that — especially ones that challenge stereotypes — are really important. Especially in a country where class is such a big factor in people’s lives.      Wait, you’re into that kind of thing? I mean, I’ve got my own little business, but I’ve always felt like education was the key to breaking the cycle. Well, I've just made some proper Sunday roast, and I thought we’d all take a break and have a chat. It's been a while since we've properly sat down together like this. Mate, I swear I just saw your brother knocking over the entire tower of soft toys again. What's the deal with him and those things? So, I was just telling my wife about the time I tried to cook Christmas dinner and ended up burning the turkey. She said I should’ve just given it to the cat. I was trying to get my car serviced, and the mechanic said, “You need to come back in two weeks.” I said, “But I only have one week.” He looked at me and said, “Well, that’s just how it is.” I said, “Tell me about it.”      You know, I’ve been thinking about my boyfriend.

Okay, I’ve got this for your birthday. I couldn’t decide what to get you, so I just bought this whole set of cookbooks. You know, since you always talk about trying new recipes.      Oh, that’s very thoughtful. But I thought you were going to get me a proper gift, not a library of food books! I mean, I already have more cookbooks than a restaurant.      You know what? You’re getting the most useful gift ever! I mean, if you start using the books, you can finally make that lasagna you’ve been talking about for years. You’re not trying to be the next Gordon Ramsay, are you? You’ll probably burn the kitchen down.      I would never burn the kitchen down. I’m a professional chef in my own right—just not in the kitchen. Or at least, not when I’m trying to make something simple.      Right, and the next thing you know, you’ll be cooking for the whole neighborhood. You’ll be the king of the block, and we’ll all be your loyal subjects.      Yeah, and then we’ll all be eating your food, and it’ll be the best thing since sliced bread. I could already taste it.      Okay, okay, I’ll take that as a compliment. So, what about your plans for the weekend? Any exciting things coming up?      Actually, I was thinking of going to that art gallery in the city. There’s a new exhibit from a local artist. I’ve heard it’s really good.      That sounds perfect! I’ve been meaning to check it out. Maybe we can all go together? You know, like a little group trip.      That’s a great idea. I’ll check the dates and let you know. But I’m telling you, if I have to cook anything, I’m bringing my laptop and a stack of takeaway menus. No pressure on me.      Deal.

I've been thinking a lot lately about how things used to be. Back when we had the heating working, and the lights and the power—everything just ran like clockwork. Now, it's like living in a village with no electricity. You can’t even boil a kettle without a generator. Oh, I know what you mean. It’s been so long since we had the power on. I remember the last time we had a party, the lights flickered, and we had to turn on all the candles. It was like we were in the 19th century again, but with modern-day furniture. That sounds like a characterful party. I'd love to have one like that. You know, the kind where you have to rely on the atmosphere and the company, not the gadgets. I’d say that’s the real sign of a good party, isn’t it? No power, no frills—just good company. Although, I suppose if you're lucky, the heating might still work, even if the lights don’t. That would be something. Yeah, and the church is still warm, I reckon. Even without the power, the warmth of the people and the place is there. It’s not the same as having a central heating system, but it’s a different kind of comfort. I remember when we used to go shopping together. It was a real thing—making a list, going to the market, and coming back with all sorts of things. Now, everything’s just delivered. You don’t even have to go out. That is a different world. I still go to the shops, but I like the feeling of being out and about. I think it helps the mind. But I can see how it might be hard for some people, especially if you don’t have the energy to go out. Energy is a big thing these days. I tell you, I used to work hard and have energy to spare. Now, it's all about rest and taking it easy. I’ve got a dog who keeps me moving, and that’s enough for me. That’s the thing with dogs—they're such a good companion. Still, I think I’d prefer a good book and a cup of tea rather than being out in the cold. But then again, I'm not sure I’d enjoy being out in the cold anyway.

I just watched this film last night, and I still can’t get it out of my head. It was  The Last of Us , right? I mean, it was so intense, wasn’t it? Oh, I saw it! I thought it was really well shot. But I couldn’t help but think about my cousin, who tried to watch it on a plane. He got so scared he had to turn it off halfway through. Oh no, really? You know, I was thinking about family the other day—my mum’s always talking about how we used to watch movies together when I was a kid. I haven’t been back to Doncaster in ages, but I was thinking about going home for Christmas. My sister’s got a new baby, and I’d love to see her. It’s been too long. That sounds amazing. Yeah, I can see that. You know, I’m planning on going to a film festival in Edinburgh next month. It’s a networking event for my job, but I’m hoping to meet some people in the industry. It’s a bit of a step up from just coordinating conferences. That sounds exciting. I might have to do something like that.

So, I was reading about the Scottish independence referendum, and it's only a few weeks away now. I think it’s a big deal, don’t you? Yeah, I heard about it. I think it's going to be a big decision for Scotland. I mean, I don’t know much about it, but I guess it’s about whether they want to be independent from the UK. Exactly. And I’ve been reading a lot about it. Some people say it’s about freedom and control over their own resources, while others think it’s a risky move. It really does depend on what you value more—national identity or economic stability. My teacher mentioned it in class last week. She said a lot of people in Scotland are in favor, especially the older generation. But I don’t know if the young people are as passionate about it. I mean, I’m just a student, so I guess I don’t have much of an opinion yet. That’s true. I remember when I was your age, the only thing I cared about was exams. But now, even as an examiner, I find myself thinking about things like this. It’s funny how the world changes, isn’t it? Yeah, it’s weird. I mean, I know my family is from York, and I’ve never thought much about Scotland. But I’ve heard some stories from my cousins who live there. They say the people there are really proud of their culture and history. I can see that. I’ve been to some of the Scottish countryside and it’s beautiful. The landscapes are different from Yorkshire, but it’s about the same in terms of the people. I think the real question is, do they want to be separate from the UK? Not just politically, but economically and socially as well. I guess that’s the thing. It’s not just about the country itself, but how the country is run. I think it’s a bit of a gamble, especially with the economy. If you leave the UK, you have to negotiate your own trade deals and all that. That’s the big fear, isn’t it? Some people are worried that the UK is too powerful and Scotland would be at a disadvantage. Others think they can manage on their own. It’s really a complicated issue.

You lot are still arguing about accents, aren’t you? I swear, it’s like we’re in a reality show. Yeah, and we’re all pretending we’re not from the same country. You think you’re so posh with that Liverpool lilt, but I’ve heard more posh than that in a tea shop in Doncaster. Oh, come on! I’m from Derby, not some fancy London borough. You think you’re the only one who sounds like a fish out of water? I’ve heard you lot talk like you’ve been to school in the Alps. Yeah, like that’s a good thing. I’m from Wakefield, and I’ve been told I sound like a Darcy from  Pride and Prejudice —only with a bit more swearing. That’s not swearing, that’s just being Yorkshire. We don’t have a word for “no,” we have “nay.” And that’s not swearing, that’s a dialect! Oh, so you’re saying you’re not swearing, you’re just… dialecting? I call it swearing, and I call it national pride. You know what I’m trying to say, though—Jeremy Kyle is the only one who can make us all stop arguing and just laugh at ourselves. Honestly, I think he’s the only TV show that can make me laugh at my own accent. I mean, you know the way he says “elided” and “sounded like” when he’s talking about people? It’s like he’s trying to play the part of the posh commentator, but he’s just doing it so badly. And we’re all just hanging on his every word like it’s the most interesting thing ever. I swear, if I could get a job on that show, I’d be talking about elision for hours. Yeah, but I think we’re all just here because we can’t stand the thought of being in the same room without arguing about accents. I mean, if we started talking about actual news, we’d probably all be arguing about something else. Exactly. It’s the only thing that keeps us from getting bored. Although I do have to say, I’ve never been more proud of my accent than I am right now. It’s like we’re all part of some weird, accidental dialect club. Yeah, and we’re all stuck in Chester, pretending we’re from somewhere else.

I can’t believe the Euros are already underway. I’ve been waiting for this all summer. Did you know they’re using the same stadiums as the Euros 2020? It’s like time is going in circles. Yeah, it’s kind of surreal. I mean, it was supposed to be in 2020, then they moved it to 2021, and now it’s 2024. I guess this is the best we can hope for. But hey, at least the atmosphere is electric. I watched the opening match online when I was in Birmingham. You should’ve seen the fans—it was like a festival. I know, right? I can’t wait to see our team play. I’ve been knitting a scarf for the Euros. I’m using the same pattern my mum used for my brother’s first scarf. It’s a bit of a tradition now. Wait, did you know she’s actually been knitting for the Olympics too? No, really? That’s interesting. I’ve been thinking about baby names lately. I remember when the London Olympics happened, there was a boom in names like Ellie and Zachary. Now I think there’s a new wave with names like Selena and Liam. Though I’m not sure if that’s just in the UK or if it’s a global thing. I think it’s a mix. I’ve been trying to come up with a name that’s both strong and unique. I’ve been thinking about names like Elise or Ethan. But I still haven’t decided. I guess it’s going to be a tough call. Yeah, it really is. But I think it’s one of those things you just have to go with your gut.

So, I just watched  The Bee Movie  again with the kids, and it made me think—what if the Queen of England was a bee? But I was thinking—do you know how much you actually pay to get into the Royal palaces, like Buckingham Palace? I mean, is it free or do you have to pay?      I think it’s free, but I’m not sure. I remember seeing a sign that said something like “Entry is free, but donations are welcome.” But I’ve never been inside, so I’m not sure.      Wait, isn’t there a museum or something?      Yes, there are some museums, but the actual palace is closed to the public most of the time. I think only certain parts are open for visits, like the State Rooms. Oh, and I remember reading that even if you pay, you can’t just walk in—you have to book a tour in advance.      That’s so fancy. I would love to visit one of those places. But I guess the problem is, how do you even get a tour? Do you need to be a member or something?      I think you just apply for a tour online. Though I wonder what it would be like to live there.      I wish I could be a Queen! Then I’d have a palace, lots of servants, and I could wear all those pretty clothes.      Or maybe you’d be a politician instead. You know, someone who can make laws and help people. But I think both jobs are complicated. The Queen has to be perfect, and politicians have to fight all the time.
