I'll talk to the manager and let you know more details next week. I think it could be a good opportunity for you. And if you're going to be busy, maybe we could catch up more often. I miss our chats. That sounds perfect. We should definitely make time. I’ve missed our conversations, especially since the break-up with Tom. It’s been hard to be so focused on work and not have someone to talk to. I know. I think it's important to keep those connections. You're not just a colleague—you're a friend.

Okay, so I was reading this old legend the other day about the Green Man, and it got me thinking—what do you two think about the idea that good and evil are more like two sides of the same coin?      Hmm, what’s a Green Man again? I’ve heard of the Green Man, but I’m not sure what it is exactly.      I think it’s like a mythical creature, right? Maybe a forest spirit or something?      Exactly! It’s a figure from old English folklore, often depicted as a man with a green face and leafy hair. Some people believe he represents nature, while others think he’s a symbol of evil or misfortune. It’s kind of like how some legends mix both good and bad elements.      So, is it like the same as the idea of a trickster? Like how some stories have characters that are both clever and dangerous?      Yeah, like the Devil? I mean, he’s not always evil, he’s just misunderstood, right?      That’s a good point. I think a lot of these legends are meant to teach lessons, not just scare people. The Green Man, for example, might have been a way to remind people to respect nature or to be cautious in the woods.      But what if the Green Man was actually a good spirit? Like, he helps people in secret?      Or maybe he’s just a part of the world, like the weather or the seasons. Some people think the Green Man is a guardian of the forest, and others think he’s a harbinger of doom. It’s all about how you see it, isn’t it?      Exactly. And that’s part of what makes these stories so fascinating. They’re not just about right and wrong, they’re about the complexity of the world. Sometimes the lines between good and evil blur, and it’s up to us to decide what we believe.      So, are you saying that there’s no real evil, just misunderstanding?      Maybe. Or maybe it’s more like there are different sides to everything. Like, a tree can be both beautiful and dangerous if it falls on your house.      That’s a perfect analogy. Stories like these remind us that life isn’t always black and white. It’s about understanding, empathy, and the roles we play in the world, whether we like it or not.

So, did you see the photos from the school filming trip? I swear, the kids were so into it. I mean, they were running around like they were in a movie, and the teacher had to chase them down just to get them to stop and sit for the camera.      Oh, I saw them. I think one of the kids even got his leg hurt during the filming. I heard he was limping all the way back from the school bus. You’d think they’d have a bit more caution with kids running around with cameras and stuff.      Yeah, I saw the message from the teacher. She said he was okay, just a bit of a bruise on his shin. My son, ANON, was asking about it all week. He said, “Dad, what if I fall and break my leg?” I told him, “It’s just a bump. You’re not a runner, you’re a thinker.”      Wait, Dad, I thought I saw you at the gym the other day. Did you go on the running machines?      Yeah, I did. I thought I’d try to get back into shape. You know, after the kids and all. I tried the treadmill, then the stationary bike. It’s actually not as bad as I thought, and I even had a doughnut while I was there. It was a good session.      Doughnut while you were working out? You’re not serious.      Oh, I am. I had a chocolate-glazed one from the vending machine. I told myself it was a reward for finishing the session. But honestly, it was about as healthy as the candy bar I had the day before.      Dad, can I have a doughnut too? I saw you eating one.      Only if you promise to eat your vegetables. And by the way, have you been keeping up with your homework? Your teacher said you fell asleep during history class.      I was just trying to figure out what the Romans ate. I thought I could memorize it by eating a doughnut. It didn’t work.      Well, if you want to get your head straight, maybe you should go to the gym with your dad. It’s not just about the doughnuts.      She’s got a point. I’ve been telling ANON we should go together. It’ll be like a family day out. And if we get hungry, we can always grab a doughnut or two.

I've been meaning to ask you, how are you holding up with everything going on? You know, with the health scare and all. Honestly, it's been a bit of a rollercoaster. I've been feeling quite run down lately, and I've picked up some bad habits. I guess being a small business owner, especially with the cost-of-living crisis, it's easy to push yourself too hard. I know what you mean. I've been trying to keep things in check as well. I've even taken up gardening as a way to unwind, but honestly, I'm not sure if it's helping much. That’s a good idea, actually. You know, I've been thinking about joining the Green Party. I think their policies on sustainability and community support are right on track. But I'm not sure if I should make the switch just yet. That's brave of you. I've been meaning to get involved in local politics more, but I always find an excuse not to. I mean, I'm not exactly a political person, but I do believe in environmental issues. I think it's about time we all took a more active role, especially with the state of the country. I've been reading a lot about the boot sales in the area. Have you heard about them? Oh yes, I remember when we used to go to those in the old days. It's sad to see them disappear. I think the community feels a bit disconnected now. But I do miss the camaraderie. Exactly. I had a friend who used to run one and it was a great social event. We'd meet people, swap stories, and even find some decent deals. I hope they come back with a new format. That would be great. Speaking of which, have you heard any news about your daughter getting a job lately? Not really. She's been looking for something stable, but it's tough out there. I've been advising her to take a job with a small business, you know, to get her feet wet. But I'm not sure if she's listening. I can see that. It's a tough time for everyone. But I think it's important to keep your head up and keep moving forward. Yeah, I guess that's the thing.

So, do you remember that time we tried growing those plants in the garden? I think it was the string of spider plants we bought from the market. I swear, after a month, they were taller than me. Oh, I remember! I was so proud of you. You were like a real gardener, talking about soil pH and all that. But then we had that weird thing with the slug. You tried to make a slug trap with a bottle and a bit of peanut butter, right? Yeah! And it was like the slugs had a secret meeting or something. They just ignored it. I was so disappointed. I thought I was gonna be the next gardening genius. You were. You still are. I mean, look at your fashion sense. You always know what to wear, even when it's just hanging out in a pub. It's like you’ve got this secret style guide. Oh, you know me. I like to look presentable. Besides, we’re in Cambridge, not Sunderland. I mean, I still wear that pasty I bought from the market last week, but at least I don’t look like a student from the East Midlands. You’ve got a point. I tried one last week, and it was so good. My roommate said it was the best thing since sliced bread. You know, I’ve been thinking about politics lately. It’s all over the news, and I can’t help but compare it to the old days. I mean, Trump—what was his deal again? It felt like we were living in a different country. I know. It’s like watching a soap opera. I can’t even watch the news without feeling like I’m in a story. And the finance stuff? It’s all so complicated. I thought I was doing okay with my savings, but then I realized I was investing in something called ‘cryptocurrency.’ I still don’t know what it is. I know. It’s like trying to understand the economy while someone is shouting about Trump. I’m a PhD student, and I can’t even keep up with the political climate. I keep thinking, what’s the point? We’re all just trying to get through the day. Yeah, I get it. But life goes on. And even though I might not be a financial whiz, I know how to pick a good pasty.

I can’t believe we’re still here, just sitting in the kitchen of ANON’s parents’ house, like it’s the most normal thing in the world. It’s been ages since we've had a proper catch-up, haven’t we? Yeah, it's been too long. I’ve been thinking about how we used to spend every weekend together, just talking and drinking wine like it was going out of style. Remember when we used to argue about the best way to teach postgrad students? Oh, don’t even start. I still remember that time when I told the class that art wasn’t just about technique—it was about  feeling . And you were the one who argued that art was about structure and form. We ended up in a full-blown debate, and the students were just watching like it was a reality TV show. You had a point, though. I mean, we’re both lecturers, and we both believe in education, but we just approach it differently. I remember that one time when I brought a few killer whales to class, or at least I tried to. I got a video of them from the BBC, and we ended up discussing their intelligence and how they live in pods. You were fascinated. I was! I think I got so caught up in it that I forgot about the lecture. I mean, who doesn’t want to learn about killer whales? Especially when you can’t find a killer whale in Norwich. Still, the students loved it. They said it made the lecture more engaging. It did. I think we both have that ability to make things interesting, even if it comes through in different ways. Speaking of which, have you seen the latest episode of  Blue Peter ? I watched it the other night, and there was a segment about squatters and their rights. Yeah, I remember. It was quite controversial, but I thought it was interesting. I mean, squatting is a real issue in cities like London, where people are priced out of their own homes. I wonder what ANON thinks about it. I think they’re more interested in the blue Peter badges. They tried to get one last year, but they lost the competition. Oh, come on! I bet they were just trying to get a badge for the sake of it. Still, I’m glad we’re back on track.

Well, I was just thinkin’ about the hostels again, you know. We had some trouble with the one in Bury last week. I don’t know how we’re supposed to manage them with all the problems we’ve got these days. Yes, I heard about that. I think it was the lack of staff, wasn’t it? They don’t seem to be able to keep up with the number of people needing help. It’s sad to see, really. I just hope they can find a solution before it gets worse. It’s a real mess, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve been in education for years and I’ve seen a lot of changes, but this is something else. I think the government needs to step in more, but I don’t know if they’re even listening. I couldn’t agree more. I remember when I was in my youth, we didn’t have these issues, you know? People had a sense of community, and now it’s all about bureaucracy and targets. Oh, I know. I used to be a childminder, and I’d say we had more accountability then. Now it’s like everyone’s too busy to care. But I guess that’s the price of living in a modern society. Speaking of society, have you seen the photos of the old school in Birmingham? I found them online the other day. They were a bit grainy, but it reminded me of my childhood. I used to walk to school every day, and I still remember the sound of the bell ringing. Oh, I still remember that too. I used to go to a school in Costessey. It wasn’t much, but we had a great bunch of kids. I wonder if any of them are still around. I bet a few are. I know some of my old friends from Harrow still live in the area. They had that big school with the tower, didn’t they? I think it was closed down years ago. Yes, that’s the one. I go there sometimes on my way to work. I wonder if anyone has ever thought about turning it into a community center. It could be useful, especially for the older people in the area. That’d be a good idea. I’m not sure I’d want to go back to school, but maybe I could help out with some of the activities.

I've been meaning to ask you about your time in recruitment. I heard you worked in that field before becoming an associate lecturer. Was it a big change? Oh, it was quite a shift! I loved the fast-paced environment and the variety of people I met. But honestly, it was a lot more stressful than teaching. I used to be responsible for hiring over 50 people a month, and I had to constantly evaluate their academic and professional backgrounds. That does sound intense. I know you mentioned you were involved in academic literacy assessments for a course. How did that compare to your work in recruitment? It was different in a lot of ways. In recruitment, I was more focused on matching candidates to roles, whereas in academic literacy, the goal is to assess how well students can engage with complex texts and arguments. I think it's important for lecturers to be able to identify gaps in students' critical thinking skills. Definitely. I've noticed that some students struggle with academic writing, especially when it comes to structuring arguments and citing sources properly. It's a skill that can take a while to develop. Exactly. One of the things I found interesting was how some lecturers might not have a strong background in academic literacy themselves. It can create a gap in how they approach teaching writing and critical analysis. That’s a good point. I think it's important for lecturers to not only have subject expertise but also the ability to assess and teach academic skills. It helps students become more independent learners. I agree. I remember one time when I was evaluating a course, and I noticed that the lecturer didn't provide clear guidelines on how to approach a specific type of essay. That made the students quite confused. It's surprising how much can be missed in the curriculum. I think more attention should be given to developing students' academic literacy, especially for those who might not come from traditional educational backgrounds. Absolutely. It's a balance between teaching content and teaching how to think critically about that content. I hope we can continue pushing for better academic literacy programs across the board. I think that's the key—encouraging a culture where academic literacy is seen as an essential skill, not just an afterthought. It benefits both students and lecturers in the long run.

So, I just wanted to say, I think I saw you earlier in the library, walking around with that big book. You looked like you were studying for something intense.      Oh, that was me. Yeah, I can relate. I’m also from England. I was born in Bolton, which is in Greater Manchester. So, I guess we’re all from the North, in a way.      Kind of, yeah. I need to get better at managing my time.      I know the feeling. I’m also juggling a lot right now. But I try to take breaks and enjoy the library’s atmosphere. It’s like a calm place. I still can't believe I got dragged into that military simulation game last night. It was like being in a war zone, complete with fog and explosions. I swear, I nearly got my phone destroyed. You're not the only one. I was in the middle of a conference call when the screen started shaking and the tank rolled onto my desk. I had to grab a pillow to stop myself from screaming. Oh no, did you get a medal for that? I got one for survival. Just barely. I told my friends I’d rather be in a real war than a virtual one, and they said I was being dramatic. But I’m telling you, the sound effects were real enough to make me jump out of my skin. I know the feeling. But then again, it’s not like we’re actually in the military. Although I did read this article about the Royal Air Force being restructured. It's weird, you know? I mean, I grew up in London, and I never thought I'd be interested in the military, but the article was fascinating. Like, did you know they’re using AI to train pilots now? Yeah, I saw that. It's insane how much technology is evolving. I mean, I work in events, so I’m used to seeing the latest trends, but that’s next-level. I still don’t get why they wouldn’t just use someone who knows how to fly a plane. But maybe it’s safer? Maybe. But then again, the military is always pushing the boundaries. I think it’s because they have to. I mean, if you’re trying to keep up with the rest of the world, you can’t afford to fall behind. Maybe. But I still think I’d rather be playing Call of Duty than flying a fighter jet. Although, maybe I should try it. You know, just to see what it's like. You ever think about joining the army? No way. I’d probably end up in the kitchen with a grenade launcher. I’d be too clumsy for that. Yeah, I think you'd be more suited to something like a magazine editor. Wait, do you read any magazines? I’m trying to catch up on some feminist publications. It’s been a while since I’ve read one. Oh, I’ve got a few.

So, do you think we should go to London for the weekend? I’ve been dying to see that new art gallery in the East End. It’s supposed to be amazing. Yeah, but I heard it’s full of posh Londoners and their fancy cars. You know how it is. They’re all like,  “Oh, we’re so much better than you.”  It’s not even a real place, it’s just another one of those trendy spots. Honestly, I think it’s just a case of people from the city being arrogant. But if we go, we can show them we’re not just some rural bumpkins. I mean, we’re not even from the same part of England, for crying out loud. I’m from Winchester, and you’re from Wirlpoole. You two are like,  “We’re the real England.”  Oh, come on, we all know that’s just a stereotype. You know, like how people from London think we’re all just working-class louts. I mean, I’m an architect, and I went to postgrad school. That’s not exactly the working class. Yeah, but I’m a film-maker, and I went to grad school too. We’re both in the same bracket. And yet, somehow, we’re still considered the ‘other’ just because we’re not from London. It’s ridiculous. You know what I hate the most? When people say,  “Oh, you’re not London-born, so you can’t really understand the city.”  It’s so full of racism, even if it’s not overt. They think we’re all just outsiders, even if we’ve been living here for years. I get that. I’ve had people tell me I don’t ‘sound’ like a Londoner, even though I’m from Watford. It’s like they think you have to be born in the city to be considered part of it. It’s so frustrating. And then there are the people from London who think we’re all just trying to  “fit in.”  Like, we’re not trying to act like them, we’re just trying to exist without being judged for where we’re from. Exactly. I think it’s time we stopped trying to prove ourselves. We’re not Londoners, but that doesn’t mean we’re not part of England. We all have our own stories, our own lives, and we’re not going to let those stereotypes define us.
